paragraphs.text: BOOK ONE.

I did not know when my writings could reach you, Cresconius, but I never gave up hope that they would. After all, yours were able to reach me in the end, though long after you wrote them. You thought you ought to write them against the brief, partial answer I had made, as best I could, to Petilian, your bishop of Cirta. He was trying to establish the repetition of baptism, and he attacked our communion not with weighty evidence but with frivolous abuse. Only a small first part of his letter had come into my hands at that time, not the whole. Why that happened there is no need to ask, since when the whole of it later reached us I was glad to answer the whole. If I did not reply to this letter you have addressed to me, you might perhaps take it as an insult; but by replying I fear in turn that you may think me contentious. You came upon writings of mine that were not addressed to you. Merely because they seemed to refute a bishop of the party of Donatus, or the party of Donatus itself, you judged it your duty to take up and publish a rebuttal, since you were conscious of having some ability and belong to that communion, though you are bound to the clergy by no office. How much less, then, was it permissible for me, given the burden of my charge, to keep silent against either Petilian or you yourself! He was attacking the Church in which I serve as a soldier, and you, in a similar work, were even composing, producing and writing a discourse addressed to me by name!

In the first parts of it you worked hard to make eloquence seem suspect to people. You seemed to praise my style of speaking, and then you seemed to fear that by this style I might persuade you or anyone else of falsehoods and so deceive them. On that basis you went on to accuse eloquence itself. You even brought testimony against it from the holy Scriptures, where you think it says, "From much eloquence you will not escape sin." But it does not say "from much eloquence"; it says "from much speaking." Much speaking is superfluous talk, a fault acquired through the love of talking. Very often the people who love to talk include those who do not know what they are saying or how to say it, whether in the soundness of their ideas or in the correct sound and order of words that is learned through the art of grammar. Eloquence, on the other hand, is the ability to speak in a way that fittingly sets forth what we think, and it should be used when we think rightly. Heretics have not used it in this way. Surely, if they had thought rightly, they would have had not only nothing bad but even something good to set forth eloquently. So it was pointless for you to accuse eloquence by bringing up those examples. A soldier should not be left unarmed for his country just because some have taken up arms against their country. Nor should good and learned physicians refrain from using medical instruments to heal just because the ignorant and the wicked misuse them to do harm. Medicine is useful or useless according to whether the things it seeks are useful or useless. In the same way, as everyone knows, eloquence, that is, skill and ability in speaking, is useful or useless according to whether the things said are useful or useless. I do not think you are unaware of this either.

I suppose, though, that you saw that some people consider me eloquent, and you thought eloquence ought to be accused in order to turn readers and listeners away from me. Anyone you had frightened would then stop paying attention to what I said, and would decide that I was to be guarded against and avoided precisely because I seemed to speak eloquently. Be careful, then, that what you have done does not belong to that evil art which, as you recalled in connection with Plato, some have rightly judged should be expelled from the city and from the society of the human race. That art is not eloquence (if only I had as much eloquence as I wish for setting forth what I think!). It is a sophistical and malicious profession that sets out to argue for everything and against everything, not from conviction but from rivalry or for gain. Of this the holy Scripture says, "He who speaks sophistically is hateful." It seems to me that the apostle Paul is restraining the young Timothy from this when he says, "Do not fight over words, for it does no good, but only ruins those who hear." And so that no one would think he had forbidden him the ability to speak rightly, he immediately added, "Do your best to present yourself to God as an approved workman who has no need to be ashamed, rightly handling the word of truth." No doubt, then, this disposition crept into your mind out of a zeal for contradicting. You declared us eloquent and found fault with eloquence, not because you really thought so, but in order to turn away from us the attention of anyone who wanted to learn. How could I believe you did this sincerely, when I know how you people regularly extol the eloquence of Donatus, Parmenian and others of yours? What could be more useful than that eloquence, if it poured forth in such an abundant stream for the peace of Christ, for unity, truth and charity? But why speak of others? You yourself have shown how insincerely, out of mere contentiousness, you found fault with eloquence. You tried to make the rest of what you wrote persuasive by means of eloquence, and you tried to accuse eloquence itself eloquently.

You say that you are not my equal in the art of speaking and are entirely uninstructed in the examples of the Christian law. What is the point of that, I ask you? Did I force you to write against my writings, so that these are the words of someone refusing and excusing himself? If you are entirely uninstructed, why do you not rather keep silent, or else speak in a way that shows you want to be instructed? You say that I am always pressing and challenging your people to debate with me in order to settle the question of the truth. Your people, you say, act more prudently and patiently: in church they teach the people only what is commanded in the law and do not bother to answer us. They know, you say, that if the divine law and so many proofs from the scriptures of the law cannot persuade us what is better and truer, no human authority could ever dispel our errors and call us back to the rule of truth. Why, then, did you think it right to speak against us when they keep silent? If they do well, why do you not imitate them? If they do badly, why do you praise them?

You say that with intolerable arrogance I believe I alone can settle what has seemed inexplicable to others and has therefore been left to God as judge. Yet a little earlier you said that after so many years, and after so many judges and arbiters, I want to settle what could not be settled before the emperors, when so many learned men among the bishops of both parties disputed it. Am I really the only one busying myself with this? Am I the only one who wants this question settled by debate? I think that if you had wanted to blame only our people for attempting it, you would not have admitted that your people too took part in that attempt. Since, at least on account of your own people, you can no longer find fault with that attempt, that wish and that persistence, I would not have you stand apart from so good a work. What is your charge? What are you criticizing? Or are you envious? That should not be rashly believed of you. The only explanation left, then, is that out of a zeal for contention you blame in me what you are compelled to praise even in your own people.

"But," you say, "to presume that what was not settled among so many men of such standing can be settled by oneself alone is intolerable arrogance." Please do not think this should be attributed to me alone. There are very many of us pressing for this to be settled, or rather for it to become known that it has already been settled. Those who said it was not settled are the ones who refused to accept the settlement. They concealed it from you, so that you too, deceived by their authority, believe it was not settled. But from the time it was settled, our people have never once stopped making that settlement known, in public and in private, in every way they could. They did so in order that no one who persists in a most destructive error could complain at the Last Judgment that God's ministers had been negligent toward him. We do not want to reopen from the beginning a case settled long ago. We want to show how it was settled, above all for the sake of those who do not know it. When the defenders of error are refuted, either they too may be corrected and set free, or at least, once they have been confuted and still remain openly obstinate, those who care more for truth than for contention may see what to follow.

Nor is this done without fruit, as you suppose. If you could see how far and wide that error had spread through Africa, and how little of it remains that has not yet been corrected and brought over into catholic peace, you would by no means consider the persistence of those who champion Christian peace and unity fruitless and empty. Even where the diligence spent on this remedy does no good, it is enough, for rendering our account to God, that we did not stop spending it. A malicious tempter who urges someone to sin will deservedly incur the deceiver's punishment even if he fails to persuade. In the same way, God forbid that a faithful preacher of righteousness should be cheated of the reward of his duty before God, even if people reject him. What is certain is done toward what is uncertain. By uncertain I mean not the reward of the one who acts, but the mind of the one who hears. We cannot be certain whether the person to whom the truth is preached will assent. But it is certain that the truth must be preached even to such people. It is also certain that a worthy reward awaits those who preach it faithfully, whether they are received or spurned, or even suffer some hardship in this life because of it. The Lord says in the Gospel, "When you enter, say: Peace to this house. If those who are there are worthy, your peace will rest upon them; if not, it will return to you." Did he make the disciples certain that the people they preached peace to would receive it? But he did make them certain that they should preach it without hesitation.

The apostle Paul too says, "The Lord's servant must not quarrel but be gentle toward all, teachable and patient, correcting with modesty those who think otherwise. God may perhaps grant them repentance so that they come to know the truth, and come to their senses and escape the snares of the devil, who has taken them captive to do his will." Notice that the man whom he did not want to quarrel he still wanted to correct with modesty those who think otherwise, so that God's servant would not take the ban on quarrelsomeness as an excuse for idleness. But many people find even correction given with modesty burdensome and annoying, either because they are indulging their own sins, or because they have no answer and still will not yield to the truth. So they call those who deal with them earnestly and do not neglect to refute their error quarrelsome and contentious. Falsehood is afraid of being exposed and refuted, and so it accuses the diligence of truth by the names of the very vices that truth condemns. Must we therefore give up this persistence? See how the same apostle binds Timothy, so that he would not grow idle in preaching because of people to whom the preaching of truth is unwelcome: "I charge you before God and Christ Jesus, who is to judge the living and the dead, and by his appearing and his kingdom: preach the word, press on in season and out of season, reprove, exhort and rebuke with all patience and teaching." Who that hears this, if he serves God faithfully and is not a deceitful workman, would stop being diligent and persistent? Who would dare to be idle under so solemn a charge? So do not let your fluency shout us down in this cause. With the help of the Lord our God we preach without reserve the usefulness, the devotion and the holiness of Christian unity. We preach it in season to the willing and out of season to those who resist. With all the strength we have, we show, both for the benefit of those we can reach and against those we can confront, that this question between us and the party of Donatus was settled long ago.

The name and the charge of contentious hostility belong to those who either use stubborn cunning to defend falsehood, or herald the truth out of envy and boasting. Let them recognize these in themselves. The apostle Paul described both kinds of contentious people. He described the first kind in Alexander, of whom he says, "Alexander the coppersmith did me great harm; the Lord will repay him according to his deeds. You too beware of him, for he strongly opposed our message." He described the second kind in those of whom he says, "Some indeed proclaim Christ out of envy and rivalry, not sincerely, thinking to stir up affliction for me in my chains." These people certainly proclaimed the very same thing as Paul, but not in the same spirit or with the same will. As he said, they did it not out of charity but out of envy and rivalry, wanting in their pride to excel in that very proclamation and to be ranked above the apostle Paul. He did not take this badly. He even rejoiced, because he saw them preaching what he wanted to become more widely known: "What then?" he says. "Only that in every way, whether in pretense or in truth, Christ is proclaimed." Their hearts were not true, since they acted not with a sincere intention but with jealous rivalry; yet they still proclaimed the truth, that is, Christ. You cannot judge what is inside our hearts. So consider only this: do we resist the truth, or do we want to refute those who resist the truth? If we urge the truth and refute error, then lovers of truth ought to rejoice, even if our own intention is not true and we are seeking worldly profit and human glory. On this occasion, too, the truth is proclaimed, as the apostle shows when he says, "And in this I will rejoice." But suppose we are engaged in the labor of this stewardship out of the devout care that charity inspires. God knows this best, and you yourself could also have known it, as far as human ability allows, if you had lived among us. In that case, I think our ministry can by no means be justly blamed if we contend with fervent spirit for the truth against any of its adversaries.

Suppose you people regard as contentious, hot-tempered and a stirrer-up of brawls anyone who has taken care to start a verbal dispute with someone, or to answer one. Then consider what you must think of the Lord Jesus Christ himself and of his servants the prophets and apostles. Did the Lord himself, the Son of God, speak about the truth only with his disciples or with the crowds who believed in him? Did he not also speak with enemies who tested him, disparaged him, questioned him, resisted him and reviled him? Was he unwilling to debate even with a single woman about the question of worship, against the opinion or heresy of the Samaritans? "But," you say, "he knew beforehand that she would believe." What then? How many times, and how much, did he speak to the faces of the Jews, the Pharisees and the Sadducees, who were not only never going to believe but were going to oppose and persecute him fiercely! Did he not, of his own accord, ask them whatever he wished whenever he wished, in order to refute them by their own answers? When they craftily asked him questions to test him, did he not answer without any ambiguity, so that they were refuted and fell silent? Yet we do not read that any of them was converted and followed him because he did this. He certainly knew, since he had foreknowledge, that nothing he said to them, about them or against them would help bring them to salvation. Perhaps, though, he was strengthening us by his example, since we cannot know in advance whether people will come to faith or remain faithless. When we speak to people who are excessively hard and perverse, without any fruit for their salvation, we must not lose heart and give up our persistence in preaching because we are weary of laboring in vain. And what of the devil himself? Not only God but not even human beings can doubt that he will never be converted to righteousness. Yet when he insidiously tempted the Son of God and set traps of questions taken from the holy Scriptures, the Son refuted him by answering from the holy Scriptures. Christ did not think it beneath him to hold a conversation with Satan about the divine oracles. What did he foresee in this, if not that what was of no benefit to the Jews and the devil would benefit the Gentiles who were going to believe?

We also read that prophets were sent to people so disobedient that God himself, who sent the prophets, foretold that those to whom he sent them would not obey their words. I pass over the fact that the prophetic spirit by which they saw the future would surely also have let them know that their words would be despised; yet they kept speaking those words with vehement persistence. The Lord says to the prophet Ezekiel very plainly, "Go, enter the house of Israel and speak my words to them. You are not being sent to a people of unknown language, but to the house of Israel, nor to many peoples speaking strange or difficult languages whose words you cannot understand. If I had sent you to such peoples, perhaps they would have listened to you. But the house of Israel will not listen to you, because they are unwilling to listen to me. For the whole house of Israel is restless and hard of heart. But I have made your face strong against their faces, and I will strengthen your struggle against their struggle." See, the servant of God is sent and ordered to speak to people who were not going to listen to him, and the very Lord who sent him and ordered him to speak foretold that they would not listen. Why, then, and to whose benefit, with what fruit or effect, is he sent into the struggle of preaching the truth against people who will fight back and not obey? Will anyone dare to say that God's holy prophets deserved the reproach you threw at me? You said, "If you know that the matter at issue cannot be settled by you, why do you take on labor in vain, why do you spend empty effort, why do you contend needlessly and fruitlessly? Is it not a great error to want what you cannot accomplish? The law warns: Do not seek what is too high for you, and do not search into what is too strong for you. And again: A hot-tempered man stirs up quarrels, and an angry man heaps up sin." You certainly would not say this to Ezekiel, who was sent with the word of God to bring a struggle to people who would not obey, who would think, speak and act against him. If you did say it, he might perhaps answer you as the apostles answered those same Jews: "Whom must we obey, God rather than men?" That is also what I myself would answer you.

At this point you may demand that I show where God has commanded me too to do what you forbid. Remember that the apostolic letters were written not only for those who heard them at the time they were written, but also for us; that is the very reason they are read in church. Note also what the apostle says: "Or do you want proof that Christ is speaking in me?" And recall what I mentioned a little earlier, which was spoken not by Paul but by Christ through him: "Preach the word, press on in season and out of season," and so on. Note also how, when he explained to Titus what a bishop ought to be, he said that a bishop must hold firmly to the trustworthy word as taught, "so that he may be able," he says, "both to exhort in sound teaching and to refute those who contradict it. For there are many who are insubordinate, empty talkers and deceivers of minds, especially those of the circumcision, who must be refuted." He does not say that only those of the circumcision are like this, but that they especially are. Yet by an unquestionable precept he established that a bishop must use sound teaching to refute and rebut empty talkers and deceivers of minds. So I recognize that this has been commanded to me too. I do it as far as my strength allows, and I persist steadily in this work, as far as he who commanded it helps me. Why do you stand in my way? Why do you shout me down, forbid me and find fault with me? Must I obey you or God?

Perhaps you think the proofs I have brought forward from the holy Scriptures should be understood in this way: that, as you praised your people for regularly doing, the people should be taught in church only what is commanded in the law. You may think that it is there that those who hold different views are to be corrected and refuted, so that each teacher, by debating and preaching, corrects only the error of his own people. But if he sets about doing anything of the kind with those who are outside, then he is to be considered hot-tempered, contentious or quarrelsome. For Ezekiel himself, you say, and the other prophets were sent with the words of God to their own people, that is, Israelites to Israelites.

To this too I reply. I have already mentioned above that the Lord Jesus himself, who gave himself as an example for his disciples to imitate, did not disdain to assert the truth and give answers from the law, not only to Jews but also to Pharisees, Sadducees and Samaritans, and to the devil himself, the prince of all deceits and errors. But you might think this was permitted to the Lord and not to his servants. So hear what we read in the Acts of the Apostles: "Now a certain Jew named Apollos, an Alexandrian by birth, came to Ephesus. He was mighty in the scriptures. He had been instructed in the way of the Lord, and, being fervent in spirit, he spoke and taught very accurately the things concerning Jesus, though he knew only the baptism of John. He also began to speak boldly in the synagogue. When Aquila and Priscilla heard him, they took him aside and explained the way of the Lord to him more accurately. And when he wanted to go to Achaia, the brothers encouraged him and wrote to the disciples to welcome him. When he arrived, he greatly helped those who had believed there, for he vigorously refuted the Jews in public, showing through the scriptures that [?] was the Christ." What do you say about him? What do you think? Would you people not perhaps accuse him of being a contentious, hot-tempered agitator and stirrer-up of brawls, if the great authority of the holy book did not hold you back?

Or is it that, because a Jew had believed in Christ, he was therefore bound to refute in public the Jews who resisted the Christian faith and denied that Jesus is the Christ, whereas we, because we were never of the party of Donatus, are therefore not bound to refute the party of Donatus when it resists Christian unity? Was the apostle Paul ever a worshipper of idols, or was he ever in the sect of the Epicureans or the Stoics? Yet he was neither ashamed nor reluctant to hold discourse with them on the question of the living and true God. Hear what is written about this in the same book: "While Paul was waiting for them at Athens, his spirit was provoked within him when he saw that the city was full of idols. So he disputed in the synagogue with the Jews and with the Gentiles and the worshippers, and in the marketplace every day with those who happened to be there. Some of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers conferred with him, and some said, 'What would this sower of words want to say?' Others said, 'He seems to be a proclaimer of foreign demons.'" See: the apostle Paul did not refuse to confer with the Stoics and Epicureans, sects that differed not only from him but from each other and were opposed to each other. He disputed with them not only outside the church but even outside the synagogue, and he was not frightened off by their abuse, nor did he cease preaching Christian truth as though to avoid quarrels and contention. For see what holy Scripture goes on to testify: "And they took hold of him," it says, "and brought him to the Areopagus, saying, 'May we know what these things are that you are saying? For you are bringing some strange things to our ears; we want to know, then, what these things mean.' Now the Athenians and the foreigners staying there had leisure for nothing else but telling or hearing something new. Then Paul, standing in the middle of the Areopagus, said, 'Men of Athens, I see that in every way you are very superstitious. For as I walked about and looked at your images, I found also an altar on which was written: To an unknown god. What therefore you worship without knowing, this I proclaim to you,'" and the rest, which would take too long to recount in full. What suffices, however, for the question we are now discussing is this: consider, I beg you, the apostle of Christ, a Hebrew of Hebrews, standing and speaking not in a synagogue of the Jews nor in a church of the Christians, but in the Areopagus of the Athenians, that is, among the most contentious and ungodly of the Greeks. For it was there that the most talkative sects of the philosophers arose. Some of these, like the very Stoics mentioned here, fight more over disagreements about words than about things, which the apostle forbade to Timothy, saying that it is useful for nothing but the ruin of the hearers. For, as you know, Tully says of them: "A controversy over a word has long tormented these Greeklings, who are more eager for contention than for truth." Yet our Paul undertook to address and correct these men. He was not frightened even by the name of the place, which echoes its derivation from Mars, whom they call the god of wars; there he fearlessly spoke words of peace to those who would believe; there, girded with spiritual arms, he stormed destructive errors; and, gentlest of men though he was, he did not fear the contentious, nor, though the simplest of men, did he fear the dialecticians.

For you know that dialectic flourished most of all among the Stoics, although even the Epicureans, who were not only unashamed of their ignorance of the liberal disciplines but actually delighted in it, boasted that they themselves above all held and taught certain rules of disputation by which anyone who used them would be least likely to be deceived. For what else is dialectic but skill in disputing? I thought this needed to be made clear because you also chose to reproach me with dialectic itself, as though it were not in keeping with Christian truth, and as though your teachers had therefore rightly judged that I, as a dialectician, ought rather to be shunned and guarded against than refuted and confuted. And though they did not persuade you of this—for you were not reluctant to dispute against us even in writing—you nevertheless accused me of dialectic, so as to deceive the unlearned and to praise those who had refused to meet me in disputation. But of course you do not use dialectic when you write against us! Why, then, have you thrown yourself into so great a danger as disputation if you do not know how to dispute? Or if you do know how, why do you, a dialectician, accuse dialectic, being thus either rash or ungrateful, so that either you do not restrain the lack of skill by which you are defeated, or you accuse the learning by which you are helped? I examine your discourse, the very one you wrote to me. I see you setting out some things fully and ornately, that is, eloquently, and arguing other things subtly and keenly, that is, dialectically. And yet you find fault with eloquence and dialectic. If they are harmful, why do you practise them? If they are not, why do you denounce them? But let us not be tormented by a controversy over a word as well. When the thing itself is understood, we need not trouble much about what people have chosen to call it. Accordingly, if the eloquent man is to be defined as one who speaks not only fully and ornately but also truthfully, and likewise if the dialectician is to be defined as one who argues not only subtly but also truthfully, then you are neither eloquent nor a dialectician—not because your diction is meagre and unadorned, nor because your argument is dull and clumsy, but because you misuse that very fluency and skill in defence of falsehood. If, however, a bad cause pleaded with fluency or with vigour can also rightly be called eloquence or dialectic, not only the truth, then you are both eloquent and a dialectician, since you say empty things fluently and argue false things acutely. But I will see to you later.

The Stoics were certainly dialecticians above all others. Why, then, did the apostle Paul not most carefully avoid them, so that they might not confer with him? And yet you praise your bishops because they refuse to hold discussion with us, as with dialecticians! Or if Paul too was a dialectician, and therefore was not afraid to have the Stoics confer with him, because he disputed not only acutely, as they did, but also truthfully, which they did not, then beware of ever reproaching anyone with dialectic as a crime, when you admit that the apostles used it. For when you reproach me with this, I do not think you are deceived through lack of skill, but are deceiving through cunning. Dialectic, of course, is a Greek name; if usage allowed, it would perhaps be called in Latin "disputatoria," just as the most learned men in both languages called grammar "litteratura" in Latin. For just as grammar is named from letters, since in Greek letters are called grammata, so dialectic received its name from disputation, since disputation is called dialogē or dialexis in Greek. And just as the ancients called a grammarian "litterator" in Latin, so one who is called a dialectician in Greek is far more commonly and acceptably called in Latin a disputant. I suppose you would not deny that the apostle was a disputant, even if you deny that he was a dialectician. So to condemn in a Greek word what you are forced to approve in a Latin one—what is that but to hold out a deception to the unlearned and to insult the learned? Or if you deny that the apostle was even a disputant, though he disputed so constantly and so excellently, then you know neither Greek nor Latin—or, what is more credible, you deceive with the Greek word those who do not know Greek, and with the Latin those who do not even know Latin. For what could be—I will not say more ignorant, since you are not ignorant of these things, but altogether more deceitful than, when you hear and read so many and so varied discourses of the apostle asserting truth and refuting falsehood, to deny that he was accustomed to dispute, when this cannot be done except by disputing?

But if you admit that he did this regularly, because his letters force you to admit it, and yet contend that these should be called not disputations but discourses or letters, why should I go on dealing with you in this way, so that those who know nothing of these matters may approve whichever of us they please and disapprove whichever they please? I teach this from the divine Scriptures themselves, to which you must yield; I bring forward their very words, the very names they give to things. You have, in this same testimony which I quoted from the Acts of the Apostles, this said of Paul himself: "So he disputed in the synagogue with the Jews and with the Gentiles and the worshippers, in the marketplace." You have in another place, though he was dealing with a Christian congregation and the brethren were gathered in church, this written: "A certain young man named Eutychus, sitting in the window, was overcome by a deep sleep as Paul was disputing." You have also in the book of Psalms: "May my disputation be pleasing to him." You have also in the prophet Isaiah: "Come, let us dispute, says the Lord." And read the many other places in the divine Scriptures where you find this word, and look at the Greek manuscripts at these same testimonies of the holy Scriptures, and you will see where dialectic got its name. Then you will not, out of foolish rashness, condemn what all the righteous do even with God—they to whom it was said, "Come, let us dispute, says the Lord"—instead of imitating it with wise devotion.

For one who disputes distinguishes by disputing what is true from what is false. Those who cannot do this and yet wish to appear dialecticians use treacherous questions to catch the assent of the unwary, so as to draw from their answers conclusions by which they may either laugh at them for being taken in by an obvious falsehood or persuade those so deceived of a hidden falsehood, which very often they themselves also take to be the truth. But the true disputant, that is, one who distinguishes truth from falsehood, first does this within himself, so that he may not be deceived by failing to distinguish rightly—which he cannot accomplish without divine help. Then, when he brings forth what he has worked out within himself to teach others, he first looks at what they already know for certain, so as to lead them from these to the things they did not know or were unwilling to believe. He shows that these follow from what they already held by knowledge or by faith, so that through those truths on which they see that they agree, they are compelled to accept other truths which they had denied. In this way, what was previously thought false is distinguished as true from what is false, when it is found to be consistent with the truth already held before.

If this true disputant does this at length and expansively, he does it eloquently, and then he is reckoned under another name and given greater honour, so that he is called an orator rather than a disputant—as in the passage that the apostle extends and expands so fully: "In all things," he says, "commending ourselves as ministers of God, in much patience, in tribulations, in distresses, in beatings, in prisons, in riots, in labours, in watchings, in fastings, in chastity, in knowledge, in long-suffering, in kindness, in the Holy Spirit, in love unfeigned, in the word of truth, in the power of God; with the weapons of righteousness on the right hand and on the left, through glory and dishonour, through ill repute and good repute; as deceivers and yet truthful, as unknown and yet well known, as dying and behold we live, as punished and yet not killed, as sorrowful yet always rejoicing, as poor yet making many rich, as having nothing and yet possessing all things." What could you easily find richer and more ornate, that is, more eloquent, than this apostolic style? But if he does it concisely and compactly, people have been accustomed to call him a disputant rather than an orator—as when the same apostle deals with the circumcision and uncircumcision of father Abraham, or with the distinction between law and grace, which some failed to understand, or rather slandered, accusing him of saying, "Let us do evil, that good may come." But whether one is an orator or a disputant, there is no oratory without disputation, since even in the breadth of eloquence truth is distinguished from falsehood; nor can there be disputation without oratory, since the very compactness of speech is certainly expressed in words and with the tongue, whether he uses continuous discourse or, by questioning the person he is dealing with, compels him to answer what is true and from this leads him to another truth that was being sought—which is where dialectic is said to reign supreme.

For when anyone is refuted by his own answers, then if he has answered badly he has no one to blame but himself, not the disputant; and if he has answered well, he is ashamed to go on resisting, no longer the disputant but himself. The Lord often dealt with the Jews in this way, refuting them when they had been caught and trapped by their own answers; but they had not heard you, nor learned from you how to hurl abuse, for they might perhaps have more gladly and more spitefully called him a dialectician than a Samaritan. Just think how twisted up and confounded they were when, wishing to catch him in his words, they took the initiative and asked him whether it was lawful to pay tribute to Caesar. They were laying a trap with a two-headed dilemma, so that he would be caught whichever he chose: if he answered that it was lawful, he would be guilty as an enemy of the people of God; but if he said it was not lawful, he would be punished as an enemy of Caesar. At this he asked to be shown a coin and asked whose image and inscription it bore. And when they answered, "Caesar's"—for the plain truth forced them to answer this—the Lord at once drew them along, bound and caught by their own answer, and said, "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's." I ask you: were they the dialecticians, who tried to win by deceiving through the trap of a question laid before him, or was he rather the dialectician, who, from the very thing they asked, drew out a true answer from them by the wisdom of his questioning, and compelled them themselves to confess that truth which they thought it would be dangerous for him to say?

If you say that they were dialecticians because they wanted to catch him in his words by questioning him deceitfully, slanderously, and maliciously—for that is how you want us too to appear—why did the Lord nevertheless answer them? Why did he give them a reasoned reply and lead them on to the confession of the truth? Why did he say to them, "Why do you test me, you hypocrites?" and not add "you dialecticians"? Why did he insist that a coin be shown to him, so that he might draw out his true judgment even from the mouths of deceivers, rather than saying, "Go away; I must not speak with you, because you put captious questions, because you want to deal with me dialectically"? He said nothing of the kind, nor did he set us such an example in dealing with captious questioners and cunning catchers at our words; rather, he set us the example of compelling them, even though they are enemies of the truth, to bear witness to the truth by watchful questioning and unanswerable reasoning. Let your people do this to us, if we are malicious and dialecticians. Or do they show that they are afraid that we might rather do this to them? But if you say that Christ was a dialectician, you will be praising dialectic, which you had cast up to me as a crime.

To avoid this, I see what you will perhaps say: that neither they nor he did anything dialectically in that conversation. If, then, neither those who converse captiously and treacherously in order to trap in words the people they are dealing with, nor those who refute such people by their own answers, are acting dialectically, tell us at last what dialectic is, and how much evil it contains, how much harm it does. Teach us how much it is to be shunned—you who slip its name spitefully before the ignorant; show its crime to those who ask. You do not want to admit that someone acts dialectically who, by questioning skilfully and rightly, leads people turned away from the truth to the truth through their own answers, lest you admit that Christ too acted dialectically with the Jews. Likewise, you do not want to say that those act dialectically who lay traps with captious questions and try to deceive the one answering, lest it be shown to you that this is how the Jews dealt with Christ—whom he nevertheless did not avoid by keeping silent, but rather overcame by speaking—and so you be forced to admit that your bishops, whom you regard as learned and wise, are wrong to refuse to hold discussion even with dialecticians in order to teach them the unconquerable truth. I see what great agonies you suffer over how to define a dialectician so that he is neither a skilled disputant, lest you be forced to praise what you have censured, nor a treacherous catcher at words, lest it be said to you, "As Christ dealt with such men, so let a Christian deal with this one." So, if you would like to be free of this worry, define a dialectician as one with whom the lawyers of the party of Donatus refuse to hold a conference. For what else is there to suggest to you, a man who reproaches us with dialectic and therefore praises his bishops for refusing to hold discussion with us?

But perhaps you can find something to say about the Jews: that, however cleverly and craftily they laid the snares of their questions, they were not dialecticians. About the Stoics, certainly, nothing of the sort can be said, for they were not only dialecticians but surpassed the other schools of philosophers in this art or skill. For, as you recall along with me, that Chrysippus was a Stoic of whom the Academic Carneades held the opinion that whenever he had to dispute with him, he thought his mind needed to be purged with hellebore, whereas he could easily defeat the rest even after lunch. So if the books of the Stoics have taught us to dispute dialectically, let your bishops bring forward the teaching of Paul against us. But let them allow us to confer with them, just as he did not repel the Stoics themselves in his day.

For this art which they call dialectic, which teaches nothing other than how to demonstrate consequences—whether true from true or false from false—Christian teaching never fears, just as the apostle did not fear it in the Stoics, whom he did not refuse when they wished to confer with him. For dialectic itself admits, and it is true, that no one is driven by a disputant to a false conclusion as a consequence unless he has first agreed to false premises, from which that conclusion follows whether he likes it or not. And therefore whoever takes care, when speaking, not to be followed by false consequences that he does not want should willingly beware of the false premises that come before them. But if he has held fast to true premises, then whatever consequences he perceives, which he thought false or about which he was in doubt, let him embrace them once he has been shown them, if he is a greater friend to the most peaceable truth than to the most contentious vanity.

I would have accomplished little unless I demonstrate what I am saying in this very conversation of ours that is going on between us. Look: in this very question about baptism, you raised the matter by asking me where it is fitting for you to be baptized, whether with us or in the party of Donatus. And since your aim is that a person ought rather to be baptized in the party of Donatus, you tried to prove this aim from the fact that we too do not deny that baptism exists there. You surely see that what you wanted to do was to draw us from what we concede to what we did not concede—that is, that because we concede that baptism exists there, we should be compelled to concede also that one ought to be baptized there.

Consider carefully whether this follows, and answer yourself. For I think that now that this has been set before your eyes, you see, with your lively intelligence, how you are inferring things that do not follow as though they followed. For we do indeed say that baptism exists there too, but we do not say that it is beneficial there; on the contrary, we say that it is even harmful. When it is asked where anyone ought to be baptized, I believe the question is asked because of what the Lord said: "Unless one is born again of water and the Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven." Since, then, baptism is to be received for the sake of this benefit, when it is asked where it is to be received, the question is not where it exists, but where it is beneficial for attaining the kingdom of heaven. It would follow that it should be received wherever it is agreed to exist, if it were shown that all who have something good have it also for their own good. But since so many people have so many good things to their own harm, who does not see that when it is asked where something should be received, the question is not where it exists, but where it does good? For just as, if you granted me that gold is good, and granted also that robbers too have gold, you would not, I imagine, want me to conclude from these two concessions that whoever wishes to have gold ought to be in the company of robbers, so, when I grant that baptism is good, and grant also that the Donatists too have baptism, you ought not to conclude from these two concessions, as though it followed, that whoever wishes to have baptism ought to be in the communion of the Donatists.

From this, I do not doubt, many things will now occur to you yourself which, although they are good and instituted for some useful purpose, are nevertheless not useful to all who have them, but only to those who use them well. For when healthy eyes and injured eyes are flooded with the same light, it is a help to the one and a torment to the other; the same food nourishes some constitutions and harms others; the same medicine cures some and weakens others; the same armour protects some and hinders others; the same garment is a covering to some and an entanglement to others. So too baptism avails for some unto the kingdom, for others unto judgment.

Here I see what may trouble you. Perhaps you will say that in all these examples I have mentioned nothing that is a sacrament, whereas baptism is a holy sacrament. So, you will say, it does not follow that because I could show of gold, light, food, arms and clothing that they suit some who have them and not others, though they are good and established for some useful purpose, baptism must also help some who have it and harm others. It remains, then, to ask whether even those good things which belong to the law of God do not all benefit everyone who has them. With this question set out, our claim is that not even these all benefit everyone who has them. See how we prove this claim from your own admissions. You grant that the apostle Paul is to be believed in everything — I hold that as one premise. You also grant that this same apostle said: "The law is good, if anyone uses it lawfully." From these two it follows that the law is good, but for those who use it lawfully. If, then, anyone has not used it lawfully, the law itself does not become bad, but it will certainly harm the wicked.

Perhaps you will say that no one can both be under the law and use the law badly, since by the very fact that he lives against the law he is shown not to be under the law. I say, on the contrary, that it is possible for someone both to be under the law and not to use it lawfully. This too I prove from your admissions. For you grant that the apostle I have mentioned cited testimony from the Psalms against those who boasted in the law and lived against the law. "As it is written," he says, "there is no one righteous, no one who understands, no one who seeks God; all have turned aside, together they have become worthless; there is no one who does good, not even one. Their throat is an open grave; with their tongues they deal deceitfully; the venom of asps is under their lips. Their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness. Their feet are swift to shed blood. Ruin and misery are in their paths, and the way of peace they have not known. There is no fear of God before their eyes." And lest they should think these things were said of those who were not under the law, he at once added: "Now we know that whatever the law says, it speaks to those who are under the law, so that every mouth may be stopped and the whole world may become accountable to God." Again in another place he says: "What then shall we say? Is the law sin? By no means! Yet I would not have known sin except through the law; for I would not have known covetousness if the law had not said, 'You shall not covet.' But sin, seizing the opportunity through the commandment, produced in me all kinds of covetousness." And again a little later: "Sin," he says, "seizing the opportunity through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me. So the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and just and good. Did that which is good, then, become death to me? By no means! But sin, so that it might be shown to be sin, worked death in me through what is good." Do you notice how, while praising the law, he rebukes those who are under the law, all who by using it badly had evil through what is good? Again, the same apostle says that a certain knowledge drawn from the law, which he said both he and others possessed, is useless and harmful without love: "Concerning things sacrificed to idols," he says, "we know that we all have knowledge. Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up." So this knowledge too, although it belongs to the law of God, puffs up and does harm if it is found in someone without love. What then? As for the very body and blood of the Lord, the one sacrifice for our salvation — since the Lord himself says, "Unless a man eats my flesh and drinks my blood, he will not have life in him" — does not the same apostle teach that this too becomes deadly to those who use it badly? For he says: "Whoever eats unworthily and drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord."

See how divine and holy things harm those who use them badly. Why not baptism in the same way? Why are heretics not, in this way, wicked while having a good baptism, just as the Jews were wicked while having a good law? I have surely now proved, with your own consent — since you believe Paul and grant that Paul said the testimonies I have quoted from the Scriptures — I have now proved, I say, from your own admissions that certain things, though good and lawful, nevertheless harm those who have and use them unlawfully. Why then does not baptism likewise, though good and lawful, still fail to benefit everyone who has it? Why did you conclude, as if it were most certain and most consequent, that a person ought to be baptized in the party of Donatus because we grant that baptism exists even there? And why did you not notice that we can say that the baptism of Christ is indeed there, just, holy and good, yet penal, hostile and deadly to the enemies of the body of Christ, which is the Church, spreading, according to the divine promises, among all nations?

Will you find anything to say here except that baptism is not to be counted among those good things belonging to the law of God which people can have and yet not be good — that the law itself, and knowledge, and the sacrifice of the body and blood of Christ are goods of the kind that people can have and yet be wicked, but that baptism is a good of such a kind that whoever has it must necessarily be good? If you wish to say this, you will be saying something false; so notice what further falsehood follows from it. I will mention it, not in order to lead you from that falsehood of yours to other falsehoods, but so that, once you recognize that this consequence is false, you may free yourself from it by correcting the premise that leads to it. What, then, is the premise? That, on your view, all who have a good baptism are good. This is evidently false, and from it follows that those were good who were making schisms by saying, "I am of Paul, I of Cephas, and I of Christ" — the ones the apostle rebuked when he said: "Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you, or were you baptized in the name of Paul?" But it is false that these people were good — except for those who said, "I am of Christ" — and yet they had been baptized with the holy baptism of Christ. Why, then, did this falsehood follow? Because a falsehood came before it: that all who have a good baptism are good. Let both, then, be rejected and both statements corrected, so that, since it is plain that those who made schisms were not good and yet had been baptized with a good baptism, it may also be plain that not all who have a good baptism are good. And therefore we are not bound to grant that anyone ought to be baptized in the party of Donatus merely because we grant that the party of Donatus, which we call wicked, has a good baptism.

Again, in order to draw me from something I agree to towards something I do not, you cited what is written: "One [God], one faith, one baptism, one incorrupt and true Catholic Church." I grant all of this, even though it is written somewhat differently. But what does that matter, since, as I said, I grant all of it? But what you try to establish from these things is not established: namely, that those who are not in the one Church cannot have the one baptism. That is utterly false. And it is all the better that you yourself have supplied the means by which I can remind you of what I wish to say. For you certainly put these forward as things I concede, from which you might lead me to your conclusion: that there is one God, one faith, one baptism, one incorrupt and Catholic Church. Since we agree on these, you think that from them you can prove what we do not agree on, namely that this one baptism cannot exist among those who are not in this one Church. But I say it can, provided it is not altered, provided the same form is kept; and it does not follow that baptism is not one because it is found also among those who are not in the one Church. And I prove this from what you set down in the same statement about the one God and the one faith. For we find that the same God is worshiped outside the Church by those who do not know him, and yet it does not follow that he is not God himself; and we find that the faith by which Christ is believed to be the Son of the living God is confessed even by those who do not belong to the members of the Church, and yet it does not follow that the faith is not one. So too, when we find the same baptism observed by those outside the Church in baptizing people, we ought not on that account to think that it is not that very baptism.

Perhaps you will reply that it is impossible for the same one God to be worshiped outside the Church, or for the same faith by which we confess Christ to be the Son of God — the confession for which Peter was called blessed — to be found in those who are not in the Church. This, then, remains for me to prove. You have it in that very speech of blessed Paul which I cited above from the Acts of the Apostles, when he spoke about God, having found inscribed on an altar "To an unknown God": "What you worship without knowing it," he says, "this I proclaim to you." Did he say: "Because you worship outside the Church, the one you worship is not God himself"? No, he said: "What you worship without knowing it, this I proclaim to you." And what did he wish to give them, except that the same God whom they were worshiping outside the Church ignorantly and to no profit, they might worship in the Church wisely and for their salvation? So we too say to you: "The baptism which you observe without understanding — its peace we proclaim to you; not that when you come to us you should receive another, but that you should have to your profit the one that was already among you." Concerning faith too, when the apostle James was speaking against those who thought their belief was enough for them and were unwilling to do good works, he says: "You believe that God is one? You do well; the demons also believe, and tremble." Demons, of course, are not in the unity of the Church, and yet we cannot say on that account that what they believe is something else, since they even said to the Lord Jesus Christ: "What have we to do with you, Son of God?" Hence the apostle Paul too says: "If I have all faith, so as to move mountains, but do not have love, I am nothing." And I do not think anyone is so foolish as to believe that someone who does not have love belongs to the unity of the Church. Just as, then, the one God is worshiped ignorantly even outside the Church and is not on that account any other than he, and the one faith is held without love even outside the Church and is not on that account any other than it, so too the one baptism is held ignorantly and without love even outside the Church and is not on that account any other than it. For there is one God, one faith, one baptism, one incorrupt Catholic Church — not the only place where the one God is worshiped, but the only place where the one God is worshiped devoutly; not the only place where the one faith is held, but the only place where the one faith is held with love; not the only place where the one baptism is possessed, but the only place where the one baptism is possessed to salvation.

So you put forward, with our agreement, one God, one faith, one baptism, one incorrupt and Catholic Church; but not only did you fail to establish from them what you wanted, you even helped us a great deal by giving us the means to remind you, from these very things, of what we wanted to say. See, then, how reasonable is the principle we follow. When people come to us from schismatics or heretics, we correct what they have corrupted, but what they have kept as they received it we recognize and approve, so that we may not, provoked by human failings, go beyond justice and do any injury to divine things. For we see that the apostle, even on an altar of the Gentiles, who worshiped idols, confirmed rather than denied the name of God that he found there. Nor is the royal mark on a man to be changed or rejected, if he has obtained from the king pardon for his error and a place in the ranks, merely because a deserter stamped that same mark on him in order to gather followers for himself; nor are the brands on sheep to be changed when they are joined to the Lord's flock merely because a runaway slave stamped the Lord's brand on them.

But if you fear these as misleading, because they are not examples taken from the Church — although you know that comparisons drawn from sheep and from soldiers are given in the Scriptures — I wish to say something from the prophetic Scriptures, which are called the Old Testament, since in the books of the New Testament no example of this matter is found either by us or by you. You will not dare, I think, to deny that the circumcision of the foreskin was observed by the ancients as a figure of the future baptism of Christ. Could a man circumcised among the Samaritans be circumcised again if he then wished to become a Jew? Would not his error be corrected, while the seal of faith was recognized and approved? And there are now certain heretics who call themselves Nazarenes, though some call them Symmachians, who have both the circumcision of the Jews and the baptism of Christians. And so, just as one of them who comes over to the Jews cannot be circumcised again, so when he comes over to us he ought not to be baptized again. To this you will say: "The circumcision of the Jews is one thing, the baptism of Christians another." But since the former was a shadow of this truth, why could that circumcision exist even among the heretics of the Jews, while this baptism cannot exist among the heretics of the Christians?

At any rate, produce from the canonical Scriptures someone who came from heretics and was baptized again. For the fact that the apostles ordered certain people to be baptized in Christ after the baptism of John is a very different case. John was no heretic — he, the friend of the bridegroom, than whom none greater has arisen among those born of women. It is a very different case, then. Otherwise, if Paul baptized after John, though both were in the unity of Christ, how much more ought your bishops, since they say they are in the unity of Christ, to baptize after their own colleagues, in whom they rightly find some conduct to censure, when Paul did this though he could find nothing to censure in John! So that is a different case, a different principle, which it would take too long to discuss now, and about which we have already said a great deal in other short works of ours. Prove, then, from the canonical Scriptures, that someone who came from heretics was baptized again. For we too cite what was said to Peter: "He who has been washed once has no need to be washed again." But you also say: "Peter had not been baptized among heretics." So, since you cannot produce from the Scriptures, whose authority we share, anyone coming from heretics who was baptized again, nor can we produce anyone received in our way, as far as this matter is concerned our case is equal.

But we have shown that many things belonging to the law of God are found among those who are not in the Church, which none of you dares to deny; and why you refuse to allow that baptism is something of this kind, I altogether fail to see, and I am confident that you cannot show. In this matter we do indeed follow the most certain authority of the canonical Scriptures as well. For it should not be considered of small importance that, when among the bishops of an earlier age, before the party of Donatus began to exist, this question was unsettled and the colleagues held differing opinions among themselves while preserving unity, the whole Catholic Church spread throughout the world resolved that what we hold should be observed. You, for your part, cite the council of Cyprian, which either never took place or was rightly overruled by the other members of the unity, from whom he did not separate himself. Nor are we better than Bishop Cyprian — if indeed he held that heretics should be baptized again — because we rightly do not do this, just as we are not better than the apostle Peter because we do not compel the Gentiles to live like Jews, as he is shown to have done, by the testimony and correction of the apostle Paul. For among the apostles there was likewise a question about circumcision, just as later among the bishops about baptism, which wavered with no small difficulty.

Therefore, although no clear example of this matter is produced from the canonical Scriptures, we nevertheless hold to the truth of those same Scriptures in this matter too when we do what has now been approved by the whole Church, which the authority of those very Scriptures commends. So, since holy Scripture cannot deceive, whoever fears to be deceived by the obscurity of this question should consult on it that same Church which holy Scripture points out without any ambiguity. But if you doubt that this holy Scripture commends the Church which spreads through all nations in the most abundant numbers — and if you did not doubt it, you would not still be in the party of Donatus — I will load you with many very clear testimonies brought forward from that same authority, so that from your own admissions, unless you choose to be excessively stubborn, you may be led to this conclusion as well. But first I shall show that you were unable to give any answer bearing on the truth to my letter, which you chose to answer from the opposing side.

Let this suffice for now. Because of people's excessive obstinacy, I thought I had to say a great deal against those who, having a bad case at its root, try to turn the judges away from examining it by a preliminary objection, saying that they must in no way speak with us. For I have proved, both from the holy Scriptures and by reasoning as clear as I could make it, that defenders of the truth need fear no eloquence, however great, nor any dialectic, of whatever kind, that would prevent them from refuting the defenders of falsehood by disputing with them and confuting them. There I also showed, regarding the point which you said troubled you apart from my letter, how little it follows that, if we grant that there is baptism in the party of Donatus, we must at the same time grant that anyone ought to be baptized in that communion. For just as the reprobate people of the Jews could have a good law, so a reprobate society of heretics can have a good sacrament. What, though, is given properly in the Church and is not given at all outside it will be shown without difficulty in its proper place. For we would not be right to deal with heretics, whom we acknowledge to have baptism, so that by all means they should come to the Catholic Church, unless by coming they received something which they cannot receive elsewhere, and without which they would have to no purpose and to their ruin whatever other things, however good and belonging to the law of God, they were able to receive anywhere. For whatever it is that, according to the Scriptures and the most certain reasoning, can be found to be given or received only in the holy Church, this will belong to the sealed fountain, the well of living water, the garden with its fruit trees. You mentioned these as best you could, but showed that you had not understood what they mean, since you think this was said of visible baptism. Although that baptism is holy and must in no way be neglected, since it excels in a most sacred significance, yet consider how many receive it — not only the good, who are called according to his purpose and conformed to the image of the Son of God, but also those who will not possess the kingdom of God, among whom, as the apostle says, are counted drunkards and the greedy. I think that, if you lay aside your stubbornness and reflect, you will readily answer yourself that I am telling the truth, so that you will look for the sealed fountain and the well of living water only where those who displease God are, by divine ordinance, not allowed to approach.
BOOK TWO.

After the long discussion of the previous book, I think I have at last persuaded you that your bishops are not to be praised or approved for refusing to confer with us about the cause of the dispute that divides our communion. They think this works like a legal plea that keeps them perfectly safe in a very bad cause. Unless I am mistaken, I have cut that plea away entirely, with true and certain arguments and above all with examples from the divine Scriptures. Through these I have shown very clearly that the holy preachers and defenders of the truth held discussions even with opponents of the truth who stood before them. They did so not only with people of the same nation as themselves, but also with foreigners and strangers, and even with those who professed dialectic most of all, the very thing you use to frighten the unlearned with empty fears. So a very diligent preacher should not be thought quarrelsome, nor a tireless debater taken for a wrangler. Following the Apostle's command, he presses on in season and out of season, so that by sound doctrine those who contradict may be refuted, idle talkers rebutted, the unruly rebuked, the fainthearted comforted and the weak supported, while the word of gospel salvation is patiently defended against all who resist it and preached without fear. I also showed that you have no reason to think a person should be baptized among you just because we agree that baptism can be had and given by you. For we also say that it is had to your harm and given to your harm. The holier those sacred things are which even the wicked can use, the more uselessly and the more to their own punishment the wicked handle them. So when such people come to the holy Church, it is they who must be corrected. The good must not violate those sacred things, since even the wicked did not change them.

Listen then, Cresconius, while I briefly show that in your whole letter you said nothing to refute mine. The one exception is perhaps that you taught me how to derive or inflect names, so that from Donatus I should say "Donatians" rather than "Donatists." Yet you admit that "Donatists" is at least a Greek formation, since Donatists would be named from Donatus just as evangelists are named from the gospel. You say this pleases you, because your people preach the gospel and so have borrowed a word formed on that model. Consider, then, whether your predecessors wanted this name precisely because they hold Donatus in place of the gospel. These people refuse to leave the fellowship of Donatus just as all the saints refuse to leave the fellowship of the gospel, and so they are pleased to be called Donatists as others are called evangelists. You actually do them an injury when you write that in Latin you will accept only the Latin rule, and that it is better to call them Donatians from Donatus, just as Arians and Novatians are named from Arius and Novatus. For my part, when I wrote, this name was already ringing in my ears, spread by I know not whom, and I did not bother to change it, since I thought it served well enough for the distinction I wanted to make. Demosthenes, the most famous of orators, belonged to a people who cared as much for words as our authors care for things. Yet when Aeschines reproached him for some unusual expressions, he replied that the fortunes of Greece did not depend on whether he had used this word or that, or stretched out his hand this way or that. How much less, then, should we trouble ourselves about the rules for deriving names! Whichever form we use, what we say is understood without ambiguity, and our chief aim is not polished speech but the demonstration of truth. If one of our people was the first to form this name, I do not think he had in mind the way evangelists are named from the gospel. Rather, a great scandal arose through Donatus. This means not only Donatus of Carthage, who is said to have done most to strengthen this heresy, but also the elder Donatus of Casae Nigrae, who was the first to set up altar against altar in the same city. So perhaps he meant to call them Donatists from Donatus in the way one might call people "scandalists" from "scandal."

But in a matter that takes nothing away from our case I am very easy to deal with. When I deal with you, I now say "Donatians." When I deal with others, I prefer to follow custom, which rightly governs such word forms. Only remember that I, to whom you attributed such eloquence, still do not know how to inflect nouns. Tell your people they can rest easy and need no longer fear me as a dialectician, since, as you see, I still need a grammar teacher. The art of disputation, whether you choose to call it dialectic or something else, teaches soberly enough that when the thing itself is agreed, one should not labor over the name. I do not care whether that art is called dialectic. What I do care about, as far as I am able, is knowing how to dispute and being able to do it, that is, to distinguish truth from falsehood in speech, for if I neglected this I would fall into the most ruinous error. In the same way, I do not care whether you are more skilfully and correctly named Donatists or Donatians. Nor do I care, in the end, whether the name we use to distinguish you when we speak should come from the Donatus who first offered sacrifice outside the Church, or from the Donatus who did most to strengthen this dissension, or from Majorinus, who was the first ordained bishop of your party in opposition to Caecilian. But you are heretics, and for that reason people must avoid you very carefully so as not to be deceived. If I do not take pains to show this thoroughly, I shall incur no small guilt of negligence in view of the burden of my office.

You think, however, that what has happened between us should be called a schism rather than a heresy. You even distinguish the two by definitions, which dialecticians seldom venture to do. I cannot adequately show how much you help us here unless I insert your own words from your letter. You say: "What do you mean by speaking of 'the sacrilegious error of heretics'? Heresies arise only among people who follow different things, and a heretic is simply a worshipper of an opposed religion, or of one interpreted differently. Such are the Manichees, Arians, Marcionites, Novatians and the rest, who hold views contrary to one another and opposed to the Christian faith. Between us, who have the same Christ born, dead and risen, one religion and the same sacraments, with nothing different in Christian observance, what has happened is called a schism, not a heresy. For heresy is a sect of people following different things, while schism is a separation of people following the same things. So you see what an error you have fallen into, in your eagerness to accuse, by calling a schism a heresy." These are certainly your words, which I have quoted from your letter.

Now, if you are not obstinate, notice how easily and briefly you yourself have settled the question between us. If we and you have the same Christ born, dead and risen, one religion, the same sacraments, and nothing different in Christian observance, is not rebaptizing a perversion? You stated three things. Had you stated only one, it would have been more than enough. But as though you were dealing faithfully against the Donatians, you made sure that no one, however clever, could try to interpret otherwise what you might have said once and briefly. So you took care to drive your statement in and press it home even into dull ears and hearts: "one religion," you say, "the same sacraments, nothing different in Christian observance." And still we are struggling against each other! At long last, restrain the dissension, mend the rent, end the quarrel, love peace. What are you rejecting? What are you exorcizing? Why do you rebaptize? There is one religion, the same sacraments, nothing different in Christian observance. If we and you do not have one baptism, how is there one religion? But you said "one religion," so there is also one baptism. If we and you do not have the same baptism, how are the sacraments the same? But you said "the same sacraments," so baptism too is the same. Again, if our baptism and yours are different, how is nothing different in Christian observance? But you said "nothing different in Christian observance," so baptism is not different either. Since this is so, we act rightly: what is one and the same and not different we neither reject, nor exorcize, nor repeat, but recognize, receive and accept. You act impiously: what is one and the same and not different you pretend not to recognize, refuse to receive and will not accept. Instead you choose to reject it, dare to exorcize it and do not fear to repeat it. On this very point, what has not been changed between us we receive and you repel. If something was given by you, we judge that it was given. If it was given by us, you give it again as though it had not been given. While you follow such different things, you disdain to be called heretics.

Pay close attention to what you say and what I say. You certainly gave a definition and said: "Heresy is a sect of people following different things, while schism is a separation of people following the same things." You also said that we and you have one religion, the same sacraments, nothing different in Christian observance. If there is one religion, the same sacraments and nothing different in Christian observance, why then do you rebaptize a Christian? And if on this point, where you rebaptize a Christian and I do not, we are clearly following different things, why do you refuse to be called a heretic? I think it is no small sign by which we recognize heretics that they admit they and we have one religion, the same sacraments and nothing different in Christian observance, and yet refuse to recognize us as baptized. Or do you contend so obstinately and resist the truth with such dissension that you separate baptism from religion, from the sacraments, from Christian observance? If you do this, you are heretics in this respect, that you will not allow baptism to belong to religion, to the sacraments, to Christian observance. If you do not do this, you are heretics in this respect, that you confess baptism belongs to religion, to the sacraments, to Christian observance, and yet you rebaptize those who have with you one religion, the same sacraments and nothing different in Christian observance. Look carefully at your definition, where you said, "Heresy is a sect of people following different things." Then see whether you are not following different things. Either you separate baptism from the religious observance of the Christian sacraments, where we join it as one of the great ones. Or you rebaptize those with whom you share one religious observance of the Christian sacraments, in which baptism too is one, and that is something we abhor.

How I would like it, if I could, to appear suddenly out of nowhere with this letter of yours at the moment your people receive one of our faithful who has been deceived, to destroy him with their wicked snares. They say that although he was baptized among us he has not even begun to be a Christian. They exorcize him as if he were a pagan and make him a catechumen, preparing him to be dipped again, or rather snuffed out. In the middle of their daring I would hold out this very passage of your letter, read it aloud and cry out: "What are you doing? Look, listen, see, read: 'We and you have one religion, the same sacraments, nothing different in Christian observance.' First ask in whose name this man was baptized. Then, if you can name someone better in your baptism, give it." Then perhaps, if the plain evidence of the facts did not make them tremble, they would at once bring out their plan, so great and so clever, and say: "Who is this man whose letter you are carrying? He is one of our laymen. Had he won, he would have won for us; as it is, he is beaten on his own account [?]." Then, if I were there, I would turn to you and say: "You at least, I beg you, tell us what these people are doing. See, they are getting ready to rebaptize someone baptized among us. Surely, then, we and you have one religion, the same sacraments, nothing different in Christian observance?" Or would you answer: "But the baptism of Christ is not religion, is not a sacrament, is not Christian observance"? God forbid such madness should enter your mind! What, then, would you answer me as I pressed you and said: "We and you have one religion. Those who do not have one baptism do not have one religion. Therefore we and you have one baptism. We and you have the same sacraments. Those who do not have the same baptism do not have the same sacraments. Therefore we and you have the same baptism. We and you have nothing different in Christian observance. Those whose baptism is different certainly do have something different in Christian observance. Therefore our baptism and yours are not different. Why is what is one rejected? Why is what is the same exorcized? Why is what is not different repeated?"

If I pressed you like this face to face, what evasions would you take refuge in? No doubt they would scorn the grammarian in your letter, and you would accuse the dialectician in ours. But in both cases the truth would overcome the heretics. It would show that the only point on which they differ from us is the one that is plainly perverse. For we recognize our sacraments and correct the error of others. You, on the other hand, confess that the sacraments are the same, yet repeat them as if they were nothing, and with great difference reject what you grant is not different.

I myself prefer a different distinction between schism and heresy. On this view, schism is a recent dissension within a congregation arising from some difference of opinion, since a schism cannot happen unless those who make it follow something different, while heresy is a schism grown old. Yet why should I labor over this, when your definitions help me so much that, if your other people granted it too, I would rather call you schismatics than heretics? For if schism is made by those who have with the people they divide from one religion, the same sacraments and nothing different in Christian observance, then your rebaptizing is all the more damnable.
