Where there is one religion, the same sacraments and nothing different in Christian observance, there cannot be another, different baptism. But what you follow differently is neither nothing nor something small. Cut off from the bond of unity, you also disagree with us about repeating baptism. So by your own definition, where you said, "Heresy is a sect of people following different things," you turn out to be both heretics and defeated. Heretics, because you are not only divided but also follow something different in rebaptizing. Defeated, because you repeat the baptism given through us as if it were not the same baptism, or no baptism at all, although you confess it to be one and the same and not different. For these are your words: that we and you have one religion, the same sacraments, nothing different in Christian observance.

So if the party of Donatus would endorse your letter, and then reflect on what you and I have said without insane obstinacy or shamelessness, it would have nothing further to think or say against us. But since it is you I am answering, I think you yourself now see that it was not out of eagerness to accuse, but to refute a ruinous deception, that I said "the sacrilegious error of the Donatist heretics." Of these four words or nouns, since you or the art of grammar prefers it, I correct and change the first, "Donatist," and say "Donatian." The other three, since I think you now see that they were spoken with complete truth, it is for you to correct and change. Change, I say, and correct the sacrilegious error of the heretics, whether you are to be called Donatians or by any other name. For you are heretics, either because you have remained in a schism grown old, or, by your own definition, because you follow something different concerning the Church, which is the body of Christ, and concerning the repetition of Christian baptism. And it is a sacrilegious error not only to separate from Christian unity but also to violate and cancel the sacraments, which by your own confession are one and the same. If you correct and change this, how can we be receiving you as you were? So you have said a great deal to no purpose. Though you have so sharp a mind, you have been dulled by the habit of listening to nonsense, so that it seems to you that when people cross over from you to us we receive them as they were. You think so because in them we approve the Christian tradition, which those who were estranged did not make foreign and those who were perverse did not pervert. Even you, though you are not such as we are, could not confess these sacraments to be anything but such, and not such in the sense of other, similar ones, but entirely the same.

Tell me, I beg you: how is someone the same as he was when he now venerates the Church he used to blaspheme, holds the unity he did not hold, has the charity he did not have, accepts the peace he rejected, and approves the sacrament he used to exorcize? Or is everything so turned upside down among false people [?] that those in whom what was different is corrected by the truth are not said to be changed, while those in whom what was one and the same is repeated through folly are said to be changed? So stop thinking about this matter not only in a carnal way but even in a childish one, as though we received your people as they were. By a turning of the will from error to truth, from division to unity, from dissension to peace, from enmity to charity, from human presumption to the authority of the divine Scriptures, they do not begin to be ours until they have ceased to be yours. This turning of the will suddenly changed not only the sinner at the tax booth but even the robber on the cross. Or do you think Christ would have wanted a bloodstained criminal with him in paradise, had not that conversion of heart made him innocent at once? So on that day, from that place, from that wood, he passed to the immortal reward of faith, on the very spot where he had received the punishment of death for his wickedness. For the mind is changed in a brief moment, whether toward evil or toward good, but what it deserves is not therefore small. Even with bodily and temporal goods and benefits, a single blow destroys a life of any age, however long it has been nourished, and an illness of thirty-eight years was healed as soon as the Lord deigned to command it. Believe sure facts, not empty words. Your people cross over to us changed. Far be it from them to be what they were! I wish you would do the same, and believe from your own experience how true this is!

You thought you were saying something important when you named Candidus of Villa Regia and Donatus of Macomades. Formerly bishops of yours, they were bishops among us as well, and after an approved life they reached the more honorable merit of old age. You speak as though the sacraments and the invocation of God's name that take place among you were themselves hostile to us. In fact, even among those outside the Church, these belong to nothing but the Church. If I were struggling with this question using my own words, yours would help me. For if you held that nothing belonging to the Church can exist outside the Church, you would not yourself have said that we and you have one religion, the same sacraments, nothing different in Christian observance. I do not agree with these words of yours entirely. You lack the Christian Church; you do not have Christian charity. I do indeed recognize Christian sacraments among you, and in them I reject and refuse the one thing that is different: that while you have these same sacraments even in schism, you exorcize the same sacraments in Catholics. The Church fully recognizes among you everything that is hers, and these things do not cease to be hers because they are also found among you. Among you they are someone else's, but when she to whom they belong receives you corrected, the things you held to your harm as someone else's become yours as well, to your salvation. Discord possesses you under the title of peace. So let discord be driven out and peace brought in. What reason is there for the title to be laid aside? "He is a bishop," you say, "and you receive him as a bishop; a presbyter, and you receive him as a presbyter." You might as well say to me, "He is a man, and you receive him as a man." For I recognize the Christian sacraments in him just as I recognize his human limbs, and I do not care who sowed them, but by whom they were created. If he chooses to use them badly, he becomes evil precisely because he offends the Creator with the Creator's own good gifts. But if he begins to use them well, he will correct himself, not change them.

Receiving bishops or clergy is indeed a separate question. When they are ordained among you, it is not the name of Donatus but the name of God that is invoked over them. Even so, they are received in whatever way seems to suit the peace and benefit of the Church. For we are not bishops for our own sake but for the sake of those to whom we minister the word and sacrament of the Lord. Therefore, since we are what we are not for ourselves but for others, we ought either to be it or not be it, as the need to govern those people without scandal requires. Indeed, some men endowed with holy humility have laid down the office of bishop, not only without blame but even with praise, because of certain stumbling blocks in themselves that troubled them out of piety and devotion. Could they lay down the Christian name and faith in the same way, and be praised for it rather than condemned? In accepting these offices there can be just reasons why someone declines to become a bishop, but there can never in the same way be a just reason for anyone to decline to become a Christian. Why is this, except that we can be saved without being bishops or clergy, but we cannot be saved without the Christian religion?

So, as far as the church's offices themselves are concerned, your bishops and other clergy have been received into catholic unity in whatever way seemed best for the people whose salvation was served either by their exercising that office or by their setting it aside. Yet even about those who have held the same offices among us as well: just as you could say, "He is a bishop; you receive a bishop," will you be able to say, "He is a heretic; you receive a heretic," or "He is a schismatic; you receive a schismatic," or "He is a Donatian; you receive a Donatian"? These names do not set a rank of honour apart from the standing of the laity. They set apart the crime of error from catholic truth. Those things, then, which are in a sense the church's gifts, though found even among outsiders, are either accepted or not accepted in those who leave you, cross over to us and so become ours. This is decided by the good of the peoples whom we serve through this stewardship. But the things that are faulty and properly your own are healed, corrected and changed. Even in heretics, however, the sacraments without which no one can become a Christian are to be treated in such a way that, when they come to the church, what was lacking is added and what is recognized is approved. Otherwise, being too deeply offended by the evils they have produced against the church, we would also persecute the good things they took with them when they left the church. For even a broken branch, if it is to be grafted back in, as the apostle says, has its root given back to it; its form is not changed.

"But since you call our people heretics and sacrilegious," you say, "which is a wicked and inexpiable crime, ought such people to be pardoned without some expiation, or can they be? Why then do you not cleanse the one who comes to you? Why do you not first wash and purify him, and only then admit him to communion with you?" What if someone else drew from these words of yours the far more fitting conclusion that such people neither ought to be pardoned nor can be? What if he showed that you have contradicted yourself, since you say that such people must be pardoned with some expiation because what they are charged with is inexpiable? How, then, is what is inexpiable expiated? How can I hope that you will listen to what I say, when you do not listen to what you yourself say a moment earlier, but contradict yourself at once by ruling that what you called inexpiable must be expiated? We, for our part, do call your error heretical and sacrilegious, but we do not call it inexpiable. Otherwise it would have been pointless for us to resolve to work on you by every means we can, so that you might abandon that error, be corrected and cross over to the catholic church. Nor should you suppose, as you write, that you are using our own word, as if we said that this evil has no pardon and no physician. We say nothing of the kind, because those who repent of this evil deserve pardon, and the physician is almighty who says through the prophet: "If you turn back and groan, then you will be saved." So if you happened to meet someone who said this to you, someone poorly instructed in these matters or not paying attention to what he was saying, even though he seemed to belong to the catholic communion, let him rather be pardoned for so thoughtless a word. So may you, who for all your liberal education and no small learning in the art of words, pay too little attention to what you are saying when you rule that what you called inexpiable must be expiated, and, more monstrous still, must be expiated precisely because it is inexpiable. It is not the catholic way to urge people to correct their error and be saved while asserting that they are in error past all expiation and past all cure. But the reason they do not seem to you to be cleansed when they cross over from you to us is that they are not baptized again. It is as if people were cleansed from error by baptism alone, which must not be repeated, since it is one and the same. They are cleansed also by the word of truth, by him who says: "You are already clean because of the word that I have spoken to you." They are cleansed also by the sacrifice of a contrite heart, by him of whom it is said: "The sacrifice for God is a broken spirit; a contrite and humbled heart God does not despise." They are cleansed also by almsgiving, by him who says: "Give alms, and see, everything is clean for you." They are cleansed by charity itself, which surpasses all these, by him who said through the apostle Peter: "Charity covers a multitude of sins." If this one thing is present, all those things are done rightly; if it is absent, they are all done in vain. And as to where charity comes from, hear the apostle: "The charity of God," he says, "has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us." So it is rightly believed that those who received the church's baptism outside the church do not have the Holy Spirit unless they themselves hold fast to the church in the bond of peace, joined to it by charity.

Now is the place to show what I had put off in the first book: what can be properly received in the church, which is the holy body of Christ, and cannot be received outside it. For of those who were causing schisms the same apostle says: "The unspiritual man does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God." Read the first letter to the Corinthians and you will find it. Baptism, then, is the sacrament of new life and eternal salvation, and many have it to their eternal punishment rather than to eternal life, because they do not use so great a good well. But holy charity, which is the bond of perfection, no one who is not good can have. No one who has it can be either a schismatic or a heretic. Whoever comes to the unity of the church and is truly joined to its members receives the Holy Spirit, through whom charity is poured into our hearts. That same charity covers a multitude of sins, so that he now deserves to have unto reward the baptism he formerly had unto judgment. How, then, can you deny that he is cleansed, unless you are entirely ignorant of what spiritual cleansing is? So we do not, as you taunt us, take in your guilty men as if into the asylum of Romulus. Those whom the city of God receives it makes innocent, when they have crossed over to it with a sincere heart. Of this city its founder says: "A city set on a mountain cannot be hidden." For its founder was not one who in anger proudly killed his brother, but one who, being killed, humbly redeemed his brothers. He gladdens this city by the cleansing of the Holy Spirit, of whom he cried out, "If anyone thirsts, let him come and drink." He was not commending the visible water that is given in the sacrament of baptism, which both good and bad can have, although without it the good cannot be saved. That water belongs to the church, yet it also flows outside, since it is found as well among those who went out from us but were not of us. In the same way, it cannot be denied that the water in any one of those four famous rivers is the water of paradise, although it is not in paradise alone, since it flowed out from there.

So it was not this water that he was commending when he said, "If anyone thirsts, let him come and drink." Under the name of water he was commending the invisible gift of God, the Holy Spirit, as the evangelist clearly testifies when he adds: "He said this about the Spirit whom those who believed in him were to receive; for the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified." And certainly, as far as the sacrament of the visible washing is concerned, he had already baptized more people than John before he was glorified by rising again, as the gospel itself says. So he says to his disciples: "John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit," whom they were to receive not many days later, at Pentecost. When this Holy Spirit came upon them, he gave at the outset a sign of this kind: those who had received him spoke in the languages of all nations. This foreshadowed that the church would be spread through all nations, and that no one would receive the Holy Spirit unless he was joined to its unity. With the abundant and invisible stream of this fountain God gladdens his city, of which the prophet foretold: "The rushing streams of the river gladden the city of God." For no stranger comes to this fountain, since no one comes to it who is not worthy of eternal life. It belongs to the church of Christ as its own, the church to which it was prophesied so long before: "Let the fountain of your water be your own, and let no stranger share it with you." For it is of this church and of this fountain that the Song of Songs also says: "A garden enclosed, a fountain sealed, a well of living water."

Your people take these words to mean the visible sacrament of baptism, and they go so far astray that they are forced against their will to admit the most absurd things. That fountain belongs to the one dove alone, and of it was said, "Let no stranger share it with you." Yet they must admit that Simon Magus, whom we read was baptized by Philip, could come to it, to the enclosed garden and the sealed well. They must admit that it was reached by all those pretenders of whom Cyprian speaks with a groan, "renouncing the world in words alone and not in deeds." It was reached, too, by all those greedy bishops of whom the same Cyprian testifies that they were "seizing estates by treacherous frauds, increasing their gains by compounding interest." These men are indeed found to have been baptized, and to have baptized others, with visible baptism. Yet that fountain belongs to the church alone, and no stranger shares it. It is the sealed fountain, the gift of the Holy Spirit, by which the charity of God is poured into our hearts. None of these men comes to it unless he is changed, and changed so completely that he is no longer a stranger. He must become a partaker of heavenly peace, a companion in holy unity, full of undivided charity, a citizen of the angelic city. So whoever turns to this city with a devout mind, laying aside the error of heresy or schism and correcting his conduct, may already have borne the sacraments, which could flow out even to the unworthy. If so, these are honoured in him, because even in strangers they are not regarded as strange. But now he is flooded by that fountain which belongs to the church alone and which no stranger shares, the sealed fountain of the Holy Spirit. Among you, anyone, however praiseworthy in the rest of his conduct, is cut off from it by the crime of schism or heresy alone.

So when your people come to us, ceasing to be yours and beginning to be ours, they receive what they did not have. As a result they begin to have, for their salvation, what they had before to their ruin, a ruin all the greater because they had it so unworthily. For first of all they receive the church itself, and within it peace, unity and charity, through the church's own invisible fountain, the Holy Spirit. Without these they would undoubtedly have perished, whatever else they had among you of the things that could be carried off outside the church. And they receive what they never yet had with readier pardon than if they had already had it and deserted it. This distinction is observed among us: those who have left the catholic church are received in one way, those who come to it for the first time in another. The former are weighed down more heavily by the crime of desertion. The latter are relieved by the bond of unity, which they did not break themselves but recognized and kept. So it can happen that those who rebaptized people they had led astray may themselves pray to the Lord for those people when they repent, if the deceivers have been joined to the church before the deceived are reconciled to it. The same can happen with worshippers of idols. Suppose some of them led Christians astray to idols and made apostates of them. If the seducers become Christians first and attain some great merit in the church, those whom they deceived may return through them, and through them be commended and reconciled to the Lord. The very people on whose account they abandoned the Lord would bring them back. For what the sacrament of baptism, rightly received, achieves in cleansing the sacrileges of pagans, the charity of unity, truly embraced, achieves in cleansing the sacrileges of schismatics and heretics. Seducers of faithful Christians who come to Christ are ranked ahead of the seduced who return, so that the seducers can even become bishops while the seduced cannot. In the same way, those deceived by heretics ought not to be surprised that, when they return to the catholic church, their deceivers, coming to it for the first time, are ranked ahead of them. For the deceivers have more excuse when they seek what they lacked, while the deceived must more humbly seek back what they once were. The deceivers we invite with greater honour to a place where they had never yet stood. The deceived we call back with greater caution from the place where they fell.

So by now you see clearly, I think, that I had good reason to speak of the sacrilegious error of the Donatist heretics, or "Donatian" heretics as you prefer. For you both dissent from the catholic church and undo the sacraments that you confess are one and the same. Yet you are not beyond pardon, nor incurable by the mercy of God. If you lay aside your quarrelsome error and turn to catholic truth and peace, you can be cleansed and healed through God's own gift, that is, his Holy Spirit, through whom charity is poured into our hearts. This will not destroy the church's sacraments in you, which you held outside, to your ruin, as things not your own. Rather, you will now hold those very sacraments inside, for your salvation, as your own.

Now let us see how you show that Petilian, or anyone else, was right to say: "It is the conscience of the one who gives in holiness that is looked to, to wash the conscience of the recipient." To this I replied: "What if the giver's conscience is hidden and perhaps stained? How will it be able to wash the recipient's conscience?" In answer you spoke at length, setting out not what you, a sharp man, would say but what your people say. All of it can be put briefly as follows. The giver's conscience is looked to, they say, not according to its integrity, which cannot be seen in it, but according to its reputation, whether true or false. It belongs, of course, to a man who may be a secret criminal, yet it is enough for the recipient that he is well thought of, not yet found out, not yet judged, not yet separated from the church. See, I beg you, over what precipice people have been driven by the plight of finding no way out. Can a giver's stained conscience really wash the recipient's conscience if it has a good reputation? And if it has gained a good reputation by deceit, will it have as much power to wash as a good conscience? Do you notice what is being said? Do you want us to pass over this point now, or shall I keep turning it over, so that you are forced to pay closer attention? Petilian said: "It is the conscience of the one who gives in holiness that is looked to, to wash the conscience of the recipient." I said: "What if the giver's conscience is hidden and perhaps stained? How will it be able to wash the recipient's conscience?" You, or rather your people, said this (for when would a man like you have said such things?): "Even if he has a stained conscience, it is enough for me, whom he baptizes, since it is hidden and I do not know of it, that I receive baptism from a man whose conscience I think innocent because he is in the church. For this reason," you say, "I look to the giver's conscience: not to judge hidden things, which cannot be done, but so that I may not be unaware of anything about him that is publicly known. This is why almighty God said: 'What is known is for you; what is hidden is for me.' So I always look to the giver's conscience. Since I cannot see it, I ask what is publicly known about it, and it makes no difference if the secret conscience holds one thing and public reputation another. For it is enough to know that the conscience of the man from whom I receive baptism has not yet been condemned."

There, I have set down your very words to show that they say what I summed up briefly and plainly in my own: that the conscience of the one who washes is looked to only so that its reputation may be known. So it is not the conscience itself that is looked to, my good man, not the conscience itself, which cannot be seen. What is looked to is the reputation, which can also be false, as you yourself confess and grant. For you too saw that a stained conscience has no power to wash. So it is not "the conscience of the one who gives in holiness that is looked to, to wash the conscience of the recipient." It is the reputation, which makes a man who does not give in holiness seem to give in holiness, and a man who does not wash seem to wash. So it is the good reputation of a bad man that washes the recipient, not the polluted conscience of the giver himself. Why then was it said, "It is the conscience of the one who gives in holiness that is looked to, to wash the conscience of the recipient"? Surely because it does not wash the recipient's conscience if the giver's conscience is not holy, if it is stained and unclean. What, then, is looked to in that case? "The conscience itself is looked to," you say, "when its reputation is looked to. If the reputation is good, it makes no difference to the washing of the recipient even when the conscience is bad; his good reputation does the washing." Tell me, I ask you: when the conscience is bad, is his good reputation true or false? False, without any doubt. So when the giver's conscience is not good and is hidden, however you imagine you are looking to it, on this view the recipient is washed only by the giver's false reputation or by his polluted conscience. Both ideas are insane; if such things delight you, choose for yourself which is the more insane. Now truth does not allow the recipient's conscience to be washed either by the giver's false reputation or by his polluted conscience. Petilian, or anyone else with your agreement, says that when the giver's conscience is holy, that is, good and clean, it washes the recipient's conscience. It remains, then, for us to ask you too what we asked there as well: by what is the recipient washed when the giver's stained conscience is hidden? I do not think you will now repeat the claim that his false good reputation takes the place of a good conscience in the washing. It is enough that you declared that this is what your people say, not you. Be ashamed of them; do not be ashamed of yourself as well. It remains, then, that in such a case either God or some holy angel does the washing. If you say this, there follows that dreadful absurdity which I pointed out in that letter of mine. I will not say you refused to see it, since you did not touch it at all; rather, you saw it all the more attentively and sharply the more you were afraid to touch it. For suppose you say that when a holy man baptizes, his holy conscience washes the recipient's conscience, but when the giver's conscience is secretly unclean, God or an angel does the washing. Then beware: those who believe you when you say this may want to find secretly wicked men to baptize them, so that they may be washed far more holily by God himself or by his angel. You saw that this absurdity, which deserves either laughter or loathing, followed from Petilian's earlier words and that I had pointed it out in my letter. So you cautiously decided to pass over so important a matter in silence, as though I had said none of it. Instead you took refuge in something even more absurd: that when the giver's stained conscience is hidden and therefore cannot wash the recipient's, the recipient is washed by the giver's false reputation, and in him falsehood produces truth.

Go on, then, and slander the dialecticians, accusing them of using some cunning trick of speech to make a statement true if it is false and false if it is true. Look, you yourself bring something of the same kind into the sacraments of Christian rebirth, and indeed something worse and more to be shunned. The dialecticians do not deal in fraud of their own, nor in the reality of things, but in the tangles of human speech. They say that certain statements appear true when they are false and false when they are true. When such statements come up in an argument, the mind can see through them, even if words cannot unravel them. You, however, are talking not about some word or other, nor some thing or other, but about the very cleansing of conscience by which we are reborn to eternal life. You say that this can truly take place in a person through the false reputation of someone else's conscience. And so that this will not be laid to your account, you who have learned dialectic, you say this is the view of your people. You have agreed with them not as a dialectician but plainly as a heretic. This, then, is the magnificent doctrine discovered or demonstrated by you or by your people. When the one who gives in holiness has a good conscience, the person baptized becomes good by it; then a good tree bears good fruit. But when the giver's conscience is bad and hidden, his good reputation, which is false, is consulted instead. So a person receives true baptism from a deceiver precisely when he has believed something false about him. Thus falsehood becomes the mother of truth, so that there may be no shortage of a tree to bear the fruit of heretical error. All this, so detestable, so astonishingly perverse and insane, is done for three reasons: so that what is God's may not be called God's, so that what is received from God may be credited to human beings, and so that the man who said, "It is the conscience of the one who gives in holiness that is looked to, to wash the conscience of the recipient," may not appear to have been wrong.

"Our people," you say, "prove this from the Scriptures, since Judas the traitor, before he was condemned, did everything as an apostle." What has this to do with Petilian's fixed and definite statement: "It is the conscience of the one who gives in holiness that is looked to, to wash the conscience of the recipient"? It only shows that this Judas is very much against you as well, when you try to defend other people's thoughtless words. Judas baptized as an apostle, and yet he was wicked, for he was a thief and used to take what was put into the purse entrusted to him. So when he baptized, it was certainly not his conscience that was looked to, but God and Christ, in whom people believed. Those who believed and received baptism were not washed by the false good reputation of that wicked man. Nor did the falsehood of human opinion produce in anyone the grace of divine truth.

And the testimony you cited from the Scriptures, "What is manifest is for you, but what is hidden is for the Lord your God," refutes these words and proves them wrong. For if hidden things are to be left to the Lord our God, how is the giver's conscience looked to, when it is hidden, so that it may wash the recipient's? And this holds not only for a bad conscience but for a good one as well. Or if the giver's conscience is not looked to when it is hidden, what do you tell the recipient to look to then, so that his conscience may be washed?

Oh, wake up at last, and now at least say: "Let him look to God." Why are you afraid of being humbled, if you glory not in man but in the Lord? "There is," you say, "something for me to fear. For if, when the conscience of the giver is hidden, I say that the recipient should look to God, and admit that it is by him that the recipient's conscience is then washed, that dreadful absurdity will follow for me: that people are washed in a holier way when they have baptizers who are secretly evil than when they have baptizers who are openly good, if a man does the washing when the giver's conscience is good and known, but God when it is evil and hidden." Then say what we say, because this is true, this is sound, this is catholic: that Christ cleanses the consciences of those who receive his baptism, whether through good ministers of it or through evil ones, since it is written of him: Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her, so that he might sanctify her, cleansing her by the washing of water in the word.

"You," you say, "answer how those whom the church has condemned can baptize." So now you are retreating from Petilian's words. For when he said, "It is the conscience of one who gives in holiness that is looked to, to wash the conscience of the recipient," and I asked who washes the recipient's conscience when the giver's polluted conscience is hidden, no answer could be given me. For to say that the giver's false reputation can wash is as contrary to the truth as to say that his conscience itself could do so.

But if you ask how those whom the church has condemned can baptize, I answer that they baptize in the same way as those whom God has condemned before the church has passed any judgment on them. For whoever, with a perverse mind, seems to be inside while actually being outside has already been judged by Christ himself. For he himself says: Whoever does not believe has already been judged; and the apostle Paul says: The church is subject to Christ. The church must not, then, set itself above Christ, so as to think that those judged by him can baptize, but those judged by itself cannot, since he always judges truly, while church judges, being human, are often mistaken. So, as far as the visible ministry is concerned, both the good and the evil baptize; but invisibly he baptizes through them, to whom belong both the visible baptism and the invisible grace. Both the good and the evil, then, can dip in water, but no one can wash the conscience except him who is always good. And so those whom Christ has condemned for their evil and polluted conscience, even without the church's knowledge, are already not in the body of Christ, which is the church, since Christ cannot have condemned members. Therefore they too baptize outside the church. Far be it, altogether, that all such monsters should be counted among the members of that one and only dove; far be it that they should be able to enter the bounds of the enclosed garden, whose keeper is one who cannot be deceived. Yet if they confess and are corrected, then they enter, then they are cleansed, then they are numbered among the trees of the enclosed garden and the members of the one and only dove, and yet they are not baptized again. So too when people come from the heretics: they come with the very baptism that they [?] outside, but not with the cleansing itself, which they receive inside, so that what was lacking may be supplied, and what has not been changed may be approved.

Your conscience, you say, stands condemned for the crime of handing over the Scriptures and of offering incense through your forebears, and for the crime of persecution through yourselves. As for the traitors and the incense-offerers, you came to believe who they were that committed this wickedness not from the holy Scriptures but from human rumor. If rumor can speak falsely well of the bad, why can it not also speak falsely ill of the good? On persecution, I will answer you briefly and once again with what I answered Petilian, which you were quite unable to refute. In holy Scripture, which deceives no one, the church of God is called a threshing floor, and we are told that the Lord himself will come with his winnowing fan and clean his threshing floor, storing the wheat in the barn but burning the chaff with unquenchable fire. So either you suffered persecution justly, or, if the Christian measure was exceeded, it was our chaff that did it, and the Lord's threshing floor ought not to have been deserted on that account. Otherwise anyone who fled the chaff on the threshing floor before the time of winnowing would be separated from the wheat and would himself become chaff. But when you tried to refute this testimony, which is not mine but holy Scripture's, you said that no persecution can be just. Here you must be pardoned for not knowing the Scriptures, which might have brought to your mind how justly it was said: "Whoever secretly slanders his neighbor, him I persecuted," and, by the Lord Jesus Christ himself in a most excellent prophecy: "I will persecute my enemies and overtake them, and I will not turn back until they fail." And there are many other divine testimonies, which it would take too long to persecute, that is, to pursue in full. I only hope you will not slander me over this word, and, because I said "it would take too long to persecute them," accuse me of being a persecutor of divine testimonies.

You cite against me words of Scripture that have so often been shown to be of no help to you: "Let not the oil of the sinner anoint my head." Yet you cannot deny that among you too there are at least hidden sinners who nevertheless baptize and are not excepted by these words, for it does not say "the oil of the manifest sinner" but simply "the oil of the sinner." You also cite: "They have become to me like lying water that has no faithfulness." Here I wonder at your good sense. How does the water of a hidden dissembler not seem to you lying water? You even believed that his false reputation could do something to cleanse another person's conscience. Perhaps you thought you would be helped by that argument which is not dialectical but plainly sophistical, the one you vainly reproached in me as though I were a dialectician: "If you are lying, you are telling the truth!" For what else are you trying to assert? You attribute baptism to man and refuse to acknowledge that it is God's, and so you say that an adulterer can give true baptism because, by concealing himself, he lies that he is chaste. So he tells the truth in baptism precisely when he lies about his sin, and his water is not lying water. And this is the water you claim belongs to the church, the church which, according to the promise of so many prophecies, is spread throughout the whole world! Yet Jeremiah did not call baptism lying water. He was speaking of lying men, according to the meaning made plain in the Apocalypse, where John asked what the waters shown in the vision were and was told that they were peoples.

Now as for the testimony that is written, "He who is baptized by a dead man, what does his washing profit?", pay a little attention to how badly you misunderstood what I wrote in that letter, and how much your own words have helped me. You thought that by "dead man" in this passage I meant a worshiper of idols, and so you argued as though I had excepted idolaters alone as unable to baptize. You did all you could, repeating the testimony about oil and claiming that the one who said "The oil of the sinner shall not anoint my head" wished no sinner to baptize, since he excepted no sinner. This only presses you all the harder, as I showed a little earlier. For if no sinner is excepted, then rebaptize those who were baptized by hidden evil men once those men have been convicted. At this point you will try to except the hidden sinner, whom holy Scripture did not except. This whole interpretation of yours, then, is convicted of falsehood by the truth, since it is also shown to conflict with your own purpose. In fact, the verse was not placed in the psalm about baptism at all, but about the flattery of a fawning man, as the preceding words make clear enough. The whole sentence runs like this: "The righteous man shall correct me in mercy and rebuke me, but the oil of the sinner shall not anoint my head." He preferred, then, to have his head struck by one who rebukes him truthfully rather than anointed by one who flatters him deceitfully. The words "oil" and "anointing" are used figuratively to signify the smoothness of the flatterer.

What I meant by this testimony in that letter, where it is said, "He who is baptized by a dead man," I will show clearly enough, I think, by repeating the very words of the letter. I was discussing how a Catholic Christian ought to answer such things, and I said: "When he hears, 'He who is baptized by a dead man, his washing does not profit him,' he will answer: 'Christ lives and dies no more, and death shall no longer have dominion over him.' Of him it was said: 'He it is who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.' Those who are baptized by the dead are those who are baptized in the temples of idols. For they themselves do not think they receive what they suppose to be sanctification from their priests, but from their gods. And since these gods were men, and are so dead that they live neither on earth nor in the rest of the saints, these people truly are baptized by the dead." Up to this point I have copied the very words of my letter. In them you can see, I think, if you will at least now pay careful attention, that I did not call the worshipers themselves dead, although in another sense they too are dead. I called dead the false gods whom they worship, because they were men, and like men they departed from the body, did not rise again, and had no claim to the life that is promised after this life. So those who are baptized by these gods are truly baptized by the dead, as I said. That is, they are baptized in the name of these gods, for they think they are sanctified not in the name of their priests but in the name of the gods about whom they hold empty opinions. Christ, however, has risen and lives. Therefore whoever is baptized by him is not baptized by a dead man, whether it is through a good minister or through a bad one who is dead in his depraved morals. For he is baptized by the one who lives for ever, and of whom it is said in the Gospel, as I also noted there: "He it is who baptizes in the Holy Spirit."

Judging by your words, you did not understand this in my letter. I would rather not say that you understood it poorly and meant to misrepresent it. But I am surprised that you did not notice the words that followed, or that you thought you should pass over them. A little later I added: "For if in this passage I take 'dead man' to mean a sinner who baptizes, the same absurdity will follow: anyone baptized even by a hidden ungodly man will have been washed in vain, as though baptized by a dead man. For it does not say, 'He who is baptized by a manifestly dead man,' but simply 'by a dead man.'" Whom would words of mine as plain as these not rouse from sleep, or rather from death itself? And yet they did not rouse you. What is more, you took what I had said against Petilian and, as though you were speaking against me, confirmed it even more forcefully. People often do this when they try to pull out an arrow that has struck them and, not knowing how, drive it in deeper. For you asserted that "dead man" must be understood only as a sinful baptizer, and that no sinner is to be excepted. And so what I was saying is concluded against you: where no one is excepted, the hidden sinner cannot be excepted either. Rebaptize, then, those who are found to have been baptized by hidden sinners, as many as are still alive and aware of it and can still be helped, so that the harm falls now only on those who either do not know or died earlier, and so could not be baptized once their wicked baptizers were later exposed. Baptize, I say, once an adulterer has been exposed and condemned, all those who are found to have been baptized by him while he was hidden. They were baptized by a dead man, for you said that every sinner without any exception must be understood as unable to baptize, and you added the testimony about the oil of the sinner. You said it, you wrote it: listen to yourself, read yourself. If every sinner is like a dead man and cannot baptize, neither can the hidden sinner. He is not alive just because he is hidden. Rather, he has been swallowed up far more deeply by the lie of his pretense. He would be less dead if he at least confessed. But in him is fulfilled what is written elsewhere: "From the dead, as from one who does not exist, confession perishes." Those who are known to have been baptized by this dead man, sunk in such depths of death, you do not rebaptize. Yet you do not hesitate to rebaptize, if you can, those baptized by people at the ends of the earth who have never heard the name of Caecilian or Majorinus or Donatus. You throw at them, "He who is baptized by a dead man, what does his washing profit him?" You call dead those whom not even a whiff of the African corpses, whoever they belonged to, could ever reach. Meanwhile you do not consider dead a man who is able to conceal his own crime, though Scripture cries out: "From the dead, as from one who does not exist, confession perishes." Is he then not dead because he is a pretender? Rather, it is precisely through his pretense that he lacks the spirit of life and has utterly expired, for Scripture says again: "For the holy spirit of discipline will flee from the deceitful." Go on defending these dead men and saying that they live, so that you may die a worse death through this very false defense.

"They are dead," you say, "but what was the person to do who came to them for baptism without knowing?" Then let him do something now, since the man has been exposed and he realizes that he was baptized by a dead man. If his conscience could not be harmed before because he did not know, it begins to be harmed now because he knows. Suppose someone unknowingly wore a tunic that had been stolen. From the moment he learns of it, that garment becomes a garment of iniquity, and he himself becomes unjust unless he throws it off. Or suppose someone unknowingly married another man's wife. From the moment he finds out, he becomes an adulterer unless he leaves her. So let this man also throw off the baptism he now knows he received from a dead man. For there is something he can do: he can still be baptized again. In the end, whether he knew it or not, he was baptized by a dead man, so what does his washing profit him? The sentence is strict, as you yourself loudly proclaim, and it excepts no one. He was baptized, I say, by a dead man, so his washing profits him nothing. You who are alive, cleanse the man by baptizing him! Or rather, cleanse yourselves of this error, so that you do not perish by holding such views. You argue, as though against me, that no one is excepted in what is written about "the oil of the sinner" and "he who is baptized by a dead man." You do not feel that by struggling you are only tightening the knot that binds you. This is exactly what I am doing, what I am pressing, and how I am driving you hard to change your empty and perverse opinion: in the oil of the sinner and the baptism of the dead man, no dead man and no sinner is excepted. You say this yourself, for me, though you think you are speaking against me. For in that case the hidden sinner is not excepted either, and everything you say is overturned. Your teachers would then be compelled to rebaptize everyone they could find in this life who had been baptized by hidden evil men.

What will you do? Where will you turn? Your own words are being read back to you. When I said this, not only did you fail to refute it, but you said the very same thing yourself in other words, as if it were your own, not realizing that what you were reading was mine. And so that it could be heard and considered more carefully, you put it in writing, where it can be read back to you as often as you like. So listen. These are certainly your words: "But if you choose to except only the worshiper of an idol, what about the one of whom it is said, 'I do not want the oil of the sinner to anoint my head'? Is the only sinner here the one who worships an idol, or is it anyone who does what is not lawful? If you think the sinner is only the worshiper of an idol, will a Christian not be said to have sinned if he does something against the law? Since nothing more foolish or absurd can be said, it was plainly foretold that not only the idol worshiper but any sinner whatever among all people must not claim for himself the right of baptism." These words I have inserted are certainly yours. I did not except the worshiper of an idol. What I said was that their gods themselves are dead, and that it profits nothing to be baptized by any of them, for these people seem to themselves to be baptized by the very gods in whose name they believe they are cleansed. You, on the other hand, excepted no sinner. If in this passage "dead man" is to be understood as a sinful mortal man who baptizes, then by excepting no sinner you undoubtedly did not except the hidden sinner either. "It was plainly foretold," you say, "that not only the idol worshiper but any sinner whatever among all people must not claim for himself the right of baptism." So listen to yourself. You said "any sinner whatever," and you excepted neither the manifest nor the hidden. With what face, then, do your people compel baptism after a manifest sinner, when they refuse it after a hidden one, while they assert that no one is excepted? Flee, then, brother, from an unsound interpretation to a sound one. In this testimony about the oil of the sinner, understand the smooth, soft words of a deceitful flatterer, as the earlier words of the same psalm direct. In that way no one will be excepted, and the hidden wicked baptizer will not drive you into an impossible corner. In the same way, with the other testimony, "He who is baptized by a dead man, what does his washing profit him?", either examine the ancient manuscripts carefully, especially the Greek ones, in case the words are written differently there and suggest another meaning in light of what comes before and after, or at any rate let us understand by "the dead," as I said, those in whose name the worshipers of idols are baptized. Then you will understand that each person is baptized by the one in whose name he believes he has been cleansed. In that way no one is excepted there either, for no dead god of the pagans can cleanse those who believe in him. But if in this passage you take "dead man" to mean every sinful man, so many consequences you do not want will follow that you will not be able to explain how you yourself are alive. For John says: "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us." You would find no one at all to baptize you if you chose to avoid every sinner.

And yet suppose you understood "dead man" to mean nothing but a heretic or schismatic, so that whoever is baptized among them is baptized by a dead man, of whom it is said, "He who is baptized by a dead man, what does his washing profit him?" You can see what headlong presumption it is to take it this way, as if it said, "He who is baptized by a heretic or schismatic." Even so, this would not be against us. We acknowledge that Christ's baptism profits a man nothing if he is baptized among heretics or schismatics and credits them with the baptism by which he is baptized. We say that it begins to profit him when he passes over to the body of Christ, which is the church of the living God. For then, under that same baptism, which was Christ's even outside but profited him nothing while he was outside, the cleansing will profit him. It comes not from the one by whose hands he was dipped, but from the one into whose members he has been grafted.

Nor will I fear that excessively severe sentence of yours in which you said that "any sinner whatever among all people must not claim for himself the right of baptism," except that you will find no one who can truthfully say in the Lord's Prayer, "Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors," without confessing that he is a sinner. I would like to question one by one those who baptize among you and ask whether they are entirely free of sin. Any one of them might answer me: "I am not a traitor, not an incense-offerer, not an adulterer, not a murderer, not a worshiper of idols, and finally not a heretic or a schismatic." But whether anyone can be found, even with heretical pride, who would dare to say or dare to think "I am not a sinner," I do not know. I do not know whether anyone is so blinded by swollen arrogance as to think, I will not say profess aloud, but silently within himself, that he has no need of the petition in which we say to God, "Forgive us our debts." For we do not ask for the forgiveness of those debts which we trust were forgiven once for all in baptism, but certainly for those without which human frailty does not exist, however watchful we may be in keeping the Lord's commandments. Finally, let anyone who wishes put on this shameless face and say: "I am not a sinner. Since everything was forgiven me in baptism, no sin can be found in me." I believe John rather than him, and I answer with much greater confidence: "You deceive yourself, and the truth is not in you." This rash and false claim does not make it so that no sins are found in you; it only makes it so that the sins that are found are not forgiven. So if you have already been baptized, I would like to know whom you found who would say against the apostle John, "I have no sin." For if you were able to find such a person, how could you have been baptized by one who was deceiving himself and in whom the truth was not? But if he did not forget humility, of whatever sort, and called himself a sinner, how could he claim for himself the right of baptism according to your sentence? For you said, and you were not at all afraid to write, that "any sinner whatever among all people must not claim for himself the right of baptism." If, however, you have not yet been baptized, either correct this utterly empty sentence or go and look for angels to baptize you.

But let us suppose that, having been refuted, you corrected it to read: "Whoever among all people is a sinner by the crime that our side alleges must not claim for himself the right of baptism." Not even this is against us. If such a man does claim it and gives baptism, I say that he ought not to have claimed it for himself, but I do not say that he has not given it. And if the one who received it was a good man receiving from a bad one, a faithful man from a faithless one, a godly man from an ungodly one, it will be ruinous to the giver, not to the receiver. For that holy thing judges the one who uses it badly and sanctifies the one who uses it well. And if the receiver also received it wrongly, even so the sacrament is not cut away but acknowledged. What harmed him while he was perverse will profit him once he is corrected.

So I will take you to have said, no longer "any sinner whatever," since unless I am mistaken you now see how rashly that was said, but rather: "A sinner of the kind our side describes, whoever among all people he may be, must not claim for himself the right of baptism." As it is written: "But to the sinner God says: Why do you recite my statutes and take my covenant in your mouth?" And to show what kind of sinner he was speaking to, so that all people who dare neither to think nor to say that they are not sinners would not hold back from preaching his word, he goes on to describe him: "But you hated discipline and cast my words behind you. Your mouth abounded in malice, and your tongue embraced deceit. If you saw a thief, you ran with him, and you threw in your lot with adulterers. You sat and spoke against your brother, and you laid a stumbling block before your mother's son." It is to such a sinner, then, that he says, "Why do you recite my statutes and take my covenant in your mouth?", as if to say: "You do this in vain. As far as you are concerned, it does you no good. It will count toward your judgment and condemnation, not toward the reward of salvation." And yet, even when such a sinner recites God's statutes and takes his covenant in his mouth, if those who hear it from his mouth believe and act and make progress, will they not be praised while he is rejected, justified while he is blamed, crowned while he is condemned? For they took care to obey the Lord, who says: "Do what they say, but do not do what they do. For they speak and do not act." So if this sinner claims for himself the right to preach the divine covenant, it does him no good, but it does good to those who hear and act, and what does them good is not he but what he preaches. In the same way, the one who ought not to have claimed for himself the right of baptism harms himself, because he wrongly claimed a good thing, but he does not harm the one who rightly received that good thing.

You see, then, not only that you could not refute what I said against Petilian, but also with how much light of truth, and in every way, what you yourself said against me is refuted. And still you go on to say that we do not make our case sound, and that we in some way confess ourselves sinners, because when we are asked by what license we claim the right of baptism, we do not argue from the merit of our actions or the innocence of our lives but say that it is lawful for anyone. Notice at least from what has been said that we do not say it is lawful for anyone. We say that the one who handles a holy thing unlawfully deserves punishment and must be corrected, and that the holy thing he handles unlawfully must not be unlawfully cut away. Just so, we want people who use the law unlawfully to be corrected, but we do not count the law itself void. Just so, we rebuke the one who unlawfully takes God's covenant in his mouth, but we do not deny or tear up the covenant itself. Nor do we confess that we have sinned because, even in a sinner, we disapprove what is his own and honor what is God's. We do not want a person who believes in God to depend on what is hidden in human beings. Instead we urge him to glory in the Lord, of whom he is certain. The apostle did not distrust his conscience as though it were evil either. He simply did not want the hope of believers to be placed in man, and he set it firmly in God when he said: "Neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but only God who gives the growth." So when we say what is written, "Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory," we are not accusing our own conscience. It is you, who want the hope of the baptized to rest on the conduct of human beings, who fail to recognize your own pride.

And what of this: you even dare to mention the blessed Cyprian, as if he, so great a defender of catholic unity and peace, were the author of your division? First be in the Church which Cyprian is known to have held and preached, and then dare to name Cyprian as the author of your opinion. First imitate the piety and humility of Cyprian, and then bring forward the council of Cyprian. For we do Cyprian no wrong when we distinguish any of his writings from the canonical authority of the divine Scriptures. It was not without reason that the Church's canon was established with such wholesome vigilance. To it belong the definite books of the prophets and apostles, which we do not dare to judge at all, and by which we freely judge all other writings, whether of believers or of unbelievers. Accordingly, the apostle, whose epistles stand in canonical authority, says: "Let those of us who are perfect be of this mind; and if in anything you think otherwise, God will reveal that also to you." So for as long as Cyprian thought otherwise (if indeed the writings you think should be brought forward on your behalf are really his), for as long, that is, as he thought otherwise on this matter than the truth, more carefully considered, has made plain, until God should reveal this also to him, he did not abandon catholic unity and peace, even with those colleagues from whom he differed. For this his charity deserves praise beyond words.

You have inserted into your letter his words from the letter to Jubaianus, to show that he held that those who had been baptized in heresy or schism should be baptized in the Catholic Church. I am not bound by the authority of this letter, because I do not hold the writings of Cyprian as canonical. Rather, I weigh them by the canonical writings. Whatever in them agrees with the authority of the divine Scriptures I accept, and I praise him for it. Whatever does not agree I reject, with all respect to him. And so, if you were reciting the words you quoted from his letter to Jubaianus from some canonical book of the apostles or prophets, I would have no grounds whatever to contradict them. But as it is, what you recite is not canonical. So, with the freedom to which the Lord has called us, I do not accept this point on which that man thought otherwise. I cannot attain to his praise. I do not compare my writings with his many letters. I love his genius, I delight in his eloquence, I marvel at his charity, I revere his martyrdom. Yet I do not accept, I say, what the blessed Cyprian held about baptizing heretics and schismatics, because the Church for which the blessed Cyprian shed his blood does not accept it. But you say that he established proofs from the Law in support of this opinion. In fact he could not establish proofs from the Law. Rather, it was by them that he himself established whatever he rightly held. So leave aside the writings of Cyprian and cite those very proofs from the Law which you say he used. If I do not show that they do nothing to help your cause, you have won. Therefore, though I am incomparably inferior to Cyprian, I do not accept this view of his, just as, though I am incomparably inferior to Peter, I neither accept nor follow what the apostle Peter did when he compelled the Gentiles to live like Jews. You, however, set the writings of Cyprian against us as if they were pillars of canonical authority. So whatever we can bring forward from Cyprian against you, you must yield to it, and it is right that, once defeated, you should fall silent and at last turn from the error of a most ruinous dissension to catholic unity.

So, not to be long, notice what I bring forward from this very letter to Jubaianus, something that overturns and destroys your error. Whether it was the holy Cyprian or whoever else wrote that letter, he was trying to persuade his readers that heretics coming to the Church ought to be baptized, on the grounds that no baptism they had received outside, among heretics, should be counted as baptism. He then raised an objection against himself and said: "But someone will say: What then will become of those who in the past came from heresy to the Church and were admitted without baptism? The Lord is able in his mercy to grant pardon, and not to cut off from the gifts of his Church those who, having been simply admitted to the Church, have fallen asleep in the Church." This simplicity is enough for us, and Cyprian himself bears witness to it. He understood the unity of the body of Christ to be so great a good that he piously presumed that even those whom he believed to be without baptism, once simply admitted into that unity, would obtain pardon from God's mercy and not be cut off from the Church's gifts. This was the custom of the Church before Cyprian's council, and not even Cyprian's council could overcome and abolish it. Those coming from heresy were admitted, not indeed "without baptism," as he puts it, since that same baptism was present in them even outside, though it did them no good, but "simply," as he also puts it. And so they obtained pardon from God's mercy and were not cut off from the Church's gifts. This simplicity, rather than a doubling of baptism, pleased the whole Church spread throughout the world.

Hear what kind of testimony Cyprian himself bears to this Church, in the letter he wrote on unity: "Tear a ray of the sun from its body: the unity of light does not admit of division. Break a branch from the tree: once broken, it cannot sprout. Cut off a stream from its spring: once cut off, it dries up." In these words of Cyprian we do not find or understand that light does not admit of division except in the saints predestined to the kingdom of God, who cannot in any way be divided from the Church. We take the broken branch's failure to sprout to mean that it bears no shoot of eternal salvation. And we recognize the drying up of the stream cut off from its spring in this: those who are separated from unity are emptied of the Holy Spirit. It does not refer to the sacrament of baptism, which both the good and the wicked can have, the wicked being separated from the holiness of the Church, openly when they are outside, hiddenly when they are inside. But note in the words he adds what Cyprian thought about the fruitfulness of the Church itself, spread throughout the whole world, a matter no one doubts: "So also the Church of the Lord, flooded with light, sends forth her rays through the whole world; yet it is one light that is spread everywhere, and the unity of the body is not divided. She stretches her branches over the whole earth in abundant fruitfulness; she spreads her generously flowing streams far and wide; yet there is one head and one source, and one mother, rich in the increase of her fruitfulness." This is the Church that Cyprian loved, held fast and commended, the Church promised in the holy Scriptures and fulfilled throughout the whole world. Lost schismatics and heretics have abandoned her in impious revolts, as though they wished to distinguish and separate themselves from the wicked. So that they might not try to wash away their impious departures with empty excuses, holy Scripture foretold: "A wicked son calls himself righteous, but does not wash away his going out." For the good, who are truly within, must not be deserted because of the wicked, who only seem to be within.

Learn what the blessed Cyprian thought on this point from the letter he wrote to the presbyter Maximus and the others, in which he congratulates them on returning to the Church from the error of schism and heresy: "For although there seem to be tares in the Church, our faith and charity ought not to be hindered by this, so that, because we see tares in the Church, we ourselves should withdraw from the Church. We must only labor to be wheat, so that when the wheat begins to be stored in the Lord's barns, we may receive the fruit of our work and labor. The apostle says in his epistle: 'In a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and of earthenware, some for honor and some for dishonor.' Let us take pains and labor as much as we can to be vessels of gold and silver. But to break the earthenware vessels is granted to the Lord alone, to whom a rod of iron has also been given. The servant cannot be greater than his master, nor can anyone claim for himself what the Father has given to the Son alone, so as to think that he can already carry the shovel or winnowing fan to winnow and clean the threshing floor, or separate all the tares from the wheat by human judgment. That is proud obstinacy and sacrilegious presumption, which a depraved frenzy takes upon itself. And while some are always taking upon themselves more than gentle justice requires, they perish from the Church; and while they insolently exalt themselves, they are blinded by their own swelling pride and lose the light of truth." You see, brother, that in accordance with the divine Scriptures Cyprian taught that the Church must not be deserted even because of the wicked, as the wheat must not be deserted because of the chaff or the tares, nor the great house because of the vessels for dishonor. Spiritually the wicked are separated from the good by their life and conduct, yet bodily they seem to be mixed with them in the Church until the day of judgment, when they will be separated bodily as well, for the punishment they deserve. You see, you hear, you perceive, you grasp, you understand what a crime it is for you to separate yourselves from the Church spread throughout the world, because of people who displease you, whether rightly or through your own mistake. And it is to this Church that Cyprian, following the divine Scriptures, bears such great, firm, clear and splendid testimony.

Therefore pay close attention to my brief argument on this whole question. Suppose those coming from the heretics are rightly received into the Church, in such a way that their own error is corrected but the divine sacrament is not undone. Then we rejoice over those who live well there, as the Lord's wheat. Suppose, on the other hand, that they do not have baptism, as you think and as you boast that Cyprian agrees with you. Then certainly, according to that same Cyprian, once they are simply admitted to the Church they obtain God's pardon because of the merit of unity itself, and they are not cut off from the Church's gifts. And all who, following the earlier custom about which Cyprian did not keep silent, simply admit them and live rightly and peaceably are counted among the same wheat destined for the barn. But those who either knowingly fight contentiously against the truth in the matter of receiving them, or live by depraved and perverse ways, are tolerated among the tares and chaff destined for the fire. Yet God commands, and Cyprian is witness, that the Church must not be deserted because of them. That Church is spreading through the whole world with abundant increase: it is the Lord's wheat, which grows together until the harvest, or is threshed together until the winnowing. So then, if the wicked defile the good through sharing in the sacraments, then in Cyprian's time or before Cyprian, when heretics were received without baptism, as you think, the Church perished. Say so, and show where you were born from! But if, as the truth teaches through Cyprian as well, the wheat is not defiled when even known tares are tolerated for the sake of the Church's peace, then "a wicked son calls himself righteous, but does not wash away his going out," because he ought not to have gone out from the Church on account of the wicked.

I say it again: look, I will not let you evade this utterly unanswerable argument. Suppose that the wicked destroy the good, who do not share in their sins, merely by sharing the sacraments with them. Then those who in the past came from heresy to the Church and were admitted without baptism certainly destroyed the good by their contagion. In that case, already at that time there was no Church for Cyprian to hold and preach, and none for Donatus to go out from later. But if that contagion did not destroy the good, then neither could the contagion of those whom you accuse destroy the Christian world. Stop slandering us in your separation, and return to the Church corrected. You must accuse Caecilian and his associates, against whom Secundus of Tigisis at that time gathered and held a council; I do not need to defend them. Accuse them with all the strength you have. If they were innocent, your windy blasts will do them no harm, for they are wheat. If they were guilty, the wheat ought not to have been deserted because of those tares, since they did the wheat no harm. Accuse as much as you can. I win if you do not prove it, and I win if you do. I win, I say, if you do not prove it, with you yourself as judge; I win if you do prove it, with Cyprian as witness. What do you want them to have been? If they were innocent, why do you, who are tares, slander the Lord's wheat? If they were guilty, why do you separate yourselves from the Lord's wheat because of tares? The Church stands visible and plain to all, for she is the city set on a mountain that cannot be hidden. Through her Christ rules from sea to sea and from the river to the ends of the earth, as through the seed of Abraham, multiplied like the stars of heaven and like the sand of the sea, in which all nations are blessed. The blessed Cyprian too commends her, saying that, flooded with the Lord's light, she sends forth her rays through the whole world and stretches her branches over all the earth in abundant fruitfulness. Either she should not have been accused in her wheat, or she should not have been deserted because of the tares. The first you can answer for yourselves; the second, learn from Cyprian's warnings. For these are his words, as he testifies: "For although there seem to be tares in the Church, our faith and charity ought not to be hindered by this, so that, because we see tares in the Church, we ourselves should withdraw from the Church."

You say that through the contagion of wicked Africans the Church has perished from the whole world, and that her remnants survive in the party of Donatus, as wheat separated from the tares and chaff. In this you plainly contradict Cyprian, who says that the good do not perish in the Church through being mixed with the wicked, and that these wicked cannot be separated from the good they are mixed with before the time of God's judgment. So, by your error, or rather your madness, you are forced to accuse not only Caecilian and those who ordained him but also the churches we read of in the apostolic and canonical Scriptures. You must accuse not only the church of the Romans, where you are accustomed to send a bishop ordained in Africa for your few followers there, but also the churches of the Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Thessalonians, Colossians and Philippians, to which the apostle Paul plainly writes. You must accuse the church of Jerusalem, which the apostle James first governed as its bishop, and that of Antioch, where the disciples were first called Christians. You must accuse the churches of Smyrna, Thyatira, Sardis, Pergamum, Philadelphia and Laodicea, to which the Apocalypse of the apostle John is addressed, and so many other churches of Pontus, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia, to which the apostle Peter writes, and all the rest that Paul testifies he filled with the gospel from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum. I say nothing of the other vast and immense regions of the earth into which the Church, reaching out from these apostolic labors and plantings, has grown and is still growing. Certainly you are forced to accuse these churches, which I have named from the divine and canonical writings, situated so far from Africa, as though they had perished through the sins of Africans. And all this rather than correct the error that drives you to so great a crime through your wicked dissension.

We, however, in order to refute this error of yours more easily, are not obliged to defend even those Africans whose false crimes you dare to pour out over the other nations too. We are not obliged, I say, to defend them. For if they were innocent, they share the kingdom with those churches overseas. But if they were guilty, then, like tares among the wheat, they could do no harm even in Africa to those who refused to separate themselves from the unity of the Church because of them, even when they knew them. Let me pass over how many believed them innocent, because their crime, if there was any, still could not be proved to them; and surely not even you can say that these could be defiled by the sins of others that they did not know about. Let me pass over these, I say. Consider instead those who knew or thought them guilty, though they were themselves settled in the African churches. They saw that the guilt of these men could not be established before the churches overseas, and that their crimes could not be proved to the members of the Church spread far and wide. Suppose they had wished, as if for fear of a deadly contagion, to separate themselves from the communion of so many nations, to whom they could not show that those men were wicked, because of men whom they knew to be wicked. Then it would not be I, nor you, nor Donatus, nor Caecilian who held them back, but the very man you dared to name, Cyprian. He would say to them the words he wrote to Maximus:

"Although there seem to be tares in the Church, our faith and charity ought not to be hindered by this, so that, because we see tares in the Church, we ourselves should withdraw from the Church. We must only labor to be wheat, so that when the wheat begins to be stored in the Lord's barns, we may receive the fruit of our work and labor. The apostle says in his epistle: 'In a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and of earthenware, some for honor and some for dishonor.' Let us take pains and labor as much as we can to be vessels of gold and silver. But to break the earthenware vessels is granted to the Lord alone, to whom a rod of iron has also been given. The servant cannot be greater than his master, nor can anyone claim for himself what the Father has given to the Son alone, so as to think that he can already carry the shovel or winnowing fan to winnow and clean the threshing floor, or separate all the tares from the wheat by human judgment. That is proud obstinacy and sacrilegious presumption, which a depraved frenzy takes upon itself. And while some are always taking upon themselves more than gentle justice requires, they perish from the Church; and while they insolently exalt themselves, they are blinded by their own swelling pride and lose the light of truth." By these words of Cyprian those who fear God would be held in the Church, even if they wished to separate from it because of wicked men they knew. By these same words you stand condemned, who have separated and accuse even the good. By these words Cyprian holds us too in the house of God, whose beauty he loved, so that we should not desert it because of the vessels made for dishonor. And this would hold even if we could know of traitors whom you had accused and proved guilty, which you have never been able to do, or of any other wicked people. By these words may that man of peace also bring you, corrected, into catholic peace. Then you will no longer take offense at any sins of others, whether real or false, and hurl such great evils against the Church of Christ, which, according to the Scriptures, is bearing fruit and growing in the whole world. Then you will not accuse the wheat because of the tares, nor desert the grain because of the chaff, nor remain outside the great house because of the vessels for dishonor.

See how much the blessed Cyprian, whom you cited, has helped us. If he thought otherwise about repeating baptism, the Lord no doubt revealed to him what needed correcting, in return for the great merits of his most ardent charity. For he remained in the vine as a branch so rich in the fruit of peace and love that, if anything in him was found that needed pruning, it would have been pruned by the knife of martyrdom, if by nothing else. These things could be more than enough to refute your error and, if you are willing, to correct it. Still, so that no one may think you put anything in your letter that I was unable to refute, or anything about which I could not show that you made no adequate reply to our writings against Petilian, let us examine the rest in the next book.
BOOK THREE

In my two previous volumes, brother Cresconius, I have answered the whole case set out in your letter, and in so many ways that even the points still left in it have already been refuted and disposed of. If I did not have to take care of slower minds, which cannot grasp this, I ought by now to have brought this work to an end. But there are many whom it is right for us to serve, and they do not think everything has been dealt with unless each point is also taken up in its proper place. So I shall briefly go through the rest of what you said, in order, and refute it.
