You thought fit to insert material from the letters of the venerable martyr Cyprian and of certain Eastern bishops, to show that they decided to reject the sacrament of baptism given among heretics and schismatics. None of this harms our case, provided we hold to the Church which Cyprian did not abandon, even when many of his colleagues refused to agree with this opinion. For in that very council he said: "judging no one, and removing no one from the right of communion if he should think differently." And he ended his letter to Jubaianus like this:

"This is our answer to you, dearest brother, according to our modest ability. We lay down no rule for anyone and pass no judgment in advance to prevent any bishop from doing what he thinks right, since he has free power of his own judgment," and so on. In the meantime, then, count us among those whom Cyprian could not persuade of that view, yet from whom he did not in the least cut off his communion, even though they thought differently on this matter. Your forebears, on the other hand, acted against Cyprian. You have yourself testified that they separated from communion with the Eastern bishops because those bishops withdrew their decision, by which they had resolved that Cyprian and that African council should be followed on this question of baptism. They ought instead to have kept the unity of communion with their colleagues, even though they thought differently on this question, as we read in his letters that Cyprian did. Your people therefore reply that Cyprian chose to speak this way so that his colleagues would not be frightened by fear of excommunication from daring to say freely what they thought, and not because he meant to remain in communion with them if they had thought differently. In saying this they openly declare that Cyprian lied. The written proceedings of the council show that he said: "judging no one, and removing no one from the right of communion if he should think differently." If he said this, and yet would not have shared the sacraments of Christ with any of his hearers who showed that he thought differently, then without doubt he was lying. He was making such promises deceitfully, not truthfully, and what is worse in that lie, he was deceiving the simplicity of his brothers with a double heart, especially since what was said was being written down. For if anyone had disagreed with that council, how could they condemn or excommunicate him by word of mouth when he could read out the opening of that same council in his own defence? So which of us thinks more tolerably of Cyprian? We say that, as a man, he could be mistaken on an obscure question about baptism. You say that, as a bishop, he chose to deceive in promising Christian communion, and deceived not just one of his brothers but the whole fellowship of bishops. But if you too think it wicked to believe this of him, then your forebears acted against his judgment when they cut themselves off from communion with the Eastern bishops because these had come to think differently on this matter.

Suppose, then, we must after all believe that fifty Eastern bishops held the same view as seventy Africans, or even somewhat more, against so many thousands of bishops throughout the world who rejected this error. Why should we not rather say that even those few Easterners corrected their decision, and not, as you put it, withdrew it? Just as it is praiseworthy not to be moved from a true opinion, so it is blameworthy to persist in a false one. The first praise is never to hold a false opinion, and the second is to change it, so that either the truth remains from the beginning, or the false opinion is changed and the truth takes its place. Nor is it relevant to our present question what we should think of the fact that the greatest part of the Christian world came to agree with the Easterners. For if what we hold and practise about baptism is true, and is to be held and kept, then we charge you with two faults of your own: first, that you are mistaken on the question of baptism; second, that you separate yourselves from those who think rightly on this matter. But if, to speak on your terms, the truth on that question is what you yourselves think, then you are certainly stained with the crime of having left the Church. For the sake of its peace you ought to have borne with those who thought differently, as Cyprian both did and urged.

Then you cry out that I have said: "Make no distinction between the faithful and the faithless; let the godly and the ungodly seem the same to you." I did not say that. What I certainly did say, and what you chose to cry out against as though I had said the other, is this: "whether someone receives the sacrament from a faithful or a faithless minister." In that statement I did not erase every distinction between the faithful and the faithless, nor did I tell anyone to regard the godly and the ungodly as the same. I said that the godly and the ungodly can have the same sacrament. You do not deny this yourself, since you grant that at least those baptized by ungodly men who are hidden are not to be baptized again. So you have no grounds for adding: "It is no use living a good life, since whatever is permitted to the righteous the unrighteous can also perform." This is false, and I never said it. Good conduct distinguishes the life of the good from that of the wicked and leads them to different ends. Nor can the unrighteous perform whatever is permitted to the righteous, for the righteous fulfil the law of Christ through love, and the unrighteous have no part in that. Yet the unrighteous can perform something that the righteous also perform: they too can baptize, certainly at least while they are hidden, if in no other case. In the same way they can preach God's commandments as the righteous do, but they cannot live by them as the righteous do. Of such people it was said: "Do what they say, but do not do what they do."

But suppose an unrighteous man who is not hidden, and is known to some good people, cannot be separated from the Church because of some sedition or faction. Listen to Cyprian: bear with the weeds, and be the wheat. How fine you thought these words of yours sounded, which you repeated in varied forms on a single point: "What could be said that is more unjust [?] than this rule: that the stained should purify another, the filthy wash, the unclean cleanse, the unbeliever give faith, the criminal make innocent?" I answer briefly. Christ is not stained, or filthy, or unclean, or an unbeliever, or a criminal. He loved the Church and gave himself up for her, cleansing her by the washing of water with the word, and he makes us secure in his own good things, so that we are not corrupted by the evils of others. For look: when a wicked minister is hidden, you do not set aside the baptism he gave. Can all these words of yours not be turned back on you? Here too the stained purifies, the filthy washes, the unclean cleanses, the unbeliever gives faith, and the criminal makes innocent. "No," you say, "he does not do it himself; his good reputation does it, empty and false though it is." Do you not want me to cry out at this: "O crime, O monstrous thing," which should not merely be "banished to the ends of the earth," as someone said, but rather driven out beyond all heaven and all lands, if that were possible? I do not mean you, whom I want to see corrected, but this error, from which I long for you to be corrected. Is it really true that to cleanse a person, when a minister lacks a truly good life, the false reputation of a bad minister is enough to do what a good life would have done? Does falsehood serve God as his minister for the sanctifying of a person when the minister's wickedness is hidden? All this is so that you need not say what we say: "whether someone receives the sacrament from a faithful or a faithless minister, only God sanctifies."

Next you quote words of mine, where I said: "Let Christ always give faith; let Christ be the origin of the Christian; let the Christian fix his root in Christ; let Christ be the head of the Christian." I certainly said it, and I say it still, and you could not answer it at all. Indeed you seem to have given way, so to speak, under the great weight of the truth, since you added: "This is what we urge too; this is what we want."

Then you again put forward a man in whom the person about to receive baptism is to place his hope. "But we ask," you say, "through whom this is better done." And since we too do not say that a person can be baptized without a minister, you ask me whether it is better for the minister to be unrighteous or righteous. My answer is that it is better for the minister to be righteous for this reason: human weakness finds what God commands hard and difficult without an example, and by imitating a good minister it may more easily be raised up to a good life. That is why the apostle Paul says: "Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ." But suppose that, for baptizing and sanctifying a person, what is received is better in proportion as the one who hands it on is better. Then baptisms would differ among those who receive them as much as the merits of ministers differ. For if Paul was better than Apollos, as everyone believes without dispute, then by this empty and perverse opinion of yours he gave a better baptism. And if he gave a better baptism, he surely begrudged it to those whom he was glad he had not baptized himself. Further, if among good ministers, where one is better than another, the baptism given through the better one is not better, then the baptism given even through a bad one is in no way bad, since it is the same baptism that is given. And so the gift of God is equal through ministers who are unequal, because it is not theirs but his.

So it is not true, as you vainly complain, that we make no distinction between the faithful and the faithless. We distinguish the merits of human beings, not the divine sacraments. Even you, compelled by the force of truth and forgetting your heretical quarrelling, said that these sacraments are not different for you [?] and for us, but one and the same.

How can you say, "We too urge and desire this: that Christ always gives faith, that Christ is the origin of the Christian, that the Christian fixes his root in Christ, that Christ is the head of the Christian," when you defend Petilian's letter? There, in commending the merit of the one who baptizes and trying to show, in the cause he had taken up, how much human righteousness counts in giving baptism, he says quite plainly: "It is the conscience of the one who gives in holiness that is looked to, to cleanse that of the one who receives. For whoever knowingly receives faith from the faithless receives not faith but guilt." And as if someone had asked him, "How do you prove this?", he went on to add: "For everything consists by its origin and root, and if a thing has no head, it is nothing." Why, I beg you, since you have fallen into defending a reckless falsehood, do you try to pour fog over things that are plain? The man says openly that the origin, root and head of someone to be regenerated through baptism can only be the one by whose ministry he is baptized. And you say, "We too want Christ to be the origin and root and head of the Christian, but we ask through whom this is better done." What you say is one thing; what Petilian said is another. What you say, even if it is true, is not what he said.

So if you too want Christ to be the origin and root and head of the Christian, resist Petilian, not me, since neither the one who plants is anything nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth. When I had set this down from the apostle in my letter, you chose to reply by saying: "It is indeed God's to give the growth, but just as only a faithful and diligent farmer is sought for planting and watering, so too in the sacrament of baptism only a faithful and thoroughly righteous worker is employed." As if what an unfaithful farmer has planted would not sprout because of his unfaithfulness! The power of the seed, the fertility of the earth and the mildness of the sky have received from God such efficacy that, to bring forth fruit, they wait only for a worker to plant or water. They do not care with what mind he works or with what intention he labors, whether he faithfully loves the owner of the field or seeks his own profit and not his master's. You also add a testimony from the prophet, saying: "I will give you shepherds after my own heart, and they will feed you, feeding you with discipline." I know it has been fulfilled. Such were the apostles, and such men are not lacking even now, though they are very few compared with the breadth of the church. But you ought to have sought out, read and pondered what is also said through the prophet Ezekiel against bad shepherds. For there he says: I will feed them, not the shepherds.

So whether he dispenses his word and sacrament through good shepherds or through bad ones, it is he who feeds, since he says of himself: that there may be one flock and one shepherd. For it is good to trust in the Lord rather than to trust in man, and: Cursed is everyone who puts his hope in man. You show that you understand what I cited in that letter in such a way that you say you look all the harder for a righteous and faithful man through whom this sacrament may be celebrated, precisely because your hope and trust are in God, not in man, and because faith and righteousness, which you always look for in his ministers, belong to God. In this you speak the truth, since of all good things we have nothing that we have not received, and so faith and righteousness come to us from God. But when you say that God cannot give you this unless the man by whom you are baptized has it, you plainly put your hope in a man, and you do not know whether he shares in righteousness. And if he does not, you then look to his reputation, and when you have found a false good reputation attached to a bad man who is hidden, you believe that it is enough for your sanctification. I beg you: if your trust is in God, not in man, and you therefore look all the harder for a righteous, good and faithful man through whom this sacrament may be celebrated because faith and righteousness belong to God, does the falseness of a reputation also belong to God? Yet you say that if a bad minister has a good reputation, that false reputation is enough for your sanctification. I would rather you trusted in a man, which I was most vehemently forbidding you to do, than in the falseness of his reputation. For a man, whatever he may be, is God's creature insofar as he is a man, but no falsehood is God's creature. Further, if cursed is the one who puts his hope in man, how much more the one who puts his hope in the falseness of human opinion, so that he falls into that other thing which is written: Whoever trusts in falsehoods feeds the winds, that is, he becomes food for evil spirits!

"If baptism given by anyone and in any manner," you say, "ought not to be undone, why did the apostles baptize after John?" How much more forcefully the question can be put this way: "If the apostles baptized after John, why does someone better or equal not baptize after any holy man you like?" From this, at least, you might be forced to understand that John's baptism has no bearing on this question! "And to the Jews," you say, "who had been baptized by Moses, Peter said: Repent, and let each of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ." If the Jews were already baptized because Moses had baptized their ancestors through the Red Sea so long before, then those born today of baptized Christians are baptized for no reason. And yet you say these things and write these things, and you are heard and read and thought to be answering our letter, as though being able to answer were the same thing as being unwilling to keep quiet.

Nor, at the beginning of this letter, did you refute, as you think you did, what you decided to pass over, namely what I said: "If those who wanted to belong to Paul were in error, what hope, pray, is there for those who chose to belong to Donatus?" For who does not see that this division arose from this very thing, and persists in this plague to this day for the same reason: hope is placed in a man's righteousness, so that the baptism of Christ is acceptable only if a person is dipped by a righteous man? Against this error, and against those who had already begun to make schisms over the differing merits of men, Paul himself cries out: I thank God that I baptized none of you, lest anyone should say that I baptized in my own name. What else is he suggesting except that the baptism of Christ belongs only to him in whose name it is given? It is therefore not made better when given by a better man, nor worse when given by a worse.

It is in vain, then, that you go on to exult and say: "It follows that I conclude that everything written in the sermon of the holy Petilian, or whoever's it is, was rightly said." For the very words you conclude were rightly said prove that they were not, since the conscience of the one who gives in holiness is not looked to so as to cleanse that of the receiver when the giver's stained conscience is hidden. Defeated at that point, when you ought to have yielded to the truth, you appealed to the man's false reputation, as to an unhappy judge deceived by a lie. But the conscience is not being looked to when it is the reputation that is looked to; and no one can be cleansed by anyone's false reputation any more than by his bad life. No one receives the Christian faith from a man, whether faithless or faithful, but from him of whom it is written: cleansing their hearts by faith. If someone hears from a faithful man what he is to believe, he imitates him, but he is not justified by him. For if the minister justifies the ungodly, it follows that it would be right to believe in the minister as well; for the apostle's statement is clear and certain: To the one who believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is reckoned as righteousness. So if the minister does not dare to say, "Believe in me," let him not dare to say, "You are justified by me."

Now as for what follows, "Everything consists by its origin and root, and if a thing has no head, it is nothing": if the origin, root and head of the baptized person is the minister who baptizes him, it is not Christ; if it is Christ, it is not the minister. Further, when the minister is secretly bad, what is the origin, what is the root, what is the head of the baptized? His false reputation? Cresconius says so, but the truth says otherwise. So if in that case the origin, root and head is Christ, he is so also when the minister is good. Otherwise, and this would be utterly absurd, a person baptized by a hidden bad man would be better off, having Christ as his head, than a person baptized by a manifestly good man, if in that case the minister is the head. I would say the same about the good seed, for there follows: "Nor does anything regenerate well unless it is regenerated by good seed."

Then you quote what follows in Petilian's letter, where he says: "Since these things are so, brothers, what perversity can it be that one who is guilty of his own crimes should make another innocent, since it is written: A good tree bears good fruit, and a bad tree bears bad fruit. Do they gather grapes from thorns? And again: Every good man brings forth good things from the treasure of his heart, and the evil man brings forth evil things from the treasure of his heart." These words show quite plainly that Petilian applied all of this only to the man through whom baptism is administered. He is to be understood as making innocent the one he baptizes, if he himself is innocent; he himself is the good tree whose fruit is the person baptized; he himself is the good man from the treasure of whose heart the sanctification of the baptized proceeds. So when this man is secretly bad, tell me, by whom is the other made innocent? Tell me, whose tree's fruit will he be? Tell me, from the treasure of whose heart will the baptized be sanctified? Or if in that case he deserves to have as the author of his innocence, as the tree from which good fruit springs, not the human minister of baptism but Christ, then he was luckier to fall in with a hidden bad minister than if he had fallen in with a manifestly good one. If that is a most absurd and insane thing to say, then whoever is sanctified by Christ's baptism is Christ's fruit, whatever minister's work he is baptized by. Unless, perhaps, he is to fall back on your advice when he runs into a minister with a stained and hidden conscience, so that you may show him, as the tree from which he is born, the falsely good reputation of a bad man. If you look for the root of that, you will find the cunning of a deceiver; and if good fruit can be born from that, God forbid, then Christ lied when he said: A bad tree cannot bear good fruit. But since Christ spoke the truth, let the good man, as a good tree, have good fruit, a good work, just as the bad man, as a bad tree, has bad fruit, a bad work. But let the one who is baptized be born not of any man but of the Spirit of Christ, if he wants to be a fruit that is not spoiled by the wind and a tree that is not uprooted. Since this is so, when you said, "Therefore it follows that I conclude that everything written in the sermon of the holy Petilian, or whoever's it is, was rightly said," I think that I, rather, conclude that none of it was rightly said.

Let us now see what you then wove into your letter: how your people taught you the case of Optatus and of the Maximianists, or rather, so that I may become more learned from you, the "Maximianensians." As for Optatus, about whom I can cite nothing in writing, I readily concede whatever you think. One thing I know: if the things that were, I will not say proved, but certainly said about him were true, then he was neither good himself nor had a good reputation. So whoever was baptized through him could be cleansed neither by his conscience, as Petilian would have it, nor by his reputation, as you would. But if envious rumor, as so often happens, spread false accusations about him, see how rightly we refuse to believe readily what you have never been able to prove to us about the traditors you accuse, since rumor is accustomed to lie even about good men. So if it is not their innocence, nor indeed, what is true and firm, God's grace and our own conscience that make our baptism valid for us, let your own judgment at least do so.

For when you spoke of Optatus, you said: "For my part, I neither acquit nor condemn Optatus." Suppose I, or rather not only I but the whole Catholic church of Africa, and still more the church overseas, spread so far and wide, were to say of Caecilian and those who ordained him: "I neither acquit nor condemn them." Do you think that would be too little for those whom they had baptized, none of whom ever saw Caecilian, when you believe it is enough in the case of Optatus for those whom he baptized with his own hands? Or is it because you cite a council of your forefathers concerning Caecilian, while we cite none concerning Optatus, that you think none of us may say, "I neither acquit nor condemn Caecilian," as you were permitted to say of Optatus? But a later judgment was held overseas in Caecilian's favor, and it was held because your people pressed for it before the emperor Constantine. Or if church judgments made earlier can no longer be overturned, what will you do about Primian, your bishop of Carthage? A hundred bishops first passed judgment against him, more, at any rate, than judged Caecilian, and they stripped him of his episcopate and installed Maximian in his place. Does Primian not rely on a later judgment, made in his favor in the town of Bagai? On the strength of that judgment he will not allow himself to be doubted, but extorts an acquittal from all of you. So we too, on the strength of the later judgment concerning Caecilian, acquit him entirely and without hesitation. Yet for our case it is enough if we say of him what you said of Optatus: "We neither acquit nor condemn Caecilian." Let those who judged him, whether yours or ours, answer for how they judged; let them give account of their own sentences; let them bear the burden of their own work, whether bad or good. Allow us at least to remain in doubt about other people's deeds, so that we are not forced to condemn in ourselves those sacraments about which no doubt is permitted. But as I have said, think what you like about Optatus. There are no grounds on which we can convict him, since what he did was not done on the public record, though he did it in such a way that he was regarded, retained and died as the chief of Gildo's henchmen. But are we also free to babble whatever we like about Felicianus and Praetextatus, associates of Maximian? Three hundred and ten of your bishops condemned them by name, together with others likewise named, in one and the same sentence of the Council of Bagai, and not long afterwards received them back as bishops, as they had been before, together with everyone they had baptized while under condemnation.

So whatever you said against us or our people, as if sparing us and passing over it, without names, without witnesses, without any documents at all, partly blaming what is not blameworthy and partly failing to prove what is, there is no need to try to clear it away. Look at these men, these men, once again; consider somewhat more carefully Felicianus of Musti and Praetextatus of Assuras. In its proper place, if the Lord permits, I will set out their whole case in such a way that, however great an enemy of the truth you choose to be, you will not be able to defend or deny the lie told by your people. For now, though, I am content to proceed on the basis of what they told you. I am not yet discussing how untrue it was; I am not yet showing with what astonishing and shameless blindness they lied. Certainly, when you read in my letter about those I called Maximianists, both condemned by your council and received back, you were, as you write, greatly disturbed, since at that time, to use your own words, you did not know what the truth was. Then at once, as you tell it, you inquired more carefully of your bishops, and through their teaching you learned the decree of the council, the sentence pronounced against those who were condemned, and the course of the whole affair. And because you believed that I too was ignorant of what had happened, you urged me to learn what the truth was, and went on to narrate everything as follows. Note that in this matter I am setting down your very words from your letter, for I very much need them.

"When error," you say, "was striving to draw as many bishops as possible to Maximian's side, our people gathered a council, and a sentence was pronounced against all who persisted in his schism, a sentence you testify that you too have read. Although this sentence was confirmed by the consent of all," you say, "it was nevertheless decided by decree of the council to grant a period of time, within which anyone who wished to be corrected would be held innocent. So it came about," you say, "that not only the two you mention but many others too returned to the church, cleared and innocent. Their baptism therefore ought not to be undone, since, having been restored within the appointed day, they were not bound by the peremptory sentence; nor, when they baptized, had they been separated from the church, since the fixed term of the time allowed had not yet passed and cut them off. But those who stubbornly persisted with Maximian even after the said day were held by the sentence of condemnation and lost both baptism and the church." These words, my Cresconius, you surely recognize as copied from the text of your letter.

So I ask you: if they had not yet been separated from the church, how was a sentence pronounced against all who persisted in Maximian's schism, a sentence which, though confirmed by the consent of all, the council nevertheless decided by decree to grant a period of time, within which anyone who wished to be corrected would be held innocent? By these words you show that, of those who persisted in Maximian's schism, anyone who wished to be corrected within that period would be held innocent. He was to be corrected, then, if he wished to be corrected, from that schism in which he had persisted with Maximian. So before he was corrected, he was in the schism in which he had persisted, even though he had not persisted in it stubbornly, since he was corrected within the agreed time. For a little later you draw the distinction in these words: "But those who stubbornly persisted with Maximian even after the said day were held by the sentence of condemnation and lost both baptism and the church." By saying "stubbornly persisted," you show that those who were corrected had also persisted, though not stubbornly. Against all of them together that sentence was pronounced, and though it was confirmed by the consent of all, you say the council nevertheless decided by decree to grant that period of time. How, then, were they in the church, when before their correction they were persisting in schism with Maximian? And if they were not in the church because they were in schism, how could they baptize? Next, how did it come about, as you say, that not only those I mentioned but many others too returned to the church, cleared and innocent, if they had not been separated from the church? What did they return to, if they had never left it? Or if they had left, tell me, please, by what right did they baptize before they returned to the church? "Their baptism therefore," you say, "ought not to be undone, since, having been restored within the appointed day, they were not bound by the peremptory sentence." Restored to what? Wake up, I beg you; tell us what they were restored to. No doubt you will say, "to the church," the church to which you said they returned. Is anyone restored to the church who has not been separated from the church? Does anyone who is not separated from the church persist in schism, for however few days? Does anyone who is not separated from the church return to the church after any length of time, however short?

I think, my dear friend, that you not only failed to consider your words before writing them, but did not even read them once they were written. Yet what could you do, when this work forced on you the task of defending, as best you could, a sentence against Maximian and his associates that was not your own but pronounced by others? For even if you had not used these words, I would quote that very decree of the Council of Bagai, where it is written: "But those whom the seedlings of the sacrilegious shoot did not defile, that is, those who out of modest reverence for the faith withdrew their hands from the head of Maximian, we have permitted to return to mother church."

So even if I had not found such words of yours, I would certainly say here, here I would cry out for the truth: how are people permitted to return to mother church who have not withdrawn from mother church? Or if they did withdraw, by what right could they baptize before they returned? The only answer is that, in your concern to repair this schism, you forgot your own empty vanity, by which you hold that, after bishops who have carried an unbroken succession from the very sees of the apostles down to these times, not one man, not one household, not one city, not one nation, but the whole world must be rebaptized. Or at any rate, since the horror [?] of this practice has always shaken the hearts even of those who do it, when so many congregations were returning to your communion from the communion of Maximian, you were glad to restore so many, but ashamed to rebaptize so many. Yet you would have done it, however much anyone detested and shuddered at it, for the sake of men's salvation—which, the more people it concerned, the less it was to be disregarded—if you ever did it out of regard for the truth and not from the prejudgment of error. You certainly see that in this return of the Maximianists to your communion it has been made plain that what we say about baptism is true. For if there is any understanding among men, whether in saying anything or in hearing it, whoever baptizes before he returns to the church plainly baptizes outside the church; and yet the baptism is not to be annulled, just as you did not annul it in their case. It is not to be altered, because each person baptizes not in his own name nor in anyone else's, but in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Next, besides the sacrament of baptism, which remains intact whether to the punishment of the perverse or to the salvation of the upright or the corrected, I want to say something about the expiation or cleansing of the corrected themselves. For you remember what you said against us: that we receive those who come to us from you out of the sacrilegious error of heretics without any expiation. Now you tell us, I ask you, by what expiation those who returned to you from the schism of Maximian were cleansed, when they were even received in their own ranks. Or, having shared in so great a crime, were they not stained by so wicked a fellowship?

Attend to what that truth-telling mouth of your bishops proclaims, what it rebukes, what it confesses in that celebrated council: "Maximian," it says, "the rival of the faith, the adulterer of the truth, the enemy of mother church, the minister of Dathan, Korah and Abiram, the thunderbolt of the sentence has struck from the bosom of peace; and that the gaping earth has not yet swallowed him up, it has reserved him for the powers above for a greater punishment. For had he been snatched away, he would have profited by the shortcut of death and escaped his punishment; now he gathers the interest of a heavier debt, since, though dead, he remains among the living." Is it really so, then, that those who persisted in his schism, as you yourself said, before they returned to your church within the period of grace, as you likewise said, had contracted no stain, or only a small one, from fellowship with this man? But hear what follows next; hear, I say, you who composed or dictated that sentence, what it goes on to add: "Nor does a just death condemn this man alone for his crime; the chain of sacrilege also drags very many into partnership in the crime, of whom it is written: 'The poison of asps is under their lips, whose mouth is full of cursing and bitterness. Their feet are swift to shed blood. Ruin and misery are in their ways, and the way of peace they have not known.' We would not indeed wish them to be cut off as though from the joints of our own body. But since the deadly rot of a festering wound finds more relief in amputation than in the indulgence of remedies, a more wholesome course has been found: lest the pestilent poison creep through all the limbs, let the wound that has arisen be cut away with a brief pain. Know, therefore, that those guilty of a notorious crime—Victorianus of Carcabia, Marcianus of Sullecthum, Beianus of Beia, Salvius of Ausafa, Theodorus of Usula, Donatus of Sabratha, Miggin of Elephantaria, Praetextatus of Assuras, Salvius of Membressa, Valerius of Melzi, Felicianus of Musti and Martialis of Pertusa, who by a deadly work of perdition glued together a filthy vessel out of collected dregs—and also the clergy, once of the church of Carthage, who by taking part in the crime played the pimp to an unlawful incest, have been condemned by the judgment of God presiding, through the truth-telling mouth of the universal council." What heavier things could you have said against them? What heavier things do you usually say against us? "But they were corrected," you say, "from so great an evil within the period of grace." I shall consider whether they were corrected, for they would truly have been corrected if they had returned to the true church. But if yours is the true church, tell us how they were expiated from so monstrous a crime. For if they were not expiated, then by your own judgment you are all stained by their crime; but if they were expiated, you concede that they could be expiated by the mere act of return, because of the charity that covers a multitude of sins, and yet you accuse us with empty slanders concerning your people when they come to us corrected. Unless perhaps, as the words of the council indicate, they had indeed already committed the sacrilege of schism, but before the date of the grace granted they had not yet been defiled by that same sacrilege, and so were not thought to need expiation.

If that is so, who would dare to oppose you, who have received such marvelous power over men? They sin when they will, and are defiled when you will. We are not quoting something obscure or little known and published. It is that sentence which, thanks to its great eloquence, is in everyone's hands and on the lips of everyone who is keen to read such things; and concerning it you can now at least see how truly I said that they ought not first to rejoice in its eloquence, lest afterward they should lament its notoriety. Attend to what it contains; hear what it thunders.

"Maximian," it says, "the rival of the faith, the adulterer of the truth, the enemy of mother church, the minister of Dathan, Korah and Abiram, the thunderbolt of the sentence has struck from the bosom of peace." If anyone, then, had knowingly shared the sacrament of the altar with this man for a single day, would he not, according to that much-vaunted severity of yours, be so polluted by so great an evil as to become his equal? What, then, were those men, or what did they become from him, who not only approached the altar with him, but themselves set him up as an ordained bishop against your Primian, raising altars against altars? But why should I question you about them? Let the sentence itself speak, whose words blaze so brightly that, if you wished to hide it, it would break through the darkness of any hiding place by its overwhelming splendor. Let us see with what a roar of condemnation it rises against Maximian's associates.

"Nor does a just death condemn this man alone for his crime," it says; "the chain of sacrilege also drags very many into partnership in the crime, of whom it is written: 'The poison of asps is under their lips, whose mouth is full of cursing and bitterness. Their feet are swift to shed blood. Ruin and misery are in their ways, and the way of peace they have not known.'" Then, a little later, after naming one by one all who ordained Maximian—among whom are read also those I am dealing with, Felicianus and Praetextatus—it adds what they had done to deserve having such things said against them: "who by a deadly work of perdition," it says, "glued together a filthy vessel out of collected dregs," meaning it to be understood that they themselves were present and themselves ordained Maximian by the laying on of hands. It adds also concerning the clergy of Carthage: "and also the clergy of the church of Carthage, who by taking part in the crime played the pimp to an unlawful incest."

I ask you, Cresconius: am I exaggerating this crime with any words of my own? Had I wished to, perhaps words would not have failed me—if not such as these, at least adequate in some fashion. I ask you, then: before these two whom I am dealing with for the present returned to the harmony of your communion, while they were bound in that chain of sacrilege, with the poison of asps under their lips, with a mouth full of cursing and bitterness, with feet swift to shed blood—how did they baptize? Was there in them the conscience of a holy giver to wash the recipients clean? Did at least a good reputation, even a utterly false one, commend them—that reputation which, in those straits of yours, offered you a way out, not one by which you might escape, but one by which you might throw yourself headlong—when so distinguished a council cries out that they are "guilty of a notorious crime"? Then, on their return before the date of grace, as you believed your bishops who told you falsehoods, how are they received in their ranks together with those whom they had baptized as schismatics, while they stood outside the church with Maximian in the chain of sacrilege? Whence are they expiated from so great a sacrilege? Whence are they loosed from that chain? Whence are their lips, their mouth, cleansed of the poison of asps, of cursing and bitterness? Whence are their feet washed of the spiritual blood they ran so swiftly to shed? Whence are their hands cleansed of the deadly work of perdition? Whence is the affection, not of the body's limbs but of the soul, purged of unlawful incest?

Plainly, in order to defend this cause, whether you will or not, you are forced to take refuge in the defense of the truth, which says that the baptism of Christ, given not only through hidden but also through open evildoers, and not only by the converted but also by the perverse, keeps the unshaken firmness of its strength; that it can indeed be present in such people but cannot benefit them unless they are corrected; and that the corrected are expiated also by the prayers of their brethren, through the charity that covers a multitude of sins. See, then: even before I show how shamelessly your bishops lied to you about the reception of the Maximianists [?], I think that, since on the basis of their very lie and your own account your whole case has been overturned, you ought no longer to be inquiring but acknowledging, nor preparing a rebuttal but rather thinking of correction. For you now see, at least, how truly I said those things to which you vainly tried to reply with falsehoods, and how rightly I said: "If for the sake of the unity of Donatus's party no one rebaptizes those baptized in a wicked schism, why is the true and complete law of Christ's inheritance not acknowledged for the sake of Christ's unity?"—since you yourself admit that those who had persisted in the schism of Maximian incurred a sentence by which they would not be bound if they returned to the church within the period of grace. From this it is clear that before they returned they baptized, in the schism in which they had persisted, those with whom they were received into your communion. You see how dead men baptized, since of those who had persisted in the schism of Maximian it had been said, before they returned to you, by the sentence of the council of Bagai: "After the manner of the Egyptians, the shores are full of the corpses of the perishing."

As for what I said—"When it was read out among them to be decreed, they acclaimed it with mouths wide open; but now, when it is read out by us, they fall silent"—see, it would now be far better for them to fall silent, since in speaking such things they entangle themselves the worse. You see how true is what I said: "At long last they ought to perceive how much must be borne for the sake of peace, and to return for the peace of Christ to the church which did not condemn what it did not know, since for the peace of Donatus they were pleased to recall the condemned." This is much more true according to your own account, for you said that even those were recalled by the grace granted of whom, named expressly, it had already been said: "Know that they have been condemned by the judgment of God presiding, through the truth-telling mouth of the universal council." For since that period of grace was established after these words, how were they not pleased to recall the condemned? Or how could those things not be unknown to us, born so long after, or even to the Christian world itself, which could not be proved against Caecilian in the overseas trial held afterward, when the things done concerning the Maximianists, both in Africa and in our own times, you, though you are an African, as you say, did not know even after so many years—and, as we shall be able to show you, still do not know, because you believed your lying bishops?

You say that in the matter of the surrender of the scriptures I wanted, by a kind of anticategoria, to throw back upon your predecessors what was done by ours, and you find fault with my doing so, as though we were discussing types of cases or questions in a school, and not seeking the truth in the church. Would you say this to the prophet Elijah, who, when a most wicked king charged him with being the one who was troubling Israel, replied: "It is not I who trouble Israel, but you and your father's house"? What does it matter to us by what name the Greeks call this kind of retorted charge in the art of rhetoric, when we find it in prophetic authority? So when someone says, "I did not do it; you did," what is needed is to speak the truth, not to fear saying it. And as for you, how you are to show that your predecessors did not do what, by the reading of their own confessions, they are shown to have done, is something you ought to think about most carefully, if you are able—not to frighten the unlearned with a Greek word so that they will not listen to us. Indeed, you have not shown that our predecessors were traditors—for you are not to be thought to have shown it simply because you said there are many letters by which it could be shown—whereas concerning your predecessors there survives the council of Secundus of Tigisis, held with only a very few at Cirta after the persecution in which the books were to be handed over, in order to ordain a bishop there in place of one who had died.

Hear what was done there; I have taken care to write below what was necessary: "In the eighth consulship of Diocletian and the seventh of Maximian, on the fourth day before the Nones of March, at Cirta, when Secundus, bishop of Tigisis, holder of the first see, had taken his seat in the house of Urbanus Donatus, he said: 'Let us first examine ourselves, and so we shall be able to ordain a bishop here.' Secundus said to Donatus of Mascula: 'It is said that you handed over the scriptures.' Donatus answered: 'You know how hard Florus pursued me to make me offer incense, and God did not deliver me into his hands, brother; but since God has pardoned me, you too reserve me for God.' Secundus said: 'What then shall we do about the martyrs? It is because they did not hand them over that they were crowned.' Donatus said: 'Send me to God; there I will render account.' Secundus said: 'Step to one side.' Secundus said to Marinus of Aquae Tibilitanae: 'It is said that you too handed them over.' Marinus answered: 'I gave Pollus some papers, but my books are safe.' Secundus said: 'Step over to one side.' Secundus said to Donatus of Calama: 'It is said that you handed them over.' Donatus answered: 'I gave medical books.' Secundus said: 'Step over to one side.'" And in another place: "Secundus said to Victor of Rusicade: 'It is said that you handed over four Gospels.' Victor answered: 'Valentianus was the curator; he forced me to throw them into the fire. I knew they were worn-out copies [?]. Pardon me this fault, and God too pardons me.' Secundus said: 'Step over to one side.'" And in another place: "Secundus said to Purpurius of Limata: 'It is said that you killed your sister's two sons at Milevis.' Purpurius answered: 'Do you think I am frightened of you as others are? What did you do, when you were detained by the curator and the town council to make you hand over the scriptures? How did you free yourself from them, unless you gave, or ordered to be given, something or other? For they did not just let you go for nothing. As for me, I killed, and I kill, those who act against me; so do not provoke me to say more. You know I take no account of anyone.' Secundus the younger said to his uncle Secundus: 'You hear what he is saying against you. He is ready to withdraw and make a schism—not only he himself, but all those you are accusing. I know they are going to abandon you and pass sentence against you, and you will be left alone, a heretic. So what concern is it of yours what anyone has done? He must render account to God.' Secundus said to Felix of Rotaria, Nabor of Centurio and Victor of Garba: 'What do you think?' They answered: 'They have God to whom they must render account.' Secundus said: 'You know, and God knows: be seated.' And all answered: 'Thanks be to God.'"

These traditors, who together with others at Carthage pronounced sentence against Caecilian and his colleagues—among them was Silvanus of Cirta too, the records of whose surrender I shall insert shortly—you will no doubt defend with splendid reasoning. For you will say of all these many men what you thought it a great thing to say about Silvanus alone, supposing that you plainly demonstrated the charge of surrender brought against him to be false because you cited the sentence he pronounced in council, among the other bishops, against Caecilian and others who shared his communion—as though it were impossible for a traditor to condemn traditors. You evidently see these things more wisely than the apostle Paul. For he charged certain people with absurd things and did not consider that what he was saying could not happen: "You who preach that one must not steal, you steal; you who say that one must not commit adultery, you commit adultery; you who abhor idols, you commit sacrilege"; and above all this: "For in passing judgment on another you condemn yourself, since you who judge do the same things." These traditors, then, whom Secundus pardoned when they confessed, because he was frightened, he had with him at the council of Carthage; and men who, though present, had not been condemned on their own confession pronounced sentence against absent men who had not confessed. This council would not have survived or lasted into the memory of posterity, had it not been copied by others while it was being kept by those who were preparing to defend themselves with it, should anyone later charge them with the same crimes that had been remitted there.

It was in the interest of Secundus himself, too, that it should be evident that he, to prevent a schism—something the peaceable are wont to guard against above all—had left all those matters to the judgment of God. He ought to have done this much more at the council of Carthage, where nothing had been established against the absent, had not Lucilla, then a very powerful and extremely wealthy woman, inflamed with frenzied hatred, vehemently pressed for another bishop to be ordained against Caecilian, as though he had been condemned. This was later brought up in the trial before Zenophilus the consular by a certain Nundinarius, a deacon of Silvanus of Cirta, then your bishop; he had been unable to come to terms, as he wished, with his bishop, whose enmity he had suffered. He had indeed pressed this matter with Silvanus's colleagues more by threatening that he would betray everything than by pleading to obtain pardon.

From the records of that trial I have inserted these few extracts: "In the consulship of Constantine the Greatest, Augustus, and Constantine the Younger, most noble Caesar, on the Ides of December, when Sextus of Thamugadi had been brought in and Victor the grammarian placed before the court, with Nundinarius the deacon also standing by, Zenophilus the consular said: 'What is your name?' He answered: 'Victor.'" And a little later, in another place: "Nundinarius answered: 'Let the records be read.' Zenophilus the consular said: 'Let them be read.' And Nundinius the clerk read: 'In the eighth consulship of Diocletian and the seventh of Maximian, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June, from the records of Munatius Felix, perpetual flamen and curator of the colony of Cirta: When they had come to the house in which the Christians used to assemble, Felix, perpetual flamen and curator, said to Paul the bishop: "Bring out the scriptures of the law and whatever else you have here, so that you may obey the command and the order." Paul the bishop said: "The readers have the scriptures, but we give what we have here." Felix, perpetual flamen and curator, said to Paul: "Point out the readers or send to them." Paul the bishop: "You all know them." Felix, perpetual flamen and curator, said: "We do not know them." Paul the bishop: "The public office knows them, that is, Edesius and Junius the clerks." Felix, perpetual flamen and curator, said: "Leaving aside the matter of the readers, whom the office will point out, you too hand over what you have here." Paul the bishop being seated, with Montanus, Victor of Castellum and Memor, presbyters, Mars and Helius standing by with Mars the deacon, there being brought out by Marcuclius, Catullinus, Silvanus and Carosus, subdeacons, and by Januarius, Marcuclius, Fructuosus, Miggin, Saturninus, Victor, Samsuricus and the other gravediggers, Victor son of Aufidius recorded it in an inventory as follows: two gold chalices, also six silver chalices,' and so on." And in another place: "After the library was opened, the cupboards there were found empty. There Silvanus brought out a silver box [?] and a silver lamp, which he said he had found behind a chest. Victor son of Aufidius said to Silvanus: 'You would have been a dead man if you had not found them.' Felix, perpetual flamen and curator of the commonwealth, said to Silvanus: 'Search more carefully, lest anything remain here.' Silvanus said: 'Nothing remains here; we have thrown all of it out,'" and so on. And in another place: "Copy of the petition handed to the bishops by Nundinarius the deacon: 'Christ and his angels are witness that you have communicated with traditors: that is, Silvanus of Cirta is a traditor and a thief of the property of the poor, which all of you bishops, presbyters, deacons and elders know; and concerning the four hundred folles of Lucilla, the most illustrious lady, for which you conspired together that Majorinus should be made bishop—and from this the schism arose. For Victor the fuller, too, in your presence and the people's, gave twenty folles to be made a presbyter, which Christ and his angels know,'" and so on. And in another place: "When these had been read, Zenophilus the consular said: 'From both the records and the letters that have been read it is established that Silvanus is a traditor.'" Likewise in another place: "Zenophilus, a man of senatorial rank, the consular, said: 'What office did Silvanus then hold in the clergy?' Victor answered: 'When the persecution broke out under Paul the bishop, Silvanus was a subdeacon.'"

Have you anything to say to this, brother Cresconius? I do not think shame has so completely vanished from human affairs that, to clear Silvanus, you still think we should read out the sentence he pronounced against Caecilian and his colleagues as traditors. That would only prompt us to quote something like the apostle's words, as I mentioned a little earlier: "You who preach that one must not hand over, do you hand over?" and: "In judging another you condemn yourself; for you who judge do the very same things." "But afterwards," you say, "when Ursatius and Zenophilus were persecuting and he refused to enter into communion, he was driven into exile." On the contrary: a man who was already a traditor chose to remain a heretic as well, so as to hold a false honour in the very party of Donatus, since he could hold none in the Catholic Church once the records of his handing over had been laid open so plainly at a public trial. You will no doubt say these things are false, and in defence of your forebears you will bring forward other things against ours, as best you can. Perhaps you will not manage even that, because you will find nothing to bring forward. But suppose you have found something, suppose you have brought it forward: are you so shameless in your madness as to insist that what you produce ought to be believed rather than what we produce? Either there were traditors on both sides, if you too read out something about a confession by our people; or, if you think our people fabricated something against yours, why do you not allow us to think the same of yours against ours? So let us who believe in one God not quarrel over human deeds that are either proven on both sides or uncertain on both sides. Let us instead agree in the grace of Christ, which is a certain and divine gift. When the records of our forebears and of yours are read out to us, born so long afterwards, and they contradict one another, what could be more unjust than forbidding us even to doubt? And if doubt is allowed, what more is needed? For although it is uncertain who started the evil of handing over, it is not uncertain who commands us to restore the good of peace.

So whoever rejects the peace of Christ on account of someone else's uncertain evil is most certainly evil himself. Cyprian did not abandon the peace of the wheat even on account of the certain wickedness of the tares mixed in with it. Writing to Maximus he said: "Although there seem to be tares in the Church, our faith and our love ought not to be hindered so that we ourselves withdraw from the Church because we see tares in it." He did not say "we suspect, we think, we judge, we guess, we believe"; he said "we see". O word that should remove all doubt, so that the body of Christ might not be divided! If you long for wheat alone, groan in the labour of the field and rejoice in the hope of the barn. Bear with the bad in the communion of Christ's sacraments, lest by tearing the nets before the time comes to reach the shore you become the very thing you refused to tolerate. I would say this if you had proved anything about the traditors you accuse. Indeed, at this point I would no longer say even this, for I am not commanded to tolerate people with whom I am no longer compelled to live. But even if a traditor were shown to me now, with what conscience could I desert so many Christian nations to whom he has not been shown? And then, if I am only now learning what I did not know a little while ago, why do you annul in me what I did know? For I knew that I had received the baptism of Christ. Even you yourselves are teaching me of another man's crime, and you grant that while it is unknown it harms no one.

Why then do you rebaptize today a man baptized yesterday, when you are teaching him today of another man's crime that he did not know of yesterday? Since he did not know what sort of man he received it from, he was not guilty on account of the baptism he received. Now he has learned this from you: why should he become guilty when his baptism is annulled? Whether or not he accepts your proofs, a man who received the baptism of Christ through the ministry of a traditor cannot rightly be baptized again even by your own rule, unless you prove that he knew whom he received it from. Now turn your mind away from party zeal and consider what a countless multitude of Christians in Africa itself do not know who the traditors were. How many more in the rest of the world! Unless you prove that this vast multitude knew it when they were baptized, either you will not dare to say they must be baptized again, or you will dare to judge the hidden things of the heart. And then where is the divine sentence you were pleased to insert: "What is manifest belongs to you, but what is hidden belongs to the Lord your God"? Believe the Christian world when it says to you: "I know the baptism of Christ; who were traditors in Africa or anywhere else I do not know. Why do you judge hidden human things in me in order to annul manifest divine things in me? Suppose you prove another man's crime to me now: when I received baptism I did not know what you are telling me. If you want to baptize me because of the men you are now exposing to me, you ought also to baptize those who unknowingly received baptism from adulterers whom you have just exposed." What can you say to this except: "Nothing is holy, nothing is clean, except what I want and when I want"?

"In this matter," you say, "the knowledge of almost the whole world bears witness." The answer to you is: in this matter the whole world has no knowledge at all. "Our forebears," you say, "received this from their parents." The answer: yes, but people in error received it from people in error or from slanderers. After all, the forebears of the Jews also received from their own forebears the story that the body of Christ was stolen from the tomb. "Not long ago," you say, "those died who knew by whom and in what places this crime of handing over was committed." The answer: our people say the same in support of their side. "There are also books," you say, "in which the course of events has been faithfully and carefully recorded; there are official records, there are letters, and we also have the open confession of many." The answer to you is that our people do not lack these in support of their side either. So either let us believe those who were able to persuade of their case the churches we read of in the divine and canonical books, or else, as you said about Optatus, let us neither acquit nor condemn what is doubtful. And let us hold fast in brotherly love to the peace of Christ, whose goodness is not in doubt.

But you say the Easterners, whom you now concede are ours, were not unaware of this crime. To prove it, you insert the opening of the letter of the Council of Serdica, where the name of Donatus, your bishop of Carthage, is found written. You think, and you claim, that this happened because the Easterners who sent this letter from their council were displeased by the crime of the traditors, had withdrawn from communion with them, and so were in communion with your Donatus. Learn, then, what you do not know. The Council of Serdica was a council of Arians. This has long been known, and we have the document in hand. It was assembled chiefly against Athanasius, the Catholic bishop of Alexandria, who more than anyone else sharply rebuked and refuted their error, which had arisen in that very city. So it is no wonder if those heretics, whom the Catholic Church was condemning throughout the world, tried to claim Donatus as one of their own. Besides, the copy we have names the bishops to whom this letter was addressed without the names of their cities. So either there was some Donatus who was not a bishop in Africa, and your people added "of Carthage" to his name, or, as I said, an Eastern heresy tried to join the African heresy to itself. This is especially credible because the Catholic East would never have written to the bishop of Carthage and passed over the bishop of Rome. They should at least have written to your bishop there, whom you are accustomed to send from Africa to Rome for your few followers. But thanks be to God that this conspiracy of Eastern heretics with African heretics, if it was ever begun, did not prevail. You yourself in your letter have placed the Arians among heretics to be detested by you and by us alike, so I have no need to contend with you on this question as well. You also posed a question to yourself as if we had raised it: "If these things are so, how is it that the Easterners later separated from communion with your people?" And you answered that in receiving ours back again they failed to stand firm in a case already condemned. Is it any wonder that your bishops, coming from such distant lands, tell you whatever they like with impunity? But even if it were entirely so, what have all those peoples done who knew nothing of these things and are nevertheless judged by you to need rebaptism? Or is it not credible that whole peoples could be ignorant even of these things? You yourself are rather more studious of such matters, yet you would not have inquired what your African party did with the Maximianists in Africa if you had not wanted to answer my letters.

I said that even if it were proved that some who died in our communion had handed over the Scriptures, something we disapprove of and which displeases us, it would not stain us in any way. How ridiculous of you to think that ridiculous and unworthy of my prudence! So now I would like to know how your prudence refuted it. Is it because you say you cannot see how we disapprove of it, or how far it displeases us, when, though the error was known, we never condemned it, placed as we are in their schism? See rather how briefly I answer this. I am in the Church whose members are all those churches which, as we know from the canonical writings, were born and established through the labours of the apostles. With the Lord's help I will not abandon their communion, whether in Africa or anywhere else. If there were traditors in this communion whom I do not know of, then once you have demonstrated it I will detest them as dead in flesh and heart. Yet I will by no means be estranged, because of the dead, from the living who remain in the holy unity of the same Church. For those men did not found this Church; within it they were wheat if they were good, chaff if they were bad. But as for you, since the tares or chaff of so manifest a Church could not stain you, what cause was there for your division except a craving for sacrilegious schism? "If it displeases you," you say, "disapprove it: flee and leave the church of the traditors; do not follow in the footsteps of your erring forebears." To this I answer: if they were not traditors, they are my forebears; if they were what I am not, they are not my forebears. I hold to a Church full of wheat and chaff. I do not mean only others, who carry their own burden: even if you showed me that I myself was a traditor within it, there I am free to change for the better, and I have no need to separate from it. If I come to know any such people in the communion of its sacraments, I correct those I can by the word and discipline of the Lord, and I bear with those I cannot correct. I flee the chaff so as not to be chaff; I do not flee the threshing floor, so as not to be nothing.

So do not toss yourself about in vain over this sentence. The apostolic precept you yourself cited rather reminds me how to do this: "Do not share in other people's sins; keep yourself pure." To show how each person may avoid sharing in other people's sins, he added: "keep yourself pure." Whoever keeps himself pure does not share in other people's sins, even though he shares with them, not their sins, but the sacraments of God, which they receive to their own judgment; by keeping himself pure he has made himself a stranger to them. Otherwise even Cyprian (God forbid!) shared in the sins of his grasping and usurious colleagues. Yet he remained in the communion of the divine sacraments with them, and he says of them: "Very many bishops, who ought to have been an encouragement and an example to others, neglected their divine stewardship and became stewards of worldly business. They left their sees, abandoned their people, and wandered through other provinces hunting for the markets of profitable trade. While brothers in the Church went hungry, they wanted to have money in abundance, to seize estates by treacherous frauds, and to swell their profits by compounding interest." Did he share in the sins of such men? Did he follow their sect? And yet he stood with them in the communion of the same sacraments. Those sacraments had not been instituted by these men, who did not hold them for salvation by holy living, but by their evil living made them serve for their own punishment.

And what do you mean by the objection you posed to yourself in my name, that I never handed over the divine testament? For you add: "But the one who did hand it over created you." Then you string together phrases that seemed to you to sound well: "The stream is drawn from the spring, and the members follow the head. When the head is sound, the whole body is sound; and if there is any disease or defect in the head, it weakens all the members. Whatever grows from a stock looks back to its origin." And after this, as though in a final conclusion, you finish: "No one can be innocent who does not follow the sect of an innocent man." In all these words of yours you have made my creator, my head, nothing but a traditor, a man you were able only to accuse, not to convict. But I do not make even his innocence my creator or my spring or my head. You, however, return to the error into which Petilian fell, as though Christ were not the origin and head of everyone born in the sanctification of baptism, and as though I would not thereby fall under the curse of which it is written: "Cursed is everyone who puts his hope in man." You find no other way out of this, and when you spring back from it you do not land anywhere else.

You also admonish me with a testimony from the Scriptures, to see what further answer I can give you on these points. You say it was for this reason that it was written: "Do not walk in the statutes of your fathers." You do not notice that this was said to the Jews so that they would not imitate the evil deeds of their fathers, not so that they would split away from that people of God. King David, Samuel, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Zechariah and the other saints and prophets of God were permitted to keep God's commandments among those who despised his law, and to hurl many fitting and true words against those very transgressors of the commandment. They were permitted not to imitate or follow, but to detest and flee, the sins of their fathers by which under Moses they so offended God that none of them was worthy to enter the promised land, and to rebuke those who committed such sins for resembling such fathers. And yet they did not set up another people for themselves, as though purged and refined, by a sacrilegious separation. If that was permitted to them, how is it not permitted to us both to refuse to imitate the deeds of who knows what people, deeds you allege rather than prove, and yet not to be separated from the holy Church, which, as the apostle says, bears fruit and grows throughout the whole world? Did the traditors institute any sacraments in which I was baptized? Did they compose books for posterity on committing or imitating the handing over of the Scriptures, and do we hold and follow their teaching? If they had done so, and allowed no one into communion with them except those who read and approved those books, they would have been dividing themselves from the unity of the Church. If you saw me in their breakaway, then you would be right to say I was in the church of the traditors. But if they had written their wicked precepts on handing over the Scriptures and yet had not gathered into a congregation and communion of their own outside the Church, they would for that reason be counted as tares, and the wheat could not rightly be abandoned on their account.

See, I say again what you forbid me to say any more: you accuse before me men long since dead, whom I never examined or judged. You reply: "You may judge even today. Judgment can be passed not only on the living but also on the dead. For although the sinner is dead, what he committed never dies." What if he corrected himself while he was alive and appeased God? Is not what he committed dead and blotted out? That is how Felician and Praetextatus, who ordained Maximian, corrected themselves of so great a crime when, as you say, they were granted a period of grace. It would be strange if their own sins do not harm people who have corrected them, yet harm others who never committed them at all; and if the question concerns us, add: "who did not even know about them." But you say I may judge even today, because judgment can be passed not only on the living but also on the dead. Look, I am willing to judge. But you do not want to argue the case itself; indeed, when we show you that it was argued at the time and without doubt settled then, you refuse to acknowledge it. But let us rather suppose that you do have people you could teach. Why do you already insist that those you have not yet taught must be rebaptized? Even once you have taught them, you ought not to baptize people who were baptized by traditors they did not know were traditors, just as you do not baptize those who were unknowingly baptized by adulterers, even after those men have been exposed and convicted.

Here perhaps you may say: "But judgment has already been given about Caecilian." The answer to you is that judgment had already been given about Primian too, by a hundred of your bishops whom Maximian had persuaded that he was utterly wicked, before you held the Council of Bagai. In the first judgment he was condemned in his absence; in the second he was acquitted in his presence. If those he baptized after the first judgment cannot be rebaptized, how much less those he baptized after the second! In the same way Caecilian was first condemned in his absence at Carthage, in the judgment of Secundus of Tigisi, and in the second judgment, that of Miltiades of Rome, he was acquitted in his presence. You still do not want us to be certain about him; at least allow us to doubt. For you are defeated not only by the one who knows Caecilian was innocent, but also by the one who does not know he was guilty. Yet you judge that both must be rebaptized, both those who say "We know" and those who say "We do not know what sort of man Caecilian was." Those whom Primian baptized after the first judgment, in which he was condemned in his absence, are not to be baptized again; yet those whom Caecilian baptized after the second judgment, in which he was acquitted in his presence, are to be baptized again! It was not lawful to condemn the man who had been condemned; let it at least be lawful to doubt about the man who was acquitted. Even if his crimes were certain to us, we are set within the Church which the Holy Spirit foretold would be like a threshing floor with chaff, and so other people's sins, which we have not imitated, would by no means stain us. And yet, even though these crimes are admitted to be uncertain to us, we are not only made out to be guilty but even judged to need rebaptism. Is this how you act? Do you twist everything like this? Do you really think you are allowed so much that whatever you wish is holy and whatever you wish is unclean? Restrain yourselves; do not advance in evil, lest you perish from among the good.

Next there is what I said: "If you are talking about persecutions, I answer quickly: if you have suffered anything unjustly, it does not concern those who, for the sake of the peace of unity, commendably tolerate those who do such things, however wrongly they act." How deceitfully you tried to refute it, without a thought that your letter would have readers of sound mind! For you answer as though I had said that you ought to be persecuted for the sake of the peace of unity. I did not say that in that passage. What I said was: "If you have suffered anything unjustly, it does not concern those by whom the men who do such things against you, however wrongly, are commendably tolerated for the sake of the peace of unity." Since this was said quite plainly, let those you wanted to deceive at least pay attention now that it has been explained. I do not think you failed to understand something so plain. You thought that because my sentence was brief it could easily be wrapped in fog, so that whatever else you said, you would seem to have answered it. And why did I say that the bad members of our communion, that is, the chaff on the Lord's threshing floor, are commendably tolerated by our good members for the sake of peace when they act unjustly against you? What need is there for me to show and defend this myself, when blessed Cyprian says it for me, most plainly and frankly: that even when the bad are seen in the Church, the Church is not to be deserted on their account? That is what I meant by saying they are to be tolerated for the peace of unity. Nor do those who persecute you unjustly persecute you more than they persecute us. To you they give a semblance of glory, false though it is, with which to deceive the unlearned; to us they give a great wound of sorrow.

Then, mentioning also certain dead men whom you say our people killed, you enlarge on the theme at great length, as though let loose on the open field of your eloquence, and there you seem to yourselves to be like martyrs. Meanwhile every day we suffer incredible deeds from your clergy and Circumcellions, far worse than those of any robbers and bandits. Armed with dreadful weapons of every kind and roaming about to the terror of all, they disturb not only the peace of the Church but the very quiet and peace of human life. In night attacks they invade the houses of Catholic clergy and leave them stripped and empty. The clergy themselves they seize, beat with clubs, cut with swords, and throw aside half-dead. Moreover, with a new and previously unheard-of kind of crime, they pour and pack lime mixed with vinegar into their eyes. They could have torn those eyes out with less trouble, but they choose to torture them longer rather than blind them more quickly. At first they used only lime for this crime, but after they learned that their victims soon recovered, they added vinegar.

I pass over all the crimes they committed earlier, which forced the enactment of those same laws against your error. Those laws were tempered by Christian gentleness rather than enforced against such great crimes with the rigour they deserved. When the Catholic bishop of Thubursicubure, named Servus, was seeking to recover a place your people had seized, and the representatives of both parties were waiting for the proconsul's hearing, your armed men suddenly rushed upon him in that town, and he barely escaped with his life. His father, a priest venerable in age and character, was so badly hurt in that assault that he departed this life a few days later. Maximianus, the Catholic bishop of Bagai, had won by a judicial sentence pronounced between the parties the basilica on the estate of Calvianum, which your people had at one time unlawfully seized. While he held it by clear right, in that very church, beneath the altar where he had taken refuge, they broke the altar over him and cruelly beat him with its timbers and with other clubs, and cut him with iron too, until he filled the whole place with blood. He had also received a great wound in the groin, from which the blood was pouring out so freely that he would have died at once, had not their greater cruelty, through the hidden mercy of God, actually helped him. For as he was being dragged along half-dead and face down, with that part of his body bare, dust quietly stopped up the gushing veins. Then, as our people were carrying him away, they rushed in again, tore him violently from their hands, beat him more severely still, and threw him down from a high tower at night. He landed softly on a heap of dung-ash below and lay there unconscious, barely holding on to his last breath. There a poor man found him as he was passing by, having turned aside to that spot to relieve himself. He recognized him when, frightened, he called his wife, whom modesty had kept at a distance, and she came carrying a lamp. Then the two of them carried him home, whether out of pity or also in the hope of some small reward, since, alive or dead, he would at any rate be shown to our people as having been picked up by them. What more need I say? He was healed by a wonderful cure; he lives, and more scars than limbs can be counted on his body.
