Rumour had reported overseas that he had been killed by your people, and the monstrousness of the crime and the grave outrage of it had stirred everyone, wherever it could be heard, with dreadful grief. After he himself followed the rumour there, his very fresh scars excused that falsehood, for a man whom those who saw him could then scarcely believe to be alive did not seem to have been rashly reported as killed. There he found his colleague of Thubursicubure, whom I mentioned a little earlier, and several others who had suffered similar or not much lesser things, and there seemed to be no possibility for them to return to their own homes. Since, moreover, the notorious frenzy of your circumcellions, who furnish your clergy with a horrifying bodyguard, had become most odiously known everywhere, a great hatred blazed up against you, and the result was that all the former laws against you were revived and these new ones were enacted. Yet the severity of all of them together, if compared with the disorderly and lawless savagery of your people, must be called a remarkable leniency. For with such great power granted to us, these laws do more to show Catholic gentleness than to punish heretical savagery. Indeed, that savagery rages against us all the more boldly and madly, devising, threatening and carrying out murders, robberies, burnings and blindings.

I wanted to recall these things, through which it came about that in our own times these imperial statutes were enacted against you, or rather against your error. For if you had any sense, what could be more in your favour? But if I wished to go back over all the cruel deeds of your people that I have learned from the writings of earlier men or have come to know myself, by which they have persecuted the Catholic Church from the beginning of your division up to this time, what tongue, what pen, how much time and leisure would suffice?

When I was dealing with Optatus, and you had wanted to excuse this rather than being able to clear it, you said that your people could not be held guilty on this account, because no one had brought charges to them so that they could punish it. So many protests by our people about the most furious violence of yours have filled the public archives sooner than those deeds have earned any punishment among you. But perhaps here too it will be said that protests were indeed lodged, but none were brought before them for punishment. Hear, then, some things I have experienced myself. When we had learned the facts about the Maximianists, whom your people had condemned and then received back, and were spreading them abroad wherever we could with fervent persistence, they could find no answer to such recent events made so plain and public. So they began, by the violence of the circumcellions and raging mobs, more often and more boldly than usual, to try to frighten us away from preaching the Catholic truth and exposing their deceit. Many who were entangled in the snares of their error, whom we were urging to be set free from it, kept answering us that we ought to take this up with their bishops, and that they earnestly wished for a conference between us, where they could see whose arguments would let the truth overcome falsehood. So at the council of all Africa at Carthage we resolved that your bishops should be peacefully approached, each by the one of ours who resided in the same place as he did, with the further testimony of public records, so that we could prove to those who demanded it that we had in no way failed their wish. The aim was that through our conference error might be removed and we might enjoy Christian and brotherly fellowship, unity, charity and peace. We had in view that, if they were willing to do this, with the help of God's mercy whatever there was in our case could very easily be made known; but if they refused, at least their lack of confidence would be plain, and not in vain, to those who had asked this of us. It was done: they were approached, and they refused. With what words, how full of guile, cursing and bitterness, would take too long to show now.

Meanwhile Crispinus, your bishop of Calama, when summoned before the public record by my colleague Possidius in the same city, had at first put the matter off to your council, promising that he would consider there with his colleagues what answer he ought to give. Then, after no short time, when the summons was repeated, he answered again on the record: 'Do not fear the words of a sinful man.' And again: 'Take care to say nothing in the ears of a fool, lest when he hears it he mock your wise words.' 'Finally, I conclude this reply of mine in the words of the patriarch: Let the ungodly depart from me; I do not wish to know their ways.' Learned and unlearned alike laughed at this reply. Here was a man saying he did not fear the words of a sinful man, when he did not dare to answer him at all. He said he did not wish to say anything in the ears of a fool, as though he were about to entrust some secret rashly to a fool's ears, when many wise people could hear what he said; it was for the sake of such people that the Lord Christ too said so much to the Pharisees, fools though they were. And he said he did not wish to know the ways of the ungodly, as though those he thought ungodly wanted to teach him their ways, and as though he himself, if he held to the ways of God, ought not rather to teach even the ungodly, as it is written: 'I will teach the wicked your ways, and the ungodly will turn back to you.' So this reply was understood by many, and shown to many as well, to be empty as far as the case was concerned, but bitter and abusive in what did not concern the case. In this way his old age, reputed among you to be most learned, was proved to have no power against the truth, and was laughed at, when a raw recruit of yesterday stood against it. Then suddenly, a few days later, as Possidius was travelling, another Crispinus, a priest of his and, as is said, a relative, laid an ambush of armed men for him. Our man had almost fallen into it already, but the men were spotted and reported, and he fled and turned aside to a certain estate, where the priest would dare nothing, or would not prevail, or, if he did anything at all, would not be able to deny it. When he learned this, he followed at once, so blinded by madness that he now thought it shameful to act in secret. He surrounded the house in which Possidius had shut himself in with his people with armed men, pelted it with stones, ringed it with flames, and tried to force an entry from every side. The crowd of inhabitants who were present, mindful of their own danger if such a crime, once begun in that place, were carried through, partly pleaded with him to spare him, since they did not dare to offend him by resisting, and partly put out the fires that had been set. But he pressed on with what he had begun, no less zealous and unmoved by entreaty. At length the door gave way under the blows. They went in, wounded and slaughtered the animals they had seen in the lower part of the house, and brought the bishop down from the upper rooms, assailing him with blows and insults. To stop them raging more savagely, Crispinus himself intervened, as if swayed by the pleas of others. But it seemed that in his anger he cared less for their pleading than he feared their testimony to the crime.

After these things became known in the town of Calama, people waited to see how Crispinus, your bishop, would punish his priest. A protest set down in the municipal records was also added, so that fear or shame might force him to exercise church discipline. But he utterly disregarded it, and your people's turmoil grew so great that they were thought about to close the roads to the preaching of the truth, which they could not answer; indeed, they were already seen doing so. Then the laws, which had not been lacking but had lain idle in our hands as though they were, were set in motion against Crispinus, your bishop, more to display our gentleness than to punish their audacity. For in no other way would it become known what the Catholic Church, with the help of Christ, was able to do against its enemies and yet did not wish to do: not, as heretical presumption does, through circumcellions raging in private fury, but, according to the truth of prophecy, through kings made subject to the yoke of the Lord God. So Crispinus was brought to court, and although he had denied to the proconsul's questioning that he was a heretic, he was very easily convicted of it. Yet at Possidius' intercession he was not compelled to pay the ten pounds of gold which the elder Emperor Theodosius had laid down as a fine on all heretics. Not content with this very mild sentence, by some counsel or other, which was said to have displeased all your people, he thought fit to appeal to the sons of that same Theodosius. The appeal was accepted. The rescript said nothing other than this: that the party of Donatus should now know that it falls under that fine in gold along with the other heretics. Because it shares such persecution with them, it must either reckon that it shares their righteousness, or, if it does not, it must not boast of being righteous because it is restrained by a penalty with which it sees also those heresies restrained which it admits to be unrighteous. Let it at last understand that it is not the penalty but the cause that makes a martyr of Christ. And let it accuse us of being such savage persecutors that even after the imperial rescript Crispinus did not pay that gold to the treasury, since the Catholic bishops obtained a pardon for him! And now, even amid these very recent laws which threaten your bishops with confiscation, he sits secure on his own property, while Catholic clergy have their homes, their livelihood, their safety and the sight of their eyes hanging in the hands of your circumcellions and clergy.

Those who do these things, to whom shall I liken them: to robbers, to pirates, to some ferocious race of barbarians, when not even the devil himself, the master of all cruelties, can be compared with them? He took away all his possessions from the holy man Job and struck him with a most grievous sore from head to foot; and yet a place remained there unharmed, with his eyes unharmed. He did not put out the eyes of the man whose whole body he had received into his power. But of course these things are not reported to your people! For Crispinus preferred to go to Carthage, to be overcome by his own stubbornness, to refuse the very mild sentence passed on him through the intercession of episcopal gentleness, to appeal to the sons of the man by whose law he saw himself caught, and to bring down on the whole party of Donatus what he alone neither wished nor was compelled to suffer, rather than punish the most audacious and most hateful crime of one priest of his by simply deposing him.

There was a certain Restitutus, a priest of yours in the district of Hippo. Moved by the reasoning of the truth, he crossed over by his own manifest choice to Catholic peace, before this was ordered by these imperial laws. He was seized from his house by your clergy and circumcellions and led in broad daylight to the nearest fortified village. There, with a crowd looking on and no one daring to resist, he was beaten with clubs at the whim of madmen, rolled in a muddy pool, and disgraced with a garment of rushes. After this had sufficiently tormented the eyes of those who grieved and satisfied the eyes of those who laughed, he was taken from there to another place, where none of our people dared to go, and was released only on the twelfth day. I complained of this myself to your bishop of Hippo, Proculeianus, and indeed did so in the municipal records, so that, if anything had to be done, he could not deny that it had been reported to him. What he answered, how he evaded inquiring into the case, and how he thought our charge should be slyly dodged afterwards even by giving no answer, the same records amply testify. And now, how can we manage to tell how much the clergy who have crossed over to us from you suffer at the hands of your people? In short, it is not that all who come to us from there abandon the truth because of persecution; rather, many do not come to us from there because they fear to suffer persecution from your people for the sake of the truth.

So put away the needless odium you stir up over the troubles you suffer by royal orders on account of your error. They are very small and almost nothing compared with the great fury of your people. And you blame us also for things done by the earthly powers themselves, out of necessity and not by choice, to drive the attacks of your people away from their own safety. For if those forty men who had sworn to kill the apostle Paul had rushed upon the armed men who were escorting him and been punished, this would not have been blamed on Paul. I pass over the fact that you lyingly lay at our door even the voluntary deaths which your people inflict on themselves. As for Marculus, I have heard that he threw himself down. This is certainly more credible than that any Roman authority could have ordered something so very unusual under Roman law, since among all the heresies that wander about under the Christian name this evil is peculiar to your heresy. What good is it, then, that your bishops boast that they have forbidden and condemned this in their councils, as you yourself mentioned, when so many crags and sheer rocks are defiled with death every day as a result of that Marculian teaching? I have told you, then, what I have heard about Marculus and why it may seem more credible; what is actually true, God knows. As for the other three, whose deaths you likewise threw in our face, I confess that I have not asked those whom I think would know what happened or how it was done.

None of the good in the Catholic Church, however, approves of anyone being treated savagely to the point of death, even a heretic. Nor do we approve when, even short of anyone's death, a lust for revenge repays evil for evil by harassment. Much more do we detest it if anyone, seizing the chance of acting as though for the sake of unity, carries off what belongs to others: not the things which ought not to be held by heretics under the name of the church, but people's private property. All these things displease the good, and they forbid and restrain them as far as they can. What they cannot prevent they endure, and, as I said, they praiseworthily tolerate it for the sake of peace, judging these deeds not praiseworthy but damnable. They do not abandon Christ's crop because of the weeds, nor Christ's threshing floor because of the chaff, nor Christ's great house because of the vessels for dishonourable use, nor Christ's nets because of the bad fish.

When kings are in error, they make laws on behalf of that error against the truth; when they are in the truth, they likewise decree on behalf of that truth against error. So the good are tested by bad laws, and the bad are corrected by good laws. King Nebuchadnezzar, while perverse, gave a cruel law that the image should be worshipped; the same king, once corrected, gave a stern law that the true God should not be blasphemed. For in this kings serve God, as they are divinely commanded to do, in so far as they are kings: if in their kingdom they command what is good and forbid what is evil, not only in matters that concern human society but also in those that concern divine religion.

It is no use your saying, 'Let me be left to my free will.' Why do you not proclaim that you should be left to your free will in murders, in sexual crimes, and in all other crimes and outrages? Yet it is most useful and most wholesome that all these should be restrained by just laws. God did indeed give man a free will, but he did not want a good will to be without fruit or an evil will to go unpunished. 'Whoever persecutes a Christian,' you say, 'is an enemy of Christ.' What you say is true, but only if he does not persecute in that person what is hostile to Christ. For when both are Christians, are not a master in his slave, a father in his son, a husband in his wife, bound to persecute vices contrary to Christian truth? Or if they do not persecute them, will they not deservedly be held guilty of negligence? But in all things a measure must be kept that suits humanity and accords with charity, so that not everything within one's power is put into force; that in what is put into force love is not lost; and that in what is not put into force gentleness is shown. And where no power is granted by divine or human laws, nothing should be ventured wickedly and rashly.

Hear now what I put off a little earlier about the Maximianists, so that you may know that your bishops have lied to you, and may know that this one case of the Maximianists settles not only the question of baptism and of tolerating the sins of others in the church without being defiled oneself, but also the odium of persecution, in which your people have surpassed against us all the laws and forces of Rome. For I am greatly amazed how you let yourself be deceived by some liar or other, if you did not find it tiresome to read that memorable sentence of the council of your three hundred and ten bishops at Bagai, which I quoted above as far as seemed sufficient. Its words show most plainly that the twelve by whose hands Maximianus was ordained in their presence were condemned along with Maximianus, and that a delay for returning to your communion was granted to those who, although they were in Maximianus' communion and had condemned Primianus, were nevertheless not present when Maximianus was ordained; for not all of them could have been present, or [?] ought to have been. You could have read aloud the very words, which are not obscure and do not demand a sharp mind to examine them, only attention to notice them, so as not to be deceived by him. But since it may be that you have not read it, and in simple good faith readily believed a bishop or bishops who suggested otherwise to you, take it, read it, and see how truly I am speaking to you. For they cannot correct it, or rather falsify it, as they please in order to cover up their lie, since they produced it in a public trial before the proconsul and so often had it inserted in the municipal records for the needs of their case, when they were proceeding against those people to have them driven out of their basilicas.

This, certainly, is how that sentence begins: 'While we were holding a council in the church of Bagai by the will of Almighty God and of his Christ, we, Gamalius, Primianus, Pontius, Secundianus, Januarianus, Saturninus, Felix, Pegasius, Rufinus, Fortunius, Crispinus, Florentius, Optatus, Donatus, Donatianus and the rest, three hundred and ten in number, it pleased the Holy Spirit who is in us to establish lasting peace and to cut off sacrilegious schisms.' Then, after it had spewed out many horrible things against them, a little further on it says: 'The thunderbolt of the sentence has struck Maximianus, the rival of the faith, the corrupter of the truth, the enemy of mother church, the minister of Dathan, Korah and Abiram, from the bosom of peace.' You see, I think, that Maximianus was condemned without any doubt. Then, after a few remarks, but very harsh ones, which it chose to declaim against him, it adds his ordainers and condemns them with him without any delay: 'Nor is he alone,' it says, 'condemned by the just death of his crime; the chain of sacrilege also drags very many into partnership in the crime.' Then, after pouring out against them too whatever it thought should be declaimed to magnify their crime, it named them and thus concluded that they were condemned: 'Know, therefore,' it says, 'that those guilty of the notorious crime, Victorianus of Carcabia, Marcianus of Sullecthum, Beianus of Beia, Salvius of Ausafa, Theodorus of Usula, Donatus of Sabratha, Miggin of Elephantaria, Praetextatus of Assuras, Salvius of Membressa, Valerius of Melzi, Felicianus of Musti and Martialis of Pertusa, who by the deadly work of perdition glued together a filthy vessel out of collected dregs, and also those who were once clergy of the church of Carthage, who, by taking part in the crime, acted as go-betweens for an unlawful incest, have been condemned by the judgment of God who presides over us, through the truthful mouth of the universal council.' What could be said more plainly, more openly, more explicitly?

Now hear to whom a delay was granted, so that you may see that these were the ones who were not present when hands were laid on Maximian at his ordination. "But those," it says, "whom the shoots of the sacrilegious plant did not defile, that is, those who in the modest shame of faith withheld their own hands from Maximian's head, we have permitted to return to mother church." You see how it does not say that these are condemned, but that they are to be held by the same sentence of condemnation only if they refuse to return once the appointed day has passed. They fix that day as follows: "And lest too short a time, with the pressure of a cramped deadline, take away the hope of salvation from those returning, we open the door of acknowledgment to all who acknowledge their fault, to whom this is permitted, the earlier statutes remaining in force, until the eighth day before the Kalends of January next coming, so that those who return may keep the foundations of their honour and faith intact. If anyone through sluggish idleness fails to enter by it, let him know that by his own will the way to every avenue of pardon has been taken from him. For the sentence pronounced will remain upon them, and a fixed penance on those who return after the appointed day."

Surely you now see, most eloquent sir, that everything you thought fit to say against us, as though we had lied about this matter, you ought rather to turn back against those from whom you heard the lie. Surely you see that the two men we are dealing with belong among those who were condemned without delay along with Maximian, twelve of them, and not among those who were granted time to return. Surely it is plain, clear and evident, and can in no way be confused, obscured or covered up, since the author of that sentence distinguished, illuminated and expressed it with such eloquence. Why are people still being deceived? Why do men still fight for a manifest error against the most luminous truth? Why do people deceive themselves? If they bind the devil's snares, which they ought to loosen and break, ever more tightly about themselves and wrap themselves in them, then hear something more, at which they may blush more deeply—and I wish it might be with some fruit of correction.

In the council of Bagai already mentioned, the day and the consul are recorded not only for the issuing of the council's decree but also for the delay itself. So from the eighth day before the Kalends of May, after the consulship of Theodosius Augustus for the third time and of Abundantius, which is the date of the council of Bagai, to the eighth day before the Kalends of January, which is the date set by the delay, nearly eight months are counted. Now there is found a petition made before the proconsul Herodes—see how long afterwards—against Felicianus and Praetextatus, for their removal from the places of Musti and Assuras. I have appended a little of it: "After the consulship of our lords Arcadius for the third time and Honorius for the second time, Augusti, on the sixth day before the Nones of March, at Carthage, in the council chamber of the praetorium, Titianus said: The priest Peregrinus and the elders of the church of the region of Musti and Assuras present the following request: When Donatus, a man of venerable memory, was defending the holiness of the catholic church from the error of faithlessness, the observance of almost the whole world, nourished in his name and practice, grew together into one. But when the poison of a certain Maximian defiled the praiseworthy and admirable purpose of that religion, an assembly of many bishops, gathered together as God breathed one mind into them, condemned that man, or rather that plague, which displeased the majesty on high, with the proper discipline of a pure mind as well. Those too whom the error of another's presumption had drawn away it restrained with an admonition of equal vigour, first offering them the harbour of repentance, if they wished to return to the path of religion within the appointed time. But wickedness delights in its own ways and does not abandon itself once it has fallen headlong. For this same Maximian feeds the audacity he has begun and joins others to himself in his madness. Among them a certain Felicianus, who at first followed what was right and is now darkened by the contamination of this depravity, being stationed in the city of Musti, thought he could hold the walls consecrated to almighty God, the venerable church, as if by a kind of siege. Praetextatus imitates him in the district of Assuras. But when the council of bishops became known to the authority of your equity, you ordered, as the records testify, that all effect of opposition being rejected, the churches claimed back from profane minds must be restored to the most holy bishops." You see, of course, that from the delay granted until the day of this petition nearly three months' time had passed. Moreover, so far as we have been able to trace from the proconsular and municipal records, this conflict dragged on up to the proconsul Theodorus, that is, up to the eleventh day before the Kalends of January of the following year. On that day the clergy and elders acting under Bishop Rogatus, who had been put in the place of the condemned Praetextatus of Assuras, cited the order of the said proconsul, while those men were still outside your communion and were being arraigned in the public courts as enemies of that same communion of yours, and their expulsion as sacrilegious men was being sought from places consecrated to the supreme God.

Whichever group they belonged to, then—although it is clear enough which one it was—since they did not restore themselves to your communion within the day fixed for the delay, how could they, estranged from you for all that time, baptize? How did they return together with those whom they had baptized outside your communion, without those people being purified by another baptism? In this matter we do not blame you: that you recognized that the baptism of Christ is in no way sacrilegious even within a sacrilegious schism; that once the perversity of men was corrected you approved what had been right even among the perverse; that you did not confuse human vices with divine sacraments; that you judged that the gifts of the church, which could be held and given outside the church as well—though to the punishment of those who have and receive them—were neither to be condemned in the condemned nor changed in those received back.

Nor do we blame you for this: that these same men, guilty of a notorious crime, even after the sentence condemning them and after the day of delay set for the others, you nevertheless believed should be gathered back without any degradation and purified by the very abundance of charity, for the sake of the weak peoples who had clung to them—remembering, I suppose, the householder's concern that the wheat should not be rooted up together with the weeds. Nor do we blame you for persecuting them, even through the earthly powers, while they were still held in the notorious sacrilege of schism. For this was done, as the outcome itself showed, out of a desire to correct, not to harm, so that, shaken by those troubles, they might be forced to reflect on their crime and, once the fury of their animosity was checked, to amend it. But it is precisely because we do not blame these things that we rightly fault, justly detest and by every argument convict the crime of your schism, by which you separate yourselves from us, or rather from the catholic communion of the whole world, by charging us with the very sort of things which, I think, you cannot deny that you did in the case of the Maximianists. For if the baptism given through Felicianus and Praetextatus, when they were separated from you and joined to Maximian and condemned with him by you for the crime of wicked schism, is the baptism of Christ and therefore in no way to be destroyed, how is it not the baptism of Christ, or how is it to be destroyed, when it is given in the church which, to use Cyprian's words, "stretches its branches over the whole earth in rich abundance"; when, finally, it is given in those churches which you have never ceased to read out in the apostolic letters, and which you have never condemned in any council as you condemned Felicianus and Praetextatus? If you saw fit to restore the condemned to their full standing in order to repair the party of Donatus, why are you offended by the unity of Christ spread through the whole world, which could not condemn men unheard, or which neither condemned nor acquitted men it did not know at all, or which believed those to be innocent whom it learned had been acquitted? If you persecuted the Maximianists who broke away from you and drove them from their sees by the orders of judges, why do you complain that you suffer undeserved treatment through the emperors who send those same judges—you who by a wicked schism have cut yourselves off from the church of him of whom it is written that "all the kings of the earth shall worship him, all nations shall serve him," and that "he shall have dominion from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth"?

See, I no longer say, "If it is not lawful to persecute, Optatus persecuted," lest you go on saying that whatever Optatus did without your people's knowledge has nothing to do with them—though your people themselves do not allow the lands most remote from Africa to say that whatever Caecilian did without their knowledge has nothing to do with them: "Who were traitors in Africa, what evil the African bishops did, we do not know." But I say plainly: if it is not lawful to persecute, your people persecuted the Maximianists in a way you cannot deny. If those who suffer persecution are innocent, the Maximianists suffered it. Will you now say this too: "The people destroyed the basilica, or rather the cave, of Maximian at the instigation of none of ours"? And yet, if one inquired what communion that mob belonged to—granted they be believed not to have been sent in by your people—perhaps they themselves would be found to be yours, or at least mingled with yours and helping them. But what is that to us? For you answer: "We did not do it, we did not send them in, we do not know who they were." Still, since it is a clear fact that the man whom you admit to be unjust suffered persecution from someone or other, the things you suffer cannot prove you just. But the proconsular records testify by whom the Maximianists, too, suffered persecution. Advocates were briefed, courts were approached and roused as though against heretics; those men, being in possession, asked for protection for themselves; your people cited the council of Bagai and demanded that the condemned be driven from the sacred sees; the matter was pressed, the case was pleaded, and in the presence of Salvius of Membressa you showed them to be heretics, you won, you drove them out. I see, then, that they suffered persecution and that you carried it out. I ask which side is just: you will claim that you are. I conclude: it does not follow, then, that he who suffers persecution is just, nor that he who carries it out is unjust.

You will again denounce the arts of dialectic; yet you will at least silently grant that I speak the truth, and you will choose to correct your own statement that no persecution is just rather than call unjust the persecutors of the Maximianists, whom you have at last recognized from the proconsular records to be your own. Indeed, it was not without fruit that you persecuted the error of your own schismatics, for by that very conflict and those troubles you corrected Felicianus and Praetextatus. And the people of Musti and Assuras are said—as I too heard from them in person—to have feared Optatus the Gildonian when he threatened them with heavier ruin, and to have forced their bishops to return to the communion of Primian. But since Optatus enforced this without any public records, why should I use such things against you, when you are ready to deny whatever you can deny? The proconsular and municipal acts survive, and by reading them we have shown how forcefully the men in question were pressed by your people to give up their places. We do not blame you, we do not begrudge it: you did not labour for nothing, you did not frighten them in vain, you did not harass them to no purpose. In their affliction their own animosity came to displease them; they were broken, they were amended, they were corrected and received back—after their own condemnation, after the delay granted to others, after your persecution. And they were received back with the honour they had held, neither purified nor degraded by the humiliation of any heavier penance—neither they themselves nor those with whom they were received back, whom they had separated with themselves against you, whom they had baptized outside you, and whom perhaps they had rebaptized after you.

You no longer have any means of heaping murky lies on people ignorant of events long past. That your people accused Caecilian before Constantine, who was then emperor, the public records proclaim. That the case was pleaded and brought to its due conclusion, as far as the clearing of Felix of Abthugni, the consecrator of Caecilian—whom they called "the source of all evils" in the council of Carthage and accused before the same Constantine with persistent petitions, as he himself indicates in his writings—the proconsular archives testify. You resist, you protest, you fight against the plainest truth; you even say that the judges overseas were bribed by Caecilian and that the emperor himself was corrupted by some favour or other—for a defeated accuser is all the more shameless when he also becomes a slanderer of the judge. Yet amid all those lies of yours with which you slander the judges overseas, we at least establish this: that your forefathers were the first to bring this case before the emperor, the first to accuse Caecilian and his consecrator before the emperor, the first to persecute Caecilian and his colleagues before the emperor. So when you stir up very heavy odium against us, as it seems to you, because in defeat you suffer what you would certainly have done as victors, it is as though those men wished to bring a charge against Daniel who, when he was set free as innocent, were themselves devoured by the very lions by which they had wanted him devoured through their false accusation. We also establish this: whatever you think or pretend about the judges before whom Caecilian, present in person, was acquitted in the trial overseas, and whatever about the emperor Constantine himself—before whom your forefathers accused Caecilian, and whose judgment they finally chose in preference to the judgment of bishops—as though he had been corrupted by favour, nevertheless all the catholic Christians then spread so far and wide, in lands near or remote, whom the report about Caecilian and his colleagues could reach, ought to have believed not the defeated accusers but the ecclesiastical judges. For where we cannot all be judges, we do better to believe those who could be, than, by believing defeated litigants whose judges we could not be, to dare to sit in judgment on the judges themselves.

Therefore, since those on whose accusation Caecilian, present in person, was acquitted have tried with the most audacious wickedness to drench with Caecilian's crimes—either invented or at any rate unproven—not only those by whom he was acquitted, but also all catholic Christians established among any nations whatever, who either knew nothing at all of that African dissension or, in it, chose to believe the judges pronouncing at their own peril, as they saw fit, rather than the defeated accusers; and since they have tried to deny that any of these are Christians: the case of the Maximianists was at long last sent to you, in which you yourselves would condemn, you yourselves would persecute the condemned, you yourselves would receive back the persecuted in the same honour, you yourselves would accept the baptism of the condemned—so that those who dared to accuse the innocent would be compelled to acquit the guilty: not men whom they had believed innocent, but men whom, as they say, they had condemned "by the judgment of God presiding, through the truthful mouth" of their plenary council. Who ever said to anyone: "Because you believed the judge who acquitted rather than me who accused, you are guilty along with those whom I accused"? And yet this is said to the Christian world—something that, if it were said to a single man, would seem, I will not say most unjust, but utterly insane. O wondrously shameful thing! Africans accused Africans of the crime of handing over the scriptures; judges overseas acquitted the accused; and the peoples of the nations became traitors because they believed the judges who acquitted rather than the accusers who brought the charge.

Deservedly, party of Donatus, has the case of the Maximianists been served to you to drink: drink the cup from the hand of the Lord who rebukes and warns. If you understand and submit, this is the mercy of one who corrects you, so that you may not fall into the judgment of one who punishes. To you it is said: You of proud and stiff neck, be reconciled to the Christian peoples everywhere whom you have unjustly accused, now that you have at least been reconciled to those you yourself condemned. Why do you cancel the baptism of Christ in those churches which the apostles founded, or in those who come from them? You have already accepted the baptism which your condemned men gave before they were reconciled to you. Why do you boast of the persecution you suffer? If it is a sign of righteousness, the party of Maximian is more righteous, for it has suffered from you and also suffers along with you. Hear the divine psalm: "Do not be like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding." For you call us your persecutors when, desiring your salvation, we pursue with medicine your wounds which we want to heal; and for this, while we are treating you, we are grievously afflicted by your clergy and circumcellions, as if by your teeth and your hooves. Do not be ungrateful for such medicine, which you yourselves have imitated: you too corrected Felicianus and Praetextatus by persecution. And would that you corrected the whole thing, and that, just as they returned to you, so you too would return to your catholic mother!

Against her, brother Cresconius, you have been carried away with such audacity that you try to refute even the divine testimonies I cited and to shout down the voice of God. For in that letter which you are attacking I set down what is in the holy book about the seed of Abraham, where God says to that father of ours: "In your seed shall all nations be blessed." The apostle calls this a testament, saying: "Brothers, I speak in human terms: even a man's testament, once ratified, no one annuls or adds to. The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed. It does not say 'and to seeds,' as of many, but as of one, 'and to your seed,' which is Christ." So abundant a fruitfulness was promised to this seed that it was said to him: "So shall your seed be, like the stars of heaven and like the sand of the sea, which cannot be numbered." To this multiplication and abundance of the church, which is spreading through the whole world, which is believed to have been prophesied in this way and is displayed in this way even before the eyes of all unbelievers, so that it shuts the mouths even of the pagans, very few of whom are left to oppose it—to this you dare to prefer the party of Donatus. You say that you have some people or other outside Africa too, though, since they are nowhere to be seen, you do not deny that you are accustomed to send them bishops from Africa—one, or two, or at most three. And you argue emptily against the most evident truth that the whole world is not in communion with us because there are still many barbarian nations which have not yet believed in Christ, or many heresies under the name of Christ estranged from the communion of our fellowship.

You do not consider, nor do you even ask those who know, how many of those very barbarian nations you mentioned have already been given over to the name of Christ, and how the gospel, as it grows, does not cease to bear fruit among the rest, until, when it has been preached among them all, the end comes. For so the Lord himself says: "And this gospel shall be preached in the whole world as a testimony to all nations, and then the end will come." Unless perhaps your insane pride drives you headlong into such a precipice that you think what was foretold is to begin from the party of Donatus, and not from those churches which the apostles planted, with which the party of Donatus is not in communion. Or will it try to rebaptize those churches too, so as to fill the world, when, as the catholic church grows everywhere, that party is shrinking every day even in Africa itself? O mad perversity of men! You think yourself praised for believing concerning Christ what you do not see, and you do not think yourself condemned for denying concerning the church what you do see, when that head is in heaven and this body is on earth.

You recognize Christ in what is written: "Be exalted above the heavens, O God," yet you do not recognize the Church in what follows: "and your glory over all the earth." You recognize Christ in what is written: "They pierced my hands and feet; they counted all my bones. They looked and stared at me; they divided my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots," yet you do not recognize the Church in what follows a little later: "All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations shall worship in his sight, for the kingdom is the Lord's, and he shall rule over the nations." You recognize Christ in what is written: "Give the king your judgment, O God, and your righteousness to the king's son," yet you do not recognize the Church in what the same psalm bears witness to: "He shall rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth. The Ethiopians shall fall down before him, and his enemies shall lick the dust. The kings of Tarshish and the islands shall offer gifts; the kings of the Arabs and of Sheba shall bring presents. All the kings of the earth shall worship him; all nations shall serve him." You recognize Christ where it is said to the Jews: "I take no pleasure in you, says the Lord Almighty, and I will not accept sacrifices from your hands"—since the coming of Christ did indeed do away with all those sacrifices of the Jews—yet you do not recognize the Church in what follows: "For from the rising of the sun to its setting my name is glorified among the nations, and in every place incense shall be offered to my name, and a pure offering; for my name is great among the nations, says the Lord Almighty." You recognize Christ in what the prophet says: "He was led like a sheep to the slaughter," and the rest that is read there about him as if in the Gospel, yet you do not recognize the Church in what he says a little later: "Rejoice, O barren one, who do not bear; break forth and cry out, you who are not in labor, for the children of the desolate woman are more than those of her who has a husband. For the Lord has said: Enlarge the place of your tent and set up your courts—there is no reason to hold back; lengthen your cords, strengthen your stout stakes; spread out again and again to the right and to the left. For your offspring shall inherit the nations, and you shall inhabit the cities that were desolate. There is no reason to fear, for you will prevail; nor be ashamed that you were once despised. For you will forget your shame forever, and you will no longer remember the disgrace of your widowhood. For I am the Lord who makes you—the Lord is his name—and he who delivers you, the God of Israel himself, shall be called the God of the whole earth."

It was certainly in these holy writings that Cyprian learned what the Church is, so that he could say: "So the Church of the Lord, bathed in light, has sent forth her rays through the whole world; in the abundance of her fruitfulness she has stretched out her branches over all the earth." Yet you, Cresconius, raise false objections against this great clarity of the divine utterances by looking at the remaining nations which the Church has not yet taken hold of; you pay no attention to how many she has already taken hold of, from which she spreads out daily to take hold of the rest. How could you fail to deny the future completion of these prophecies, when you do not hesitate to deny the great progress to which that completion will be owed—and to deny it, I will not say against the divine voices, but now even against your own? For the great force of truth itself wrung even from you, without your knowing or noticing what you were saying, the statement that the whole world is daily turning to the Christian name. Why then does the party of Donatus not hold communion with this Church, which spreads by growing throughout the whole world? Clearly, so as not to be polluted by sinners. Then what becomes of Cyprian's words? He refused to forsake—not this church of yours, which stays in Africa and slanders the world, or travels out of Africa to live abroad among a few hidden people, but that Church which in the abundance of her fruitfulness stretches out her branches over all the earth—even though in her communion sinners not only exist but are plainly visible; and he said: "For although there seem to be tares in the Church, neither our faith nor our charity ought to be hindered, so that, because we see there are tares in the Church, we ourselves withdraw from the Church."

You too must answer this, if you care to answer anything true. And how will what is written be fulfilled: "A wicked son calls himself righteous, but does not wash away his going out"? Let this expose the wicked son: let him condemn and persecute the Maximianists, and then be reconciled with those he condemned and persecuted—and so let him be convicted, so let him be put to shame, or so let him be corrected. "How," you ask, "is the whole world full of your communion, when there are so many heresies, not one of which is in communion with you?" On the contrary, the world is full not only of heretics but of other wicked people as well, and the world is also full of holy and faithful servants of God, just as the sea is full of bitter waves and is also full of sweet fish.

"Truth," you say, "is often found among the few; error belongs to the many." And so that your words would not seem to contradict the great fruitfulness of that barren woman to whom it was said, "The children of the desolate woman are more than those of her who has a husband," you brought in a testimony from the Gospel: "For few are those who are saved." Then solve the question: how does the Lord himself say, "How narrow and strait is the way that leads to life, and few there are who find it," and yet the same Lord says elsewhere, "Many will come from the east and the west and will recline with Abraham and Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven"? How, too, is there shown in the Revelation their multitude which no one can number, from every nation and tribe and tongue, wearing white robes and carrying palms, who had endured tribulations for the faith of Christ? How are the same people both few and many? For it is not that one of these is true and the other false, since both were spoken by divine truth. The only answer is that the same good and true Christians who are many in themselves are likewise few in comparison with the bad and false. In the same way, we call the many grains with which great barns are filled few in comparison with the chaff. In the same way, too—to speak of God's own covenant made with Abraham concerning his seed, which is Christ—we call the many stars, which we cannot count and with which the vast sky shines all around, few in comparison with the sand of the sea. Perhaps the stars signified spiritual Christians and the sand of the sea carnal ones, through whom and from whom heresies and schisms also arise. Yet the world is full of both kinds, for the same Lord says, "The field is this world," and you yourself, with truth wringing it from you, said, "The whole world is daily turning to the name of Christ." Throughout the whole field, then—that is, throughout the whole world—there is wheat, and throughout the whole of it there are tares, since he who cannot be deceived said of both: "Let both grow until the harvest."

So let the impious deserters of the wheat that grows in such abundance throughout the whole world restrain themselves, and not dare to boast of the fewness of some separated tares. If they do boast, then even on this very point those same Maximianists stand against them, set there by divine judgment to put them to shame in every respect and, if they have any sense, to correct them. For the Donatists, trusting in their own numbers, persecuted the far fewer Maximianists, and by persecuting them brought some of them back into their own communion—and so left the rest all the more righteous for being so very few.

"The East," you say, "is not in communion with Africa, nor Africa with the East." Not, indeed, in the heretical chaff separated from the Lord's threshing floor; but in the catholic wheat and in the chaff still inside, the East is wholly in communion with Africa and Africa with the East. For some heretics here, others there, and others somewhere else again are in conflict with the catholic unity spread everywhere. She is everywhere, and from her went out those who could by no means be everywhere, saying, as was foretold of them, "Look, here is Christ; look, there he is," some in this place and others in another, each displaying their own little fragments of their presumptions, or rather their amputations, and with impious pride denying the root from which they were broken off. To this Church, then—which with abundant success, as she spreads throughout the whole world, bears from every nation, tribe and tongue a multitude clothed in white and bearing palms, which no one can number, as is written in the Revelation—to this Church, I say, with which the party of Donatus is plainly not in communion, your forebears ought to have proved whatever true documents they had about the traditors. Had they done so, they would themselves be within her, and those they accused would be outside her. But now, since we see that the accused remained within her, what good can we think of the accusers, whom we see outside her? And so, in that fourfold division of mine—where I said that when documents concerning the traditors are produced by both sides, either both sets are true, or both are false, or ours are true and yours false, or ours are false and yours true—since you saw that in the first three you would be defeated very easily, you chose this last one in vain, as though it were a way of escape. For although you notice how shameless it is to say so, even so, those true documents of yours, if any such human documents existed, ought to have been proved before that Church which the divine documents prove.

Tell me, I beg you—but do not pour fog over the unlearned, so that, since you cannot convict the accused traditors, you keep trying to accuse the arts of dialectic instead—tell me, then, I ask you: was this case of yours, with your true documents, brought to the judgment of the churches overseas that were founded by the labor of the apostles, or was it not? If it was brought, did you win in that judgment or were you defeated? If you say you won, why did you not hold communion with those churches in whose judgment you won? But if you were defeated—as the very estrangement of your communion from them shows clearly enough—why do you quarrel with us over a case that was lost, whether it was bad or good? Your greatest crime is this: you smear the Christian world with the crime of traditors whom, even producing true documents, you were utterly unable to convict in the judgment of the churches overseas—and you do it because, in a case at which the world could not be present, it chose to believe the judges rather than the defeated accusers. So you are not guilty because you lost a good case (to speak your way) in the judgment overseas, but because you do not hesitate to charge the crime of the accused—and, to concede you far too much, of the judges as well—against so many innocent Christian peoples spread far and wide through so many nations. Holding fast to their communion as to the Lord's wheat, you ought, according to the Gospel writings and with Cyprian too admonishing you, to have tolerated as chaff until the time of winnowing both those men, traditors as you call them, and those judges, wicked as you think them, so as not to perish by deserting the threshing floor. But if that case of yours, with its true documents (the option you chose), was not brought to the judgment of the churches overseas, how could so many bishops, established among their own congregations, be rightly condemned by those churches in a case they never examined and that was never brought before them at all? Or how ought the African Christians—I do not mean those who had thought these men innocent, but even those, if there were any, who knew them to be traditors—to have separated themselves, because of the tares they saw in the Church, from the plain innocence of the wheat growing so far and wide and knowing nothing of these men? For then, because of another's crime, by which they would not have been stained had they tolerated it for the sake of unity, they would have been condemned for the crime of violating unity itself.

What good, then, does it do your case to have chosen, out of those four propositions, that your documents are true and that those we produce against your people are to be reckoned false? See, here too you are beaten, because the traditors could not be convicted where they ought to have been by what you take to be your true documents—whether those documents were hidden by your own people, or the traditors themselves hid from the judges by some cunning, or they were hidden by the corrupt judges themselves. Look at the seed of Abraham, which according to God's covenant is growing through all nations like the stars of heaven and like the sand of the sea, and then dare to say, dare to believe—dare, if there is any fear of God in you, even to think—that so abundant a harvest throughout the field of the world could have perished because of some African tares or other, concealed for whatever reasons.

You exaggerate the persecutions you claim to suffer, though you are spared with wonderful gentleness while you rebel with such sacrilegious and open obstinacy against the peace of the holy Church. And you say in the opening parts of your letter that when Caecilian's crime became plain to the emperor Constantine, he too condemned him by his own sentence to live in exile at Brescia. Who could doubt that in this you are either deceived or deceiving, when you also claimed that Felix of Aptunga was convicted of surrendering the Scriptures in the proconsul's court by some Ingentius or other?

Here I insert the sentence of the proconsul Aelianus, by which Felix was cleared and acquitted. If you want to read the whole proceedings, get them from the proconsul's archive. Aelianus the proconsul said: "From the statement of Caecilianus, who says that the records are false and that much was added to the letter, it is clear with what intention Ingentius did these things, and he will therefore be taken back into prison, for he is required for a stricter interrogation. But it is clear that Felix, the devout bishop, is free of the charge of burning the divine documents, since no one has been able to prove anything against him, namely that he handed over or burned the sacred scriptures. For the interrogation of all those named above makes it clear that no divine scriptures were found, damaged or burned. The records show that Felix, the devout bishop, was not present at that time, gave no consent, and ordered no such thing to be done."

I also insert the rescript of the emperor Constantine to Probianus, which attests this very thing and shows how troublesome your forebears were to him as accusers of the innocent. "The Emperors and Caesars Flavius Constantine, Maximinus, and Valerius Licinianus Licinius, to Probianus, proconsul of Africa. Your predecessor Aelianus, acting in place of Verus, one of the perfectissimi and vicar of the prefects, who was at that time held by ill health in our Africa, rightly judged that among other matters this affair, or rather this ill-will, which appears to have been stirred up against Bishop Caecilian and the catholic church, should be brought back for his examination and decision. For when he had caused Superius the centurion, Caecilianus the magistrate of Aptungi, Saturninus the former curator, Calibius the younger, curator of the same city, and Solus, the public slave of that city, to be present, he gave a proper hearing. As a result, since it had been objected against Caecilian that he appeared to have been raised to the episcopate by Felix, who seemed to be charged with betraying and burning the divine scriptures, it was established that Felix was innocent in the matter. Further, since Maximus contended that Ingentius, a decurion of the city of Ziqua, had forged the letter of Caecilianus the former duumvir, we saw from the attached records that this same Ingentius had been put on the rack but not tortured, because he asserted that he was a decurion of the city of Ziqua. We therefore wish you to send this same Ingentius under suitable escort to the court of me, Constantine Augustus, so that, in the hearing and presence of those who are now pleading here and who do not cease to petition day after day, it may be shown and made known to them that they have tried in vain to stir up ill-will against Bishop Caecilian and to rise violently against him. In this way it will come about that, once such disputes have been dropped, as is fitting, the people may serve their own religion with due reverence and without any dissension."

I further insert the words of Constantine from his letter to Eumalius the vicar, where he testifies that he examined the case between the parties and found Caecilian innocent. For after relating, in the earlier part of the letter, how the parties were brought to his tribunal following the judgments of the bishops, he says: "In which I saw clearly that Caecilian was a man endowed with every innocence, fulfilling the due duties of his religion and serving it as he ought; and it plainly appeared that no crime could be found in him such as had been fabricated against him in his absence by the deceit of his adversaries."

Why did you not insert the sentence of Constantine by which, you say, Caecilian was condemned and placed in exile at Brescia, most eloquent sir? How much more fitting it would have been to insert this than something or other about the Council of Serdica, which can be shown to have nothing at all to do either with you or with the case that is between us and you! For why Caecilian was at Brescia—which you most slanderously call exile—when he preferred that the church should lack his presence rather than peace, what need is there for me to say? Meanwhile you cite no sentence of an emperor condemning him, and yet you think it right rashly—I will not say to listen to or to say, but even to write—that Caecilian was condemned by the emperor. Nevertheless, taking your words as they stand, see, I picture Caecilian in exile under the emperor's condemnation. At least answer: at whose accusation? And now put to me the question which, after many empty things, you set down just as emptily in your letter: "Who agrees less with the testament that has been produced, the one who suffers persecution or the one who inflicts it?" These are certainly your words. Look, then, at Caecilian suffering persecution and, as you yourself said, placed in exile; look also at your own people, who, as the emperor himself testifies in his own words, did not cease day after day to petition against Caecilian; and answer me when I ask you in those very same words of yours: who agrees less with the testament that has been produced, the one who suffers persecution or the one who inflicts it? If you read everything carefully you will find that Caecilian suffered persecution from your people even before the emperor. But you will not find that he was condemned by the emperor; on the contrary, you will find that he was acquitted.

Moreover, as to the point you chose as a great matter, namely that the documents you produce on the crimes of handing over the scriptures are true while those we produce are false: even here the truth of God overcomes you. As it foretold, so it shows the church bearing fruit and growing throughout the world, because documents about the crimes of others, even if true, do not prejudice it. Such documents, in the hands of the nearer bishops overseas, through whom the report of such things either passes or does not pass to more distant regions, either were not demonstrated as they should have been, or were not believed by those to whom they could have been demonstrated, or were believed but concealed and so never reached others. Nor can anyone—not even one man, much less so great a number of Christians settled among so many nations—be guilty of sharing in another's crime if he has learned of no true documents about it, or if someone feigning innocence has deceived him with false documents. If, then, as I had begun to say, even on this point which you chose as a great matter, granting that the testimonies you produce about the traditors are true and those produced against you are false, you have no power against the catholic church spread throughout the whole world and against the providence of God, by which, to use your own words, the whole world is daily turning to the Christian name, how much more do your accusations fail! For this very handing over—whose name those who made this schism pretended to shudder at, while, cut off from the body of Christ, they handed themselves over to the devil—we charge against you, as I said in that letter and say now, much more plausibly. We only ever hear you speak the names and crimes of traditors, whereas we produce both the ecclesiastical records in which they confessed about themselves and the municipal records in which they are read to have done it!

But you, a shrewd examiner and weigher of words, teach us the force of the comparative degree, and exult like a victor, because, you say, I could not have said "we charge you with handing over more plausibly" unless I admitted that you charge us with it plausibly. "For if you," you say, "more plausibly, then we plausibly." And you teach this: that "plausibly" and "more plausibly" are like saying "truly" and "more truly," and that this degree increases what is set before it and does not disprove what was said before it. You add other words to help us understand this more clearly, saying: so it is with "well" and "better," "badly" and "worse," "horribly" and "more horribly," thereby showing that "plausibly" and "more plausibly" work in the same way. From this you think it follows that, if I charge what is false more plausibly, it remains for you to confirm that you have charged what is true plausibly. Do I say here that, in an ecclesiastical question or debate, you are trying to teach us the technicalities of grammar—the force of the comparative degree, that it increases what is set before it and does not disprove what was said before it? For I see how ineptly I would charge you with what you yourself refused to see when you thought you should charge me with anticategoria as if it came from the art of rhetoric—a kind of argument, in which one says, "I did not do it, but you did," that I showed to be found even in the authority of the prophets.

Yet consider more carefully whether you may not find in the authors of the Latin language, whom the technicalities of the grammarians serve, that this degree does not always increase what is set before it, but sometimes is set above its opposite. An example of this usage occurs to me for the moment from the letter of the apostle which he wrote to the Hebrews. For when he was speaking of the blessing of the land which, having received the rain, yields fruit, he then added: "But if it bears thorns and thistles, it is rejected and near to a curse, and its end is burning." And lest he should seem to have wished this on those he was addressing, he says: "But we are confident of better things concerning you, dearest brothers, things that belong to salvation." You surely notice how he said "better" here, not because the things he had mentioned above—bearing thorns and thistles and deserving to be burned—were good, but rather because they were bad, so that, avoiding them, his hearers might choose and desire better things, that is, good things opposed to such great evils. But perhaps you think the apostle should be heard as he says of himself, as a man who, though unskilled in speech, is not so in knowledge, and that therefore the authority to be followed in him is not that of words but that of matters and thoughts; and you contend that he ought to have put "good" where he put "better." What if I too, now accustomed to these scriptures and having forgotten the literature I learned as a boy, spoke in the same way: "You charge us with handing over; we charge you with this very thing much more plausibly," as if I were saying "plausibly," putting the comparative for the positive—not because you charge it plausibly, but rather because you charge it implausibly—just as he said "better," not because those things were good, but rather because they were bad? Why do you so rashly conclude that, because I said "we more plausibly," I confirmed "you plausibly"?

And yet you would not reprove me for misusing the word even by the standards of the grammarians, if you had been willing at least to read attentively, or to recall from memory, the authors of those very words. For the schoolboy's books contain—though it was said by no unskilled boy—"May the gods grant better things to the pious, and that madness to their enemies!" and "they were tearing at their own mangled limbs with bare teeth." How then "better things" for the pious, as if those things were good, and not rather great evils, for men who were tearing at their mangled limbs with bare teeth? Surely you now see that, just as the poet could wish better things for the pious even though the things in comparison with which he wished them were not good, so I too could say, "we charge you with handing over more plausibly," even though you did not charge us with it plausibly. But I will pass over the point that, when something is called plausible, it does not follow that it is true. For things are so called that can happen and usually do, and are therefore approved, that is, accepted and believed, even if they have not happened; whereas what is true, when it is shown, is necessarily plausible, and certainly more plausible than the other. Look again at the book where you learned these words: you will surely find that I am not deceiving you.

Hence, even if I conceded that your people plausibly charged ours with handing over, I would not therefore maintain that they charged it truly; and I would rightly say that we charge it more plausibly, since we are used to hearing traditors merely named by you, but never shown by any records, ecclesiastical or public, read out and proved to have confessed; whereas we produce both the public records, in which your people handed over the scriptures, and the ecclesiastical records, in which, having confessed, they were left to God as their judge.

But I will not pass over the very obvious help you give us, by which, even without knowing it, you do us a great favor in teaching the rules of the comparative degree: that it increases what is set before it and does not disprove what was said before it. For according to this rule of yours, and according to certain words of yours in your letter, we have won our case without any difficulty. You said in the first part of your letter, as though accusing us of obstinacy, that so many legal documents could not persuade us of what is better and truer. From this I conclude, according to your technicalities, that we already hold what is true and good, if we cannot be persuaded of what is truer and better. Since, then, we do not annul your baptism, which, to speak your way, is truer and better, why do you annul ours, which is true and good? Again, when you had said, "We too want this, that Christ should be the origin, root and head of the Christian," you immediately added, "but we ask through whom this is done better." In saying this you certainly conceded that it is done well through a bad minister, but better through a good one. Since, therefore, we do not annul the baptism which you say is given through your minister as a good one, why do you annul the baptism which you contend was given through ours as a bad one? For you said, "we ask through whom it is done better," and your rule is that this degree increases what is set before it. Hence, if it is done better, as you think, through your minister, then it is done well through ours; and so, when you rebaptize someone baptized by us, you annul with sacrilegious presumption what by this rule of yours you concede was done well.

I fear I may press your modesty too hard if I show how frivolously and scurrilously, as though you were witty and sharp-tongued, you thought fit to mock even certain words of mine that I used figuratively: "brow" for shame, "mouth" for speech, "the trident weapon" for a speech in three parts, "the three-headed beast" for an error raging with three slanders against the innocence of so many peoples. Keep childish things for children instead. Nor am I troubled that you say Neptune's weapon, because it is a trident, does not befit a bishop, since it is also a fisherman's tool and therefore apostolic, for the Lord made his apostles fishers of men. For Scripture also says that our God has both wings and arrows, and yet we do not worship Cupid.

You even reproach me for not keeping the gentleness I promised at the outset, because, stirred by the mention of the Manichees, I said: "Just as, in the Lord's words, Satan cannot cast out Satan, so the error of the Donatists cannot overturn the error of the Manichees"—as though I had compared Petilian to Satan, and not the error from whose snares I long for him to be set free. It is good that the apostle armed us against such slanders in the very place where he urges us to be gentle, patient and modest when we correct someone who disagrees with us. For when he had said, "The Lord's servant must not quarrel, but be gentle toward all, ready to teach, patient, correcting with modesty those who think otherwise," he immediately added, "in the hope that God may grant them repentance so that they come to know the truth and recover their senses, escaping from the snares of the devil, by whom they are held captive to do his will." See the apostle's mildness! The very people with whom he commanded us to deal calmly, patiently and modestly he describes as taken captive by the devil; and yet he did not lose the gentleness he was commending, because he refused to keep silent about the truth he was teaching.

But see for yourself whose part you are playing, when, by accusing my words of being abusive and savage, you try to rouse to quarreling those whom you do not want to come together for debate; for I would rather not say that you too take pleasure in quarreling. More sparingly and modestly, it is true, but as if obliquely, you charge me with things that have nothing at all to do with me. As for what I think of the most pestilential folly of the Manichees, which all Christians must anathematize: even if I were only in the habit of saying so, and did not also bear witness to it in many books of many kinds, not even then would there be any ground for your slander against me. For it would be no wonder that I, a catholic, am falsely accused by you, since by you the whole Christian world, with so many churches—even those first planted by the labor of the apostles—is accused of false crimes. But since anyone who wishes can read all that I have written against the Manichees, who once deceived me when I was a young man, no one is so foolish as to believe your words about me rather than his own eyes and senses.

"But," you say, "not a few of our people have the letter of your primate in which he wrote something or other about you when he did not want you to be ordained." I would not care about that letter at all, even if there were not read, from the very man by whom it is said to have been written, a clear sentence in our favor condemning that slander and falsehood. How much less does the catholic church care about it, whose case we are pleading against you! It relies on so many divine testimonies that no human testimonies about any man, whether true or false, can take from it the truth in which it rejoices. Stop such talk: I am one man. It is the church's case that is being argued between us, not mine—the church's, I say, which has learned from its Redeemer to place its hope in no man. And yet even concerning me myself, you, my enemies, would not rightly be believed, even if you knew my way of life. As regards men's opinion, there is an ample supply of witnesses who know me; as regards the sight of God, there is only my conscience. And though I hold it unafraid against your accusations, I still do not dare to justify myself before the eyes of the Almighty, and I look to him for the overflowing abundance of his mercy rather than for the strict scrutiny of his judgment, mindful of what is written: "When the righteous king sits on his throne, who will boast that he has a pure heart, or who will boast that he is clean from sin?"

But what has the kind of man I am to do with the question at issue between us, since on the Lord's threshing floor I am straw if I am bad, and grain if I am good? Yet if you were grain, you would not flee from the chaff mixed with you before the time of winnowing, as Cyprian himself also warns. Accordingly, if we find any known bad man among us, we rightly hold it up against you; for your whole defense rests on this, that you separated yourselves so as not to perish through contagion from the sins of others. Hence you boast that you have made a new kind of threshing floor, one that either has only wheat or on which only wheat appears, and which needs not a winnower but a searcher. For your Parmenian too, setting your splendid purity against our impurity as its opposite, dared to bring in the saying of the prophet Jeremiah where he says, "What has chaff to do with wheat?"—which the prophet said, as the passage itself shows, against those who were putting their own dreams on a level with divine oracles. Yet your arrogance and dreadful pride are made plain in the writings of Parmenian, where, against the divine scriptures and against the warnings of Cyprian, he proclaimed you to be wheat already purged of chaff before the final winnowing which the world awaits.

What more fitting answer to this most deceitful pride, then, could have been arranged for you than the case of the Maximianists? Whatever you are accustomed to say against us as traditors, you said even worse things against the Maximianists when they were condemned—the very men whom, though condemned, you took back. You stir up ill-will against us over the emperors as persecutors: you yourselves persecuted the Maximianists before judges whom the emperors themselves had sent. You contend that the church's baptism cannot be given outside the church: you did not annul the baptism which the Maximianists gave while guilty of the crime of schism, when you received back those to whom they had given it. If these things ought to have been done for the sake of the peace of unity, you find nothing to accuse us of; but if they ought not to have been done, do not accuse us unless you condemn yourselves. I do not want you to spread yourself over many points; for I too could briefly recall what has been said against you. Think only of this: set the case of the Maximianists before your eyes. If you can answer us on this, go on to the rest; but if you cannot, you would do better to keep quiet than to kick against the goad.
BOOK FOUR

I have already answered your letter, Cresconius, carefully and adequately in three books, and not short ones. In that letter you thought you should defend Petilian's writings against my replies, which refuted them. Even so, I have undertaken in this shorter work to deal with you on the single case of the Maximianists, and from this one case to show how vainly and emptily you said everything you put in that letter. For we must not despise the kindness of God, who has deigned to provide this both to shorten our labour and to help your correction, if you have any sense. Without your knowing it, and without any effort on our part, he so ruled the minds of your bishops that certain things followed. They charged the Christian world with being stained by the sins of others through communion in the sacraments, though those sins were themselves false and unproven. Yet in Maximian's case they were forced to admit that certain men had not been stained by the sins of those they condemned, although they stood in one communion of the sacraments with them. These were the men to whom they gave a period of grace to return, as though they were innocent: men who had not ordained Maximian, but who stood in his party and had condemned Primian. Again, they refused to acknowledge the baptism of Christ even when it was given in the churches which the labour of the apostles spread and founded. They contended that baptism cannot be given outside the one church, and blamed us for not rescinding baptism given by those whom we deny to be in the true church. Yet they received people baptized in Maximian's sacrilegious schism and did not dare to rescind baptism in them. Again, they accuse us of the crime of persecution because of the laws of the Christian emperors which order their perversity to be corrected. Yet they themselves approached judges sent by those very emperors, gravely accused Maximian and his associates before them, cited in proconsular proceedings the council by which they had condemned them, and obtained highly effective orders to drive them from their sees. Though they did all these things themselves, they still try to throw fog over the unlearned. Yet they have been overcome most plainly, not only by the holy Scriptures and by many sure records of the earlier events when they separated themselves from unity, but also by their own very recent deeds and examples.
