From this point, then, I will make my whole case, and from this point I will answer every part of your letter, as far as the Lord helps me, without any difficulty and indeed with great ease. First, contradicting yourself, you chose to attack eloquence eloquently, as though it were the enemy of truth and rather the patron of falsehood, so as to show the unlearned that I, as an eloquent man, was to be guarded against and avoided. Suppose my eloquence really were as great as you claim, though you claim it as an accusation. Then when the decree of the Council of Bagai is read out, would you not be compelled to praise eloquence? In that decree, as is written there, "the thunderbolt of sentence has struck from the bosom of peace Maximian, rival of the faith, adulterer of truth, enemy of mother church, minister of Dathan, Korah and Abiram." Again, if that subject were set before me, when could I ever say: "Although the hollow of a poisoned womb has long hidden the harmful offspring of viper's seed, and the moist clots of the crime conceived have slowly steamed with sluggish heat into the limbs of asps, yet the poison conceived could not be hidden by a vanishing shade. For though late, wishes pregnant with crimes have given birth to their public outrage and their parricide"? When would I force myself to search out such words? When would I pour them out in speech? When would I stir the mind of reader or hearer to hatred of the guilty with such force and such sound? Yet are these words any less truly said of those against whom they were said? Does this eloquence lessen the credibility of so great a council or shake its authority? Surely that text was chosen above all because it seemed the more eloquent. All wished it to be their own, so that through this one voice the silent mouths of three hundred and ten might resound. See: you denounced eloquence. You warned that it should be loathed and avoided as seditious, and even used a Greek term to call it maliciously artful. Yet it so charmed so many of your bishops that in their plenary council none of them wished to put forward his own opinion. Instead they all made their own the one opinion which one man could express more eloquently and ornately. Let us, then, be allowed without resentment to argue against the errors of men not altogether without polish, if so many great bishops of yours were allowed to condemn the men themselves so eloquently and ornately.

We have often wished to confer with your people, so that error might be removed and brotherly love might rejoice in the bond of peace. You censure this zeal to contend for the truth under the faulty name of contentiousness and animosity. But I ask you: would it not be better for the cause of truth and unity to be handled between bishops, in peaceable words and in more peaceful places, than to be litigated in the forum by bishops through advocates? Yet that is exactly what the party of Primian, your bishop of Carthage, did against Maximian and against those condemned with him at the Council of Bagai, before the legate of Carthage and before four or more proconsuls. Certainly in a conference for discussion one must take care that it does not break out into a quarrel, and the modest and gentle can avoid this and usually do. But when a dispute is fought out in the forum, with advocates struggling on both sides, then without doubt it is litigation. I do not fault your people for this, if they were driven to it not by love of litigation but by the need to protect their interests. Yet I urge you, a man of good intelligence, to notice, to perceive and to understand this. They used the din of the forum and the wrangling of the courts to convict and expel men whom they had already condemned in council. They did not shrink from this but took it up and pursued it. Such men could much more easily have conferred with us peaceably, had they not preferred to cover a bad cause with excuses rather than settle it by discussion.

Before you come to my argument against Petilian, you ask me in the meantime by whom you ought to be baptized. Should it be by the one whom I too affirm to have baptism, or by the one whom your man contends does not have it? This question too has been taken out of the empty chatter of the unlearned by the case of Maximian, at least as far as you are concerned, for among the Maximianists themselves it still remains. Your people condemned Maximian for the sacrilege of schism. Primian had condemned him when he was his deacon, and through him Primian had himself been condemned when a great many colleagues conspired against him. With Maximian they at once condemned, by the same sentence, twelve men who had ordained him. Two of these were Praetextatus of Assuras and Felicianus of Musti. Your people accused these two in the proconsul's court, and through their advocates they cited that same sentence to show that the two had been condemned at the Council of Bagai. By order of the proconsul they tried to drive them from the places they held, and they utterly failed. Afterwards they received them back in such a way that they held communion with them with their ranks intact. Their congregations were brought back to peace along with them, and your people rebaptized none of those whom these two had baptized in schism.

The decree of the Council of Bagai still exists, cited before the proconsul by the advocate Nummasius. He was seeking to have the church of Membressa handed over to Primian's communion and Salvius expelled, who had long held it and had obtained the episcopate there in the party of Donatus. Salvius' expulsion was sought on the ground that, as Nummasius read out, he had been condemned by the Council of Bagai as one of the twelve who ordained Maximian. Nummasius got the number wrong and called them eleven. Titianus later read out this petition of Nummasius when he was pleading expressly and by name before the same proconsul against Praetextatus and Felicianus. The words of this advocate are these: "But iniquity," he says, "delights in its own practices and does not abandon itself once it has fallen headlong. For the same Maximian nourishes the audacity he began and draws others into partnership in his madness. Among them is a certain Felicianus, who at first followed what was right but has been darkened by the contamination of this depravity. Settled in the town of Musti, he has believed that he may hold, as though by a kind of siege, the walls consecrated to almighty God, a venerable church. Praetextatus imitates him in the district of Assuras. But when the fellowship of the bishops became known to the authority of your equity, you ordered, as the records attest, that all effect of opposition be rejected, and that the churches be reclaimed from profane minds and restored to the most holy bishops." A little later, to show what had been ordered, the same advocate reads out the petition of Nummasius which I mentioned above. In it the proconsul said to Nummasius, "Read the bishops' judgment," and the judgment of Bagai was read, in which Maximian is condemned in these words: "The thunderbolt of sentence has struck from the bosom of peace Maximian, rival of the faith, adulterer of truth, enemy of mother church, minister of Dathan, Korah and Abiram. That the earth has not yet opened and swallowed him, heaven has reserved him for a greater punishment. Had he been snatched away, he would have gained a shortcut to his penalty through death. Now he gathers the interest of a heavier usury, since though dead he is present among the living." Then the sentence of Bagai is pronounced against his twelve ordainers as follows: "Nor," they say, "does the just death due to his crime condemn him alone. The chain of sacrilege also drags very many into partnership in the crime, of whom it is written: 'The poison of asps is under their lips; their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness. Their feet are swift to shed blood. Ruin and misery are in their ways, and the way of peace they have not known. There is no fear of God before their eyes.' We would not wish to be cut off from them as from a joint of our own body. But the pestilent rot of a festering wound finds more relief in cutting it away than in the gentleness of medicine. So a more wholesome course has been found, lest the pestilent poison creep through all the limbs: the wound that has arisen must be cut away with brief pain. Know, therefore, that by the judgment of God presiding, through the truthful mouth of the universal council, the following have been condemned as guilty of a notorious crime: Victorianus of Carcabia, Marcianus of Sullecthum, Beianus of Beia, Salvius of Ausafa, Theodorus of Usula, Donatus of Sabrata, Miggenes of Elefantaria, Praetextatus of Assuras, Salvius of Membressa, Valerius of Melzi, Felicianus of Musti and Martialis of Pertusa. By the deadly work of perdition these men glued together a filthy vessel out of the dregs they collected. Also condemned are certain clergy formerly of the church of Carthage, who were present at the crime and acted as panders to an unlawful incest." Among those condemned we read the names of Praetextatus of Assuras and Felicianus of Musti, with whom, as I said before, your people came to terms after they had obtained proconsular orders against them. After condemning these men, the same Council of Bagai gave a delay, fixed to a definite day, to the others who stood in that same schism of Maximian. These too had condemned Primian, but they received the delay merely because they had not been present at Maximian's ordination. The delay is set out in these words: "But those," they say, "whom the shoots of the sacrilegious slip did not pollute, that is, those who out of a modest shame for the faith withdrew their hands from Maximian's head, we have permitted to return to mother church. For just as we are cleared of responsibility for the death of the guilty, so we rejoice at the return of the innocent. And lest too short a time, with the pressure of the day, take away from those returning the hope of a salvation cut short, we open the door of recognition to all who are allowed to acknowledge their fault, the previous decrees remaining in force, until the eighth day before the Kalends of January next. Those who return will have the foundations of undiminished rank and faith. If anyone fails to enter this door through sluggish idleness, let him know that by his own will he has cut himself off from every avenue of pardon. For the sentence pronounced will remain upon such men, and fixed penance will await those who return after the appointed day."

From all this you do not deny that some men returned to your communion. The events are so recent, and the men concerned are still living, that the facts are widely and clearly known. Two groups baptized outside your church during that whole time. The first were those to whom the delay was granted. As the words of that same council make plain, your bishops invite them to return to mother church and rejoice at their return as at the return of innocent men. The second were those whom your bishops condemned with Maximian without any delay at all. These baptized up to the deadline, while they were in communion with Maximian and stood in his schism. They also baptized after the deadline had passed, when the advocate Titianus demanded by name that Praetextatus and Felicianus be expelled from their basilicas, the same men with whom Primian afterwards came to terms with their rank intact. How, then, do you now dare to say that the one baptism cannot be given except in the one church? You acknowledged and received, without any dispute, the baptism these men gave in a sacrilegious schism, and you did not dare to rescind it. Yet you cannot say that you conferred nothing on those whom you received with that same baptism. So if I ask what you conferred, you will doubtless answer: "They were not to perish by the very sacrilege of schism. They were not to hold the baptism of Christ to their judgment rather than their reward, to their ruin rather than their salvation, as deserters still bear the military mark. So we conferred peace, we conferred unity, we conferred the fellowship of the church. Thus they might be worthy to receive the Holy Spirit, through whom love is poured out in our hearts. Without him no one reaches the kingdom of heaven, even if he has received all the lawful sacraments." You would be answering truly if you held the true church. Yet to admonish you it is enough that you understand the following. Some were baptized by these bishops in Maximian's sacrilegious schism and came back with them from there to you. You believed that they received something in your communion, and you yourselves will receive that same thing in the true church. You too, then, though you have received the baptism of Christ, are to be punished if you do not hold to the unity of the catholic church. In the same way, you would have no doubt that those baptized in Maximian's schism were certainly to be punished if they were not joined to your communion. Yet when they came to you from there, you judged that their baptism should not be rescinded. You see, then, that this point too, which troubled you about the sacrament of baptism, has already been settled in the case of the Maximianists.

Now let us look at the arguments by which you believed you had refuted my letter. First, you ask why I call your people Donatists. You add that Donatus was not the author and founder of a church which had not existed before, but one of the bishops of an ancient church descended from Christ. You do not notice that Maximian says the same of himself, and yet you name his whole communion after him. You have no term to distinguish the schism he made from yourselves or from other sects except "Maximianists" or "Maximianenses" or some other name derived from Maximian. Or, more simply and without fear of the grammarians' rods, you call it the party of Maximian. What will you say to this, except that Maximian made a schism from your communion, whereas Donatus did not make one from the catholic communion? But that is not what Maximian says. He claims rather that Primian and all of you made a schism from the party of Donatus, in which he himself remained. He reads out the decrees of two councils. The first was held at Carthage by forty-three bishops, and there Primian was condemned in advance. At the second, a hundred or more of your bishops of that time met at Cebarsussi, and there he was condemned completely and more fully. When Maximian produces such documents, what will you answer? Only that the Council of Bagai has greater authority. There three hundred and ten bishops condemned that same Maximian and his associates. At that council Primian did not plead his case before them as a man needing to be cleared. He sat with them as a most innocent judge. He pronounced sentence against Maximian and the twelve associates in whose presence Maximian was ordained. And by granting a delay he recalled to his own peace, as innocent men, so many others who had themselves condemned him.

In this conflict of yours, what do you want us to judge as neutral parties, since we are bound neither to Maximian's communion nor to yours? What, I ask, do you want us to judge here, except this? There are two councils by which Primian was condemned, and one later Council of Bagai by which Maximian was condemned. You want the later council to prevail on Primian's behalf, presumably because you think that, being later, it was the firmer and could judge the earlier ones. Very well: in this we take your side. Our quarrel with the Maximianists is another matter, if we should dare to decide it. We take your side, I say. The third judgment, at Bagai, was made for Primian against Maximian and his colleagues, and since it was later it could rightly annul the earlier ones. Even so, we neither read nor hear of any appeal by Primian from the two earlier judgments to the third. We hear only that he was absent when he was first condemned in advance and then condemned at the second council. But the most eloquent sentence of Bagai was likewise pronounced against Maximian and his associates in their absence. Moreover, the forty-three at Carthage testified that they had acted with greater moderation, caution and care. They sent envoys to Primian not once but a second and a third time, asking that if he would not come to them himself, he would at least let them come to him. He refused both. As they write, he treated the envoys with an insulting rebuff. They then felt it necessary at last to provide for the church. Yet they did not dare to rush into a final judgment. They took counsel by a kind of preliminary judgment, so that if he trusted his cause, room would be left for him to answer and clear himself at a later, larger council. When he refused to come to that council, they judged it necessary to condemn him without any suspension of sentence. But in the decree of the Council of Bagai we read of no envoys mistreated by Maximian. We do not even read that any were sent to ask him to come. Yet we do see what happened. Altar was raised against altar, and a bishop was ordained against the bishop who sat in the chair where he had been ordained. That bishop had not been deserted by the assembly of his people, and most of the other bishops had not cut off communion with him. This act, once the sacrilege of schism had been committed, stirred such indignation that the condemnation of Maximian and of those who ordained him could be put off no longer.

Even so, none of this moves you on Caecilian's behalf. Majorinus was ordained against him while he remained in office and presided over his people, and altar was raised against altar. Against him you do not produce two judgments, as the Maximianists did against Primian, but one, rushed through with the haste of a horrifying rashness. Unlike Primian, he did not refuse to let his colleagues come to him. On the contrary, he invited them to come, and even they could not keep silent about this in the decree of the council they drew up against him. On his behalf four later judgments are read out, not one as for Primian. His adversaries were refuted in their presence, not in their absence as Primian's were. They were refuted before the judges they had agreed to accept, and even before the emperor Constantine himself. They first accused Caecilian before Constantine. Later they complained to him that the bishops he had appointed to hear the case had not judged rightly. They appealed to him again from a second episcopal judgment, so that they were defeated when he himself heard the case between the parties after the first and second episcopal judgments. They did not lack even a fourth conviction. For once they had been exposed as false accusers regarding Caecilian's own alleged crimes, they brought against him the charge that Felix of Abthugni, who ordained him, had handed over the Scriptures. Felix too was cleared by a proconsular judgment, after that same Constantine, whom they wore out with constant petitions, ordered his case to be examined. The Maximianists did not inflict such evils on Primian. They were not defeated so many times, nor defeated in person, nor defeated before judges they had chosen themselves. And yet they plainly made a schism from your communion, while you refuse to notice that your own party did the same thing to the catholic communion. With what shamelessness, born of utterly empty animosity, I simply do not know. You want everything you say about Caecilian and Felix his ordainer to be true because about seventy bishops judged the matter. Then why do you not want what is said about Primian to be true? In his case first forty-three bishops and then a hundred gave judgment, and the later judgment confirmed the earlier preliminary one. But if you hold that the charges against Primian are false because the Council of Bagai, held later on his behalf against his enemies, is read out, why will you not admit that the charges brought against Caecilian are utterly false, when so many later judgments are read out on his behalf? If Caecilian, once judged against by those seventy, should not have found any opportunity to clear himself before other judges, neither should Primian. Far more than seventy had condemned him at a second hearing that confirmed the first. But if a third judgment made in his favour gives ample support to a man condemned twice, then with what brazen face do you claim that a second, third, fourth and fifth judgment are not enough to acquit a man condemned once? Perhaps it is numbers that impress you, so that you think the Council of Bagai outweighs the hundred who condemned Primian because three hundred and ten took part in it. Then why will you not agree with the whole world, which has a so much greater number of bishops?

You charge Caecilian with that unforgivable sin against the Holy Spirit, of which the Lord says: "It will not be forgiven, either here or in the age to come." We too could show that you charged Felician of Musti with a sin against the Holy Spirit when you charged him with the sacrilege of schism, as the sentence of the Council of Bagai loudly declared. Yet you now have him as a bishop alongside Primian, though he was one of Maximian's ordainers and one of Primian's own condemners, and you did not rebaptize those he baptized even in sacrilegious schism. You think that those you accuse of handing over the divine Scriptures to persecutors to be burned sinned against the Holy Spirit with that unforgivable guilt, because holy men of God spoke those same Scriptures as they were moved by the Holy Spirit. In just the same way we could bring this same charge against your own traditors instead, whom the records convict. We could also show, as I said, that you laid this charge against Felician when you accused him of the crime of sacrilegious schism. For the unity of love and peace is kept in the Holy Spirit, as the apostle says: "Bearing with one another in love, eager to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace." Anyone who commits schism certainly violates that unity. But we do not charge you with the guilt of that indissoluble and eternal sin committed against the Holy Spirit, for we do not despair that you can be healed if you are corrected while you live. Nor do we charge it to your people who handed over the holy books to be burned, unless they remained cut off from unity with an impenitent heart to the end of this life. Nor do you show that you charged Felician and Praetextatus with it, though you later entered into communion with them. The record says that the truthful mouth of your plenary council condemned them, dragged along with Maximian by the chain of sacrilege into partnership in his crime. It is also proven that they were received after the deadline of the grace period, which was granted not to them, since they were already condemned, but to others who were regarded as innocent.

You object to the derivation of the name by which they are called Donatistae from Donatus, and you think that by the rule of Latin usage it should be formed differently. I do not reject your advice. But go and find grammarians as judges, and before them argue this point of the art with the Maximianenses and defeat them. I no longer even wish to call them Maximianistae, so as not to offend your very learned ears. As far as I can judge, they will certainly not give way to you as easily as I do and start calling 'Claudianenses', or something else, the people they called 'Claudianistae'. They listed it among the other charges on which they both condemned Primian in advance and then condemned him that he had received these people into communion. At the same time, recognize that this way of forming the word has not pleased me alone, as you complain. Perhaps I am the only one who has given way to you so readily on a matter that has nothing to do with the case.

You thought I should be rebuked more sharply because I spoke of "the sacrilegious error of the Donatist heretics", calling it a heresy when you would rather have it considered a schism, and yet we receive such people into communion without their being cleansed of sacrilege. You rebuke us so severely in this matter, so answer this: how did your people cleanse the sacrilege of Felician and Praetextatus? Afterwards they entered into communion with them, joined them to themselves and restored them as bishops just as they had been before. And they did not rebaptize any of those whom these men had baptized in the sacrilege of schism. Or were they perhaps not stained with sacrilege at all, as some of your people foolishly claim, saying that they sinned against a man and not against God? But sacrilege is all the graver a sin because it can only be committed against God. And the only reason you thought I should be pressed in your argument about our receiving those who come over to us from you in this way was that I called your error sacrilegious. So read the Council of Bagai. These are certainly its first words: "By the will of almighty God and of his Christ, our Saviour, we came from all the provinces of Africa and held a council in the holy church of Bagai: Gamalius, Primian, Pontius, Secundianus, Januarianus, Saturninus, Felix, Pegasius, Rufinus, Fortunius, Crispinus, Florentius, Optatus, Donatus, Donatian and the rest, three hundred and ten in number. It pleased the Holy Spirit who is in us to establish lasting peace and to cut off sacrilegious schisms." Do you hear? Do you notice? Are you paying attention? "To cut off sacrilegious schisms," they say. When this sentence was pronounced, was Maximian the only one in that schism held guilty of the crime of sacrilege, committed through wicked perversity against God and not against a man? Read a little further what they say about his associates, among whom are written the names of the men we are discussing: "Not only is he condemned," they say, "by the just death his crime deserves; the chain of sacrilege also drags very many others into partnership in the crime."

What now, most eloquent sir? What have you to say to me? Read what follows. Among the very many whom the chain of that sacrilege drags into partnership in the crime, see Praetextatus and Felician bound fast. I see sacrilegious bishops. What will you do if you cannot prove they were cleansed? You are surely forced to yield to the truth we teach: your people are cleansed when they come to us by the very bond of brotherly peace, and charity covers their sins, as it is written: "Charity covers a multitude of sins." And what about the people these men baptized when they were separated from your communion and bound with Maximian in the fellowship of that sacrilegious chain? You received them into peace and concord together with these bishops, in that same baptism. Will you give any answer except that you were right to approve in them the same sacraments that we also approve in you? You will be more consistent if you give that answer and do not fight against the words of your own letter. There, trying to show that what divides us is a schism rather than a heresy, you said that we and your people have one religion and the same sacraments, with nothing different in Christian observance. You could not have condemned the repetition of baptism more severely than with those words. For when people are led away from us, your people rebaptize them, and yet you think, say and write that they have the same sacraments. By what shameless wickedness, then, do you refuse to respect, in those the Christian world baptizes in holy unity, what you respected in those Praetextatus and Felician baptized in sacrilegious schism? You have therefore already settled by your own verdict the case we have against you. These men had been struck down by your condemnation. They had urged the people most insistently not to come over to you. They had even held that people must be baptized again after you. Yet you received them into fellowship at the altar without any loss of rank, together with those they had baptized while they stood outside your communion in the sacrilege of schism, and without repeating their baptism. And you believed they had been cleansed of that crime of sacrilege by nothing other than the holy fire of charity. That would truly happen if you held that same charity in true unity.

But let us also look at the words of Petilian's letter, which you wanted to defend against me, and see how you get yourself out of this case of the Maximianists, which is the only matter I have now decided to take up against your writings. He certainly wrote these words: "What is looked to is the conscience of the one who gives in holiness, which is to cleanse the conscience of the one who receives." To which I replied: "What if the giver's conscience is hidden and perhaps stained? How will it be able to cleanse the recipient's conscience?" Petilian's words do not resolve this inescapable question at all, so you took it upon yourself to resolve it in your own. In doing so you spoke not against me but against the man you wished to defend. For he says: "What is looked to is the conscience of the giver, which is to cleanse that of the recipient." You, however, admitted that a hidden conscience cannot be seen. So you said that it is looked to in a way that does not see the conscience itself but only what is known about it from public reputation. From this it follows that it is no longer true that the giver's conscience cleanses the recipient's conscience. According to you, it is his reputation that cleanses. Yet reputation certainly deceives the observer when it calls the worst of men good, an adulterer chaste and a sacrilegious man devout. So it cleanses precisely when it lies. If reputation tells the truth about a secret criminal, then it does not cleanse but stains whoever has received baptism from him. See, then, what sort of thing this reputation is that you chose as patron of so bad a cause: when it lies it cleanses, and when it tells the truth it pollutes. Thus, by your marvellous argument, the water is not "lying water" in its eyes precisely when reputation itself is lying.

But why say more about this, when Felician sits today among your bishops? While he was separated from them and joined to Maximian in the chain of sacrilege, he baptized people, and no one rebaptized any of them after him. I ask Petilian what kind of conscience he had then. And I read the decree of the Council of Bagai, where it is written: "Not only is he condemned by the just death his crime deserves; the chain of sacrilege also drags very many others into partnership in the crime. Of them it is written: 'The poison of asps is under their lips; their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness.'" Felician is counted among these very many. Yet his water, coming from such lips and such a mouth, you did not spit out, did not annul, did not destroy. Because it was consecrated with the words of the gospel, in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, by whatever tongue and conscience, you acknowledged it and accepted it as truthful rather than lying. And I ask you: what was this Felician's public reputation at the time when he baptized in the chain of sacrilege, with so evil a conscience? And again I recite the council itself, where it is written: "Know therefore that those guilty of a notorious crime, Victorianus of Carcabia", and among the others, whom it would be tedious to repeat, "Praetextatus of Assuras and Felician of Musti, who by the deadly work of perdition have glued together a filthy vessel out of collected dregs", and a little later: "have been condemned by the truthful mouth of the plenary council."

What is your answer to this? If someone separated from your communion cannot baptize, I read that men dragged along with Maximian into partnership in the crime did baptize. If someone who sins against God cannot baptize, I read that men bound together in the chain of sacrilege did baptize. If what is looked to is the conscience of the one who gives in holiness, which is to cleanse that of the recipient, I read that men poisoned by the bites of asps did baptize. If what is looked to is the giver's public reputation, so that his conscience can cleanse, I read that men guilty of a notorious crime did baptize. Felician is still alive. With him are all those he baptized in the sacrilege of schism, who were received into your communion and rebaptized by no one. Against Petilian's view, a man stained by a sacrilegious conscience baptized. Against yours, a man guilty of a notorious crime baptized. How, I ask, can you defend yourselves, unless your own deeds finally convict you into saying what we also say? Neither the conscience nor the reputation of the giver cleanses the conscience of the recipient. What cleanses is the faith of the recipient himself, and the giver is the grace of God, not of man. And if the recipient has not made the appeal of a good conscience, and his faith has wavered either wholly or in part, then people's conduct must be corrected and the sacraments must not be destroyed. For you admit that these sacraments are not different or merely similar, but entirely the same. In the same way, you judged that the life and will of those whom Felician and Praetextatus baptized in sacrilegious schism had to be corrected so that they would not remain in that sacrilege of schism. But you judged that baptism must not be violated, even though it was ministered to the most unworthy by the most unworthy.

So it was in vain that you chose, with your abusive tongue, to accuse our conscience as if it had been exposed and condemned for the crime of offering incense, of handing over the Scriptures and of persecution, as though this proved that we cannot give baptism. Your charges are false. And whatever the truth of the matter, a conscience condemned for the crime of the Maximianists' sacrilege was certainly able to give baptism, and you were afraid to annul that baptism. Your own conduct also shows that baptism can be given even by persecutors. You persecuted those same Maximianists most fiercely, and yet you not only baptize but claim that you alone ought to baptize.

You say it is written in the law: "Let not the oil of the sinner anoint my head." That is not what is written, nor is it to be understood as you think. But is not the oil of the sacrilegious Praetextatus and Felician the oil of a sinner? You also say it is written: "If someone is baptized by a dead man, what does his washing profit him?" You do not read this carefully, and you do not understand its meaning from the context of the passage. But listen to what that most eloquent sentence of Bagai proclaims: "The joined brotherhood of peace and concord," it says, "is indeed to be desired, as it is written: 'Righteousness and peace have kissed each other.' But the truthful wave has cast the limbs of some, shipwrecked, onto the rough rocks. Like the Egyptians who perished, the shores are full of their corpses, and their punishment is greater in death itself, for after the avenging waters have wrung the life from them, they do not even find burial." How then could these men baptize, when they were not only dead but, what is worse, unburied? If the text must be understood as you think, how did the washing profit those whom these dead men baptized? You received them in that same washing and did not wash them again. You also suppose that in my letter, to which you think you are replying, I made an exception only for the idol-worshipper as guilty of the gravest sin. And you press hard to prove that no sinner is excepted in the text you claim is written: "Let not the oil of the sinner anoint my head." Then look at Felician and Praetextatus. Were they not sinners when so great a council declared that they were being dragged along with Maximian by the chain of sacrilege? Dare to assert it, dare to argue it, dare at least to say that they were sinners but secret ones, when I read there that they were guilty of a notorious crime. And yet even if they had sinned only lightly, even if their sin had been hidden, you are trying in this argument to wring from your text about the sinner's oil the conclusion that no sinner is excepted. If that is so, where will you stand? Where will you flee? In what hiding places can you conceal yourselves, with your sacrilegious men, with your men guilty of notorious crime, with your unburied corpses?

You say that when we are asked by what licence we claim the right to baptize, we do not appeal to the merit of our deeds or the innocence of our lives but say that anyone may do it. And you say that in trying to show that sinners too have the power to baptize, we openly confess that we have sinned, like men already judged guilty of crimes. As if we had to speak against God on the strength of our own merits, making baptism exactly as righteous as we are! No human being should presume on his own righteousness. In fact, our chief proof that baptism belongs to Christ and not to men is that it does not vary with the varying merits of men. I would argue this more fully if I did not prefer to use the shortcut you have provided. At the Council of Bagai the Maximianists were called asps, vipers, parricides, Egyptian corpses and whatever else was declaimed against them with grandiloquent mouths, which made our case very easy. Yet you received and did not destroy the baptism they gave. By doing so you yourselves have judged clearly enough that baptism does not stand by the merits of those who minister it or of those to whom it is ministered. It stands by its own holiness and truth, because of him who instituted it, bringing ruin to those who use it badly and salvation to those who use it well.

I wonder, though, how they managed to persuade even you to mention Cyprian in your argument. His letters about destroying the baptism given among heretics or schismatics, which you say are his, overturn your whole case. But that is a point we should argue against the Maximianists, or against others who do not accept baptism given either among you or among us. You, however, have already settled this question with remarkable ease. You have already accepted the baptism given in Maximian's sacrilegious schism, along with Praetextatus and Felician, among their congregations. You have already acted without any hesitation against the letters you attribute to Cyprian and against anyone else who held this view. You say that the Easterners were separated from communion with your people because they later came to agree with us and chose to rescind the judgment they had held on baptism. Whether that can be shown is another matter. But if some few Easterners did this, they certainly corrected their judgment. You too rescinded your old position when you accepted the baptism given in Maximian's schism. Yet you remain in communion with one another and refuse to be in communion with the Easterners.

But evidently you think you have found a place to spread out your eloquence when, at what I set down in my letter, "whether someone receives the sacrament of baptism from a faithful or a faithless steward, let all his hope be in Christ," you cry out and say: "O splendid command of a bishop! O praiseworthy precepts of justice from a good father! 'Make no distinction,' he says, 'between the faithful and the faithless; let the godly and the ungodly seem the same to you.' There is no profit in living a good life, since whatever the just man may do the unjust can also perform. What could be said more unjust than this precept: let the stained purify another, the filthy wash, the unclean cleanse, the unbeliever give faith, the criminal make innocent?" These are certainly your words, with which you find fault with my opinion, though I neither held nor wrote any such thing. For there is a very great difference between the faithful and the faithless: not with respect to the sacrament, if both have it, but with respect to merit, since the one has it for salvation and the other for punishment. Nor can the unjust man perform whatever the just man may, because even if the unjust man can baptize, the unjust man cannot enter the kingdom of heaven. Nor does the one who administers baptism purify, wash or cleanse anyone, or make him innocent; that is done by the grace of God who gives and by the good conscience of the one who receives. But consider whether there was no difference between Primian and Felician when Primian sat among the three hundred and ten. By them it was said of Felician that the venom of asps was under his lips, that his feet were swift to shed blood, that ruin and misery were in his ways, that he did not know the way of peace, and that there was no fear of God before his eyes. Was he not then stained, unclean and filthy, he who glued together a filthy vessel out of collected dregs? Was he not faithless, with the venom of asps under his lips? Was he not a criminal, guilty of a notorious crime? And yet he himself now sits with Primian as your bishop, and those whom he baptized then, never washed again afterward, he now has with you.

And still you fight against the truth and will not grant that it is always Christ who gives faith, Christ who is the origin of the Christian, in Christ that the Christian fixes his root, Christ who is the head of the Christian. To these words of mine, set down in that letter against Petilian, you append your own and say: "This we too urge, this we want; but we ask through whom it is better done." And you do not notice that this is not what Petilian urges, the man to whom I was then replying and whose letter you are trying to defend and uphold against my reply. For he said plainly: "What is looked to is the conscience of the one who gives in holiness, which is to wash the conscience of the recipient. For whoever takes faith from a faithless man receives not faith but guilt." Tell me, what place has he left to Christ for washing the conscience of the baptized, or from whom does the baptized receive faith, when he says that the conscience of the giver is looked to, which washes that of the recipient, and that whoever takes faith from a faithless man receives not faith but guilt? You do indeed seem to yield to the great weight of the truth, and you say that you urge and want this: that Christ gives faith and that Christ washes the Christian so that he may enter upon a new life. But you ask through whom that is better done which ought not to be done without a minister. Petilian, however, did not say, "The conscience of the minister is looked to, through which Christ washes that of the recipient, or through which Christ gives faith"; rather, he meant that the recipient's conscience is washed by the very conscience of the giver. Nor did he say, "Whoever takes faith through a faithless man receives not faith but guilt," so that the man might seem to take it from Christ, though through another. He said outright, "takes from a faithless man," and to this he added, as if by way of proof: "For everything consists by its origin and root, and if something has no head, it is nothing." By this he meant the minister himself, whose conscience he said is looked to, not as that through which Christ washes, but as that which washes the recipient; he was making the minister himself, quite simply, the origin, root and head of the baptized.

Accordingly, here I am replying not to Petilian, whose words you have not defended, but to you, who in support of your own opinion said something or other different from what he said. For you, as you write, want and urge this: not, as he said, that the conscience of one who gives in holiness washes the recipient or gives faith to the recipient, nor that it is itself the origin, root and head of the believer, but that through it Christ washes, through it Christ gives faith, through it Christ is the origin of the Christian, through it the Christian fixes his root in Christ, through it Christ is the head of the Christian. That is why you ask through whom that is better done which you grant is done by Christ. And here you too, as far as I can see, do not deny that this can be done even through a bad minister, but say that it can be done better through a good one. For what else does your statement mean: "This we too urge, this we want; but we ask through whom it is better done"? On this view, Christ washes even through the stained conscience of one who does not give in holiness, but better through the clean conscience of one who does; Christ gives faith even through a bad minister, but better through a good one; Christ becomes the origin of the Christian even through a faithless steward, but better through a faithful one; the Christian fixes his root in Christ even through a reprobate farmer, but better through an upright one; Christ can be the head of the Christian even through Felician, but better, you think, through Primian.

So there is little or perhaps no disagreement between us on this matter. For I too say that the divine sacraments are better dispensed through a good minister than through a bad one. But this is better for the sake of the minister himself, so that his life and conduct may agree with the things he ministers. It is not better for the sake of the recipient, who, even if he comes upon a bad minister dispensing the truth, receives assurance from his Lord, who warns him and says: "Do what they say, but do not do what they do; for they say and do not do." I add also that it is better in this respect: the one to whom it is ministered may, by loving the uprightness and holiness of a good minister, more easily imitate it. But the things ministered are not truer or holier because they are ministered through a better man. For they are true and holy in themselves, because of the true and holy God whose they are. And so it can happen that someone coming into the fellowship of God's people finds one man by whom he is readily baptized and chooses another whom he may imitate to his profit. For he is sure that the sacrament of Christ is holy even if it is ministered through a less holy or an unholy man, but that he himself will be punished by the holiness of that very sacrament if he receives it unworthily, if he makes bad use of it, if he does not live in a way that fits and accords with it.

For I ask you: suppose that someone whom Primian baptized in your communion lives very wickedly, while someone whom Felician baptized in Maximian's schism lives very well. To which of them do you think the kingdom of God lies open? To the bad man whom, on your view, a good man baptized, or to the devout man whom, on the view of the Council of Bagai, a sacrilegious man baptized? But perhaps you say, and say truly: "One who is placed in schism cannot be devout." I agree. Yet someone baptized by Primian, whom you believe to be devout, can be sacrilegious, even secretly, within your communion. Further, if the man whom Felician baptized in the chain of sacrilege were to abandon the sacrilege of schism and be set right in the communion of the Church, would you dare to say that baptism would become better in him, though you would not dare to deny that the man himself could become better? You judged this by your very action, since all whom Felician and Praetextatus baptized in a schism whose sacrilege you had condemned and abhorred, you received along with those two when they returned to you, without any annulling or repetition of baptism. But if, in saying "but we ask through whom it is better done," you put the comparative degree for the positive, as if you meant "we ask through whom it is done well," intending it to be understood that through a bad minister it is done badly, I do not press you on the word. Rather, I point out that you ought to have said "we ask through whom it is done" rather than "we ask through whom it is done well," as though it were possible for Christ to give faith not well, for Christ to be the origin and head of the Christian not well, for the root to be fixed in Christ not well. For either it is not done at all, or, if it is done, it is without doubt done well.

Still, we discuss these things so that the unity of the wheat itself may not be abandoned on account of bad stewards. They are stewards not of their own sacraments but of the Lord's, and they must remain mixed in until the time when the Lord's threshing floor is winnowed. But to make a schism from the unity of Christ, or to be in schism, is certainly evil, and a great evil. Nor can it possibly be that Christ gives a schismatic, not faith, but sacrilegious error, or that a schismatic has fixed his root in Christ, or that Christ is origin or head to a schismatic. And yet, if a schismatic gives the baptism of Christ, it will have been given; if he receives it, it will have been received. But it will be received not for eternal life but for eternal punishment, if he persists in that sacrilege. This is not because he turns the good that he has into evil, but because, as long as he is evil, he has the good to his own harm.

Perhaps you ask me to prove this. What else shall I say to you than what I have set out to do in this work? Read the decree of Bagai; look at Felician and Praetextatus. Schismatics gave, schismatics received; both were taken back and gathered in by you, the givers without being degraded and the receivers without being rebaptized. Now surely you no longer ask whether it is better done through a just minister or an unjust one, since the baptism given by Primian, just in your view, is not better than that given by the unjust Felician. Surely you are now forced to understand how the apostle could say: "Neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the growth." And you recall that you said in vain: "Just as in planting and watering only a diligent and faithful farmer is sought, so also in the sacrament of baptism only the most righteous workman is approved." See: Felician was neither diligent nor faithful nor most righteous, but rather careless of his own salvation, faithless and most unrighteous, when, allied with Maximian and, as your three hundred and ten proclaim through the most eloquent mouth of one man, bound in the chain of sacrilege, he administered the baptism which you did not dare to annul.

Surely you see that the testimony you cited from the prophet has no bearing on this case: "I will give you shepherds after my own heart, and they will feed you, feeding you with discipline." For Felician, a sacrilegious man, was not after God's heart, nor did he feed his sheep with discipline in a sacrilegious schism. And yet he baptized them, and when you received them you recognized that what he gave was not his but God's. Surely you perceive the point of my citing from holy Scripture that it is better to trust in the Lord than to trust in man, and that your answer was empty, as far as this case is concerned. You answered that you inquire all the more whether the one through whom this sacrament is celebrated is just and faithful precisely because your hope and trust are in God, not in man, and because faith and righteousness, which you always look for in his ministers, belong to God. See: in Felician, when he was guilty of a notorious crime, there was neither righteousness nor faith, and yet there was baptism. And of those to whom he gave it, when they were gathered in by you, you say that righteousness was added to them; you do not say that baptism was lacking.

Accordingly, as to what you next ask me, "If baptism given by anyone whatever and in any manner whatever must not be annulled, why did the apostles baptize after John?": solve that question yourself, if, as you say, the apostles baptized after John. Why did your people not baptize after Felician those whom he had baptized in a sacrilegious schism? And from this learn at least that whatever is read or argued about the baptism of John has nothing whatever to do with this case. I do not know, moreover, what possessed you to say that the Jews to whom Peter said, "Let each of you be baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ," had already been baptized by Moses, though they were born so many generations after that servant of God led their ancestors across the Red Sea. Or if they had baptism from Moses because they were descended from those whom the apostle says were baptized in Moses, then dare to say that all who are born of faithful Christians already have Christian baptism. You see, I think, how empty a thing that is to say. But however that matter stands, even if the apostles had baptized after Moses the servant of God, I would press you to give the reason why your people did not baptize after Felician, the sacrilegious Maximianist.

Next, what I set down — "If those who wished to belong to Paul were in error, what hope, pray, is there for those who wish to belong to Donatus?" — I think you did not refute in the earlier parts of your letter, as you yourself recognize from what we have said sufficiently above. So it is not the case, as you suppose, exulting as though you were certain, that you rightly conclude that everything said by Petilian or anyone else was rightly said. Rather, following the very order in which you briefly ran through those points, as if recalling and reviewing them, I conclude in this case of the Maximianists that they were not rightly said. For there was no conscience of one giving in holiness in Felician when, clinging to Maximian, he was dragged along in the chain of sacrilege; and those whom he baptized were baptized by a man guilty of a notorious crime, and therefore by a manifestly faithless man. Nor was a sacrilegious man an origin, root and head unto salvation for them. Nor was he a good tree, condemned as he was in the fellowship of a sacrilegious schism and still remaining in that same sacrilege. Nor was he a good man bringing forth good things from the good treasure of his heart, since it was said of him and his other associates: "Whose mouth is full of cursing and bitterness." And yet, when your people came to terms with him, they at last, terrified by the force of the truth, acknowledged that the baptism such a man had given was not his but Christ's.

Come now, let us see, in its proper place in your letter, how you extricate yourself in the case of the Maximianists. For all who read this correspondence are surely waiting to see what you said on this point where you said it, or what I replied. As for your answer to my charges about Optatus the Gildonian, I do not wish to discuss it; I do not wish to dwell any longer on the case of a man about whose condemnation by your people I am not concerned. I certainly give up this charge, and perhaps it will be a real loss among posterity, once his memory has faded. But for now, as long as there are people who knew his life and conduct, they will complain that I said too little about him rather than that I said something false. For they do not read our writings as you do, you who ask me what the man I called a raging wave swallowed up, when you have Praetextatus and Felician right there. For my words there run thus: "These men," I said, "indeed insult their own schismatics so far as to call them dead and unburied. But surely they ought to have wished them buried, lest, out of the multitude of unburied corpses lying on the shore, Optatus the Gildonian, advancing with a column of soldiers like a raging wave leaping beyond its bounds, should afterward suck Felician and Praetextatus back in." When you read these words of mine there, why did you not quote them in full when you tried to answer them? Why do you charge me, as it were, with not saying what that raging wave swallowed, when you see written there: "should afterward suck Felician and Praetextatus back in"?

For when this reception of the condemned Praetextatus and Felician is held against your people, what else do they usually reply, as if it were a great defense, but "Optatus wanted this; Optatus did this"? This the towns of Musti and Assuras themselves attest: they say that, fearing the Gildonian soldiery because of Optatus's threats, they forced their bishops to return to the communion of Primian. But you, since you saw that it could not be denied without shamelessness that he did this, denied that I wrote it, perhaps thinking that my writings were more likely to be unknown than that event. But grant that your bishops, by some Donatian or Numidian privilege, were allowed to be ignorant of whatever all Africa was crying out about their colleague, while they will not allow the charges brought by Africans against Africans, never proven and so often dismissed, to be unknown to the farthest bounds of the earth in east and west. Let the baptism given by Optatus be valid among you, the man you were unwilling to condemn, yet in such a way that you did not dare to acquit him. And let baptism not be valid when given in the churches founded by apostolic labor, those of the Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Colossians, Philippians, Thessalonians and the others written of in the holy Scriptures which you too read, where perhaps not even Caecilian's real name has been heard, let alone that false charge against him. Let Optatus have had the conscience of one giving in holiness in that life which, as your writings show, you were ashamed to condemn on our account and yet afraid to acquit on God's account, and amid that public notoriety in which you thought a hidden conscience could still be looked to. And let the conscience of so many great Christian nations stand accused because it knew nothing of the remotest quarrels of the Africans. But could they likewise have been ignorant of the crimes of these men too, namely Felician and Praetextatus, whom the three hundred and ten condemned in a plenary council?

And you still throw at Catholic unity some deeds or other of our people, which are either false, or not sins, or, even if true and sinful, cannot defile the fellowship of the good. For the good do not share in the sins of others, since they certainly do not consent to their being committed. Until those who commit them are separated like chaff from the Lord's threshing floor by the final winnowing fan, the good share with them not their sins but God's sacraments. Within the same net, like good fish with bad until the separation that is to take place on the shore, that is, at the end of the age as at the edge of the sea, they are set apart from them not by bodily segregation but by difference of life and conduct. So the eleven apostles did not share in the thefts of Judas, and yet with him they visibly clung to the same Lord, heard the same master, received the same gospel to be believed and took the same sacraments, mingled with him in bodily assembly, separated from him by spiritual unlikeness. So the apostle Paul did not share in the contentiousness and envy, that is, the devilish vices, of those who proclaimed Christ insincerely; yet with them he preached the same Christ and partook of the sacraments of the same Christ, and he said of them: "Whether in pretense or in truth, let Christ be proclaimed." For the martyr Cyprian, a most ardent lover of unity, both understood and wrote that these men were not separated by any schism or heresy but were mingled with the brethren in bodily assembly. So that same Cyprian did not share in the avarice, plundering and usury of his colleagues. He said that they wished to have money in abundance while the brethren in the church went hungry, that they seized estates by treacherous frauds, and that they increased their gains by multiplying interest, an evil he even compared to idolatry. Yet he did not flee their bodily assembly, but stood at the same altars and took the same most holy food and drink. For they ate and drank judgment not on others but on themselves, while he shared with such men not their sins but the mysteries of Christ, most closely joined to them in assembly, most widely parted from them in conduct. This is why those similitudes and examples were set before us in the Scriptures: so that we might learn to be wheat and not desert the Lord's threshing floor because chaff is mixed in; to be good fish and not break the nets and go outside because bad fish are mixed in with us; to be vessels of mercy, made for honor and cleansed, and not flee from the great house because of the vessels of destruction and dishonor. For in the temporal gathering and mixture of both, there is no reason why the bad should be tolerated, and praiseworthily so, except that the good may not be deserted, to the deserter's damnation. And since you too do this, under the same necessity, with your own evils, so many and so manifest, you can easily see, if you wish, that it is only sacrilegious animosity that separates you from the Christians of so many great nations.

So, then: suppose that not only Optatus, notorious for his alliance with Gildo, but any obscure member among you has done something wrong, and you know it. Since you cannot separate him from your communion, either because no one believes you when you accuse him or because you dare not accuse him for fear you will not be able to prove it, then either you must leave the party of Donatus, or you will be just like the man whose sin you know, however differently you live. This is said to you with perfect justice, not according to the true principle but according to your own. For who does not know that you have no part in his wickedness if you do not share his sin by consenting to it? But from this you are forced to recognize how impiously you charge the Christian world with the crimes of Africans, crimes that are either false or at any rate unknown to it, when you yourself do not want to be charged with what you know about another man, because you cannot convince of it those whose fellowship you do not wish to leave. So, in order not to desert those whom you think good, you are forced to put up with those whom you know to be bad. And through this the truth convicts as wicked all those who, on account of other people's crimes, whether true or false, yet unknown to everyone else and incapable of harming themselves, tore apart the unity of so many nations and deserted the good. So that you could not in any way excuse this enormous outrage of the party of Donatus, the case of the Maximianists was arranged for you, so that, seeing your perversity in it as in a mirror, you might correct it, if you are willing. But if you are not willing — I do not want to say anything harsher, since I know you have a heart. For what are you going to say against all this?

It is good that you yourself write that when you read all I had included in my letter about the Maximianists who were condemned and then received back, you were deeply disturbed. I believe it; I can see clearly that the matter was one that ought to disturb you deeply. Let us see, then, by what explanation this disturbance of yours was calmed. You say that you immediately made careful inquiries of your bishops, and that from their instruction you learned the decree of the council, the sentence pronounced on those who were condemned, and the whole course of the affair. Then, believing that I was still ignorant of what had happened, and urging me to learn what the truth is, you told me plainly not what the truth is, but what your people pass off as truth to the careless and the negligent. For you say that when Maximian's error was striving to draw as many bishops as possible to its side, your people convened a council and a sentence was pronounced against all who persisted in his schism, a sentence which you mention that I too have read. Although this sentence was confirmed by the consent of all, the council nevertheless decreed that a period of grace should be granted, within which anyone who wished to be corrected would be held innocent. So it came about, you say, that not only the two I mention but many others too were cleared and restored to the church as innocent; and for this reason you think their baptism ought not to have been annulled, because, having been restored within the appointed day, they were not bound by the final sentence, nor, when they baptized, had they been separated from the church, since of course they were not cut off until the limit of the appointed time had passed. Here, in this very falsehood of your account — for I have set down not only your meaning but your very words — I marvel at your intelligence, and I marvel at a mind fighting against its own intelligence. Never anywhere has it been so plain how strongly the prejudice of human presumption can work, whether to keep one from seeing the most obvious truth or to make one assert the most shameless falsehood. Do you not realize that you have stated things so openly contradictory that it is scarcely believable one man could say both? You say, of course, that a sentence was pronounced against all who persisted in Maximian's schism, and that it was decided to grant a period of grace within which anyone who wished to be corrected would be held innocent. How then can you also say that they did not baptize outside the church before they had corrected themselves from that schism? So when they were with Maximian, were they not outside the church? Do you notice what you are saying? Can you find a way out, a place of refuge? Where will you hide?

Surely you see that, while you try to defend other people's obvious errors, all you achieve is to add your own, which are even more obvious. Look, read your own words — I quote them exactly as you wrote them: "When Maximian's error," you say, "was striving to draw as many bishops as possible to its side, our people convened a council and a sentence was pronounced against all who persisted in his schism, a sentence which you testify that you too have read. Although this sentence was confirmed by the consent of all, the council nevertheless decreed that a period of grace should be granted, within which anyone who wished to be corrected would be held innocent." In saying this, do you so close your mind against yourself that you fail to notice that all these men, who deserved to have the council's sentence passed against them precisely because they were allied with Maximian, remained in that same schism before they corrected themselves within the period of grace? There, then, they were also baptizing. I beg you: why do you spread an empty fog over plain facts, a fog which your own words, no less plainly, scatter again? For what I say is that Praetextatus and Felicianus, who ordained Maximian, baptized within the sacrilegious schism they had committed, and that those they baptized were received along with them without their baptism being annulled — the baptism they had given in schism, which they had administered as men of sacrilege, which they had consecrated with a mouth full of cursing, with lips bearing the poison of asps. For such are the things said against them in that sentence, which you do not deny was pronounced against them all.

Here you reply that not only the two I mention but many others too were cleared and, as innocent, returned themselves to the church within the day of grace. With these words you help me; with these words you join me in asserting the truth, and you dispel the fog you were trying to spread. For when you say that they returned themselves to the church, you undoubtedly admit that they had been outside the church. Where they were before they returned to the church, then, there they baptized; therefore the baptism they gave was outside the church. While you try to wriggle free of this inextricable tangle, you get entangled again. For you say that their baptism ought not to have been annulled because, having been restored within the appointed day, they were not bound by the final sentence. How then can you say that before the day of their restoration they had not been separated from the church, when you admit they were restored to the church before the day of grace expired? If we are human beings, if we have any reason at all, if we have human sense, if we are not cattle talking to cattle, not wood and stones talking to wood and stones, then it stands out, it is evident, it shines forth, not only from my words but from your own, that your people did not dare to annul baptism given in Maximian's sacrilegious schism — the same people who do not hesitate to deny that men baptized in the churches which the apostles spread by their own labor through the grace of the Lord are Christians, to exorcise them with breathing, and to rebaptize them. You say it, you write it — listen to yourself, read yourself — you, I say, say and write that your people convened a council and pronounced a sentence against all who persisted in Maximian's schism; you say and write that, although this sentence was confirmed by the consent of all, it was nevertheless decided to grant a period of grace within which anyone who wished to be corrected would be held innocent; you say and write that not only the two from that party whom I mention but many others too were cleared and, as innocent, returned themselves to your church; you say and write that their baptism ought not to have been annulled because, having been restored within the appointed day, they were not bound by the final sentence. How [?]

Why, why does so bad a cause prevail so strongly over so good an intelligence, you man of sense, you man of letters? These men, against whom that sentence was pronounced precisely because, as you yourself say, they persisted in Maximian's schism — before they were restored, as you put it, where they were, there they celebrated the sacraments, there they baptized; and, to use rather the words of that plenary council, there they were warming with slow heat the noxious brood of viper's seed; there they were bringing forth the pregnant longings for crime born of their public outrage and parricide; there they were in labor with injustice, conceived trouble and gave birth to iniquity; there, the forest of crimes no longer confused, their names were being marked out for punishment; there, at the end of indulgence, while the line of clemency was being paid out, the case had already found whom it would punish; thither the truthful wave had cast their shipwrecked limbs as onto jagged rocks; there, as they perished, were the shores full of corpses, after the example of the Egyptians, who did not find even burial; there the thunderbolt of the sentence had struck from the bosom of peace not only Maximian, rival of the faith, adulterer of the truth, enemy of mother church, minister of Dathan, Korah and Abiram — nor did a just death condemn him alone for his crime, but the chain of sacrilege was also dragging very many into partnership in the crime; there was the poison of asps under their lips; there their mouth was full of cursing and bitterness; there their feet were swift to shed blood; there ruin and misery were in their ways; there they did not know the way of peace, and there was no fear of God before their eyes; there lay the severed limbs which a pestilent rot had so corrupted that there was more comfort in cutting them off than in the relief of medicine; there were those guilty of the notorious crime, Victorianus of Carcabia and the twelve others with him, among them Praetextatus of Assuras and Felicianus of Musti — whose reception is our subject — who had been present to ordain that same Maximian, that is, who "by the deadly work of perdition had glued together a filthy vessel from collected dregs," where the clergy of Carthage acted as pimps for so great a crime, as for an unlawful incest. Such ministers of the sacraments baptized in Maximian's schism while not yet corrected, not yet returned and restored to you; and after such ministers of the sacraments were corrected, returned and restored, your people did not rebaptize.

Why does animosity alone prevail among you? Let the truth be attended to at last, listened to at last. Why throw out the utterly empty fog of the period of grace that was granted? It was not granted to the very men of whom it was said, "Know that they are condemned," and of whom it had already been said what sort of men they were, what they had done, and why they had to be condemned at once without any grace period — namely, because they had been present and laid hands on Maximian to ordain him. That is what they meant by saying that "by the deadly work of perdition they had glued together a filthy vessel from collected dregs." The grace period was granted instead to those who had not taken part in Maximian's ordination, although they were in his fellowship and schism, simply because, having been absent, they had not laid hands on him. For in that same sentence of the council they are distinguished from his condemned ordainers in this way. Having said of the former — whose names they also wrote down — "Know that they are condemned," they go on: "But those whom the shoots of the sacrilegious sprig did not defile, that is, those who out of the modest shame of faith withheld their own hands from the head of Maximian, we have permitted to return to mother church." What could be plainer, more distinct, more open? Of the former, those guilty of the notorious crime, who "by the deadly work of perdition had glued together a filthy vessel from collected dregs," they say, "Know that they are condemned"; of the latter, "those whom the shoots of the sacrilegious sprig did not defile, that is, those who out of the modest shame of faith withheld their own hands from the head of Maximian," they say, "we have permitted to return to mother church." And since two of those condemned were afterwards received with their rank intact, no way can be found to defend this except by saying that the grace period was granted to everyone.

But let it be granted to everyone. Clearly, all who returned to you from that schism were there before they returned, and baptized there; and by coming back to you from there without the destruction of their rank or of their baptism, they have shut your mouths — if you have any shame left. For when we ask where they were before they had returned themselves to the church, as you yourself put it, and before they were restored within the appointed day, what other answer does the fact itself force you to give but "in Maximian's schism," the very reason that sentence was pronounced against them all? There, then, they baptized those in whom, when they came to you together from there, you did not dare to annul Christ's baptism, because you were forced to recognize it. Hence, by your own deed, your own action, your own judgment, it is rightly and justly concluded against you that Christ's baptism must be recognized even if it has been given outside the church, and therefore that we act with piety in recognizing it among your people, and you act impiously in annulling it among ours.

But perhaps you regret having used words that press this truth too hard, since you said: "It came about that they returned themselves to the church and, having been restored within the appointed day, were not bound by the final sentence," so that the reply could be made to you: "How did they return themselves to the church, how were they restored to it, if they had not been separated from it? Or if they had been separated, how could they baptize?" But what else could you say than what you had heard from those you consulted when you were deeply disturbed by my letter on this matter? And yet perhaps they will blame and rebuke you for using such words carelessly. There is something that will protect you against them above all and console your sadness. For they themselves put words of this kind in the decree of that same council. So if, after reading this little work of ours, they choose to answer us that the words of their layman do not prejudice their case, we will at once quote their own words: "But those," they say, "whom the shoots of the sacrilegious sprig did not defile, that is, those who out of the modest shame of faith withheld their own hands from the head of Maximian, we have permitted to return to mother church." For when they are asked, "These men whom you permitted to return to mother church — where were they before they returned?", they are pressed just as you were pressed a moment ago by the words you had used. For where will they answer that they were, except in Maximian's schism? But let them maintain they were wherever they like: certainly those who were permitted to return to the church were not in the church. Therefore they baptized outside the church; and when baptizers and baptized returned to the church together, the former did not lose the ranks they had held outside, nor the latter the baptism they had received outside.

You, indeed, spoke as cautiously as you could in a bad cause, saying: "The council nevertheless decreed that a period of grace should be granted, within which anyone who wished to be corrected would be held innocent." They, however, did not even say that those to whom the grace period was granted needed correction; rather, when they extend this very period, they speak of them as though they had been entirely undefiled and innocent while in Maximian's fellowship. For what else do they mean by saying, "But those whom the shoots of the sacrilegious sprig did not defile we have permitted to return to mother church," than "Those whom fellowship with Maximian did not defile we have permitted to return to mother church"? And as if that were not enough, see what they add: "For the more we are cleansed by the death of the guilty, the more we rejoice at the return of the innocent." Why then do you say that it was decided to grant a period of grace within which anyone who wished to be corrected would be held innocent, when you see that it was granted to the undefiled and innocent? Evidently you were afraid of being asked, "Why was a grace period granted to those whom Maximian had not defiled?" So you held that they were to be corrected through that grace period. They were afraid of being asked, "Why were you willing to receive the defiled in their ranks?" So they said they had granted the grace period to the undefiled.

So each of you feared something different, but each position is attacked by the other. For it is said to you: "How can you think that those whom your own people proclaim undefiled needed correction?" And it is said to them: "How can you assert that those men were undefiled who, even if they did not lay hands on Maximian's head, were nevertheless stained by communion in his schism?" But whose spirit, whose strength, whose tongue is equal to expressing so unbearable a grief? So that the torn party of Donatus might be patched together again, Maximian did not defile his African associates in Africa; so that broken branches might not be allowed to return to the very root of unity, Caecilian from Africa defiled so many far-distant nations.

From the day of the Council of Bagai, that is, 24 April, to the day of the grace period granted, that is, 25 December, eight months are counted. During this long interval, were those to whom the grace period was granted stained by fellowship with the condemned Maximian or not? If they were stained, how can it be said, "But those whom the shoots of the sacrilegious sprig did not defile we have permitted to return to mother church"? If they were not stained, how could the contagion of other people's sins — sins unknown to us, not to call them false — stain us and all the Christian nations everywhere? "But," you say, "the grace period was granted so that, if it passed without their returning, they would then be stained and would incur the penalty of condemnation."
