So it was not the sin of that fellowship that stained them, but the fixing of a day. If, then, no day had been fixed, they would certainly have remained unstained. What has the whole world done to deserve ill of you? Why do you declare it stained by other people's sins, when you fixed no day of grace for it, since your power is so great that people are allied with sinners when they wish, and defiled when you wish? Those who were given a grace period in Maximian's party were innocent and undefiled; if they came back to you within its term, they would keep the foundations of their honor and faith intact; but if that day passed without their returning, then they would be defiled, then criminal, then lost; then they would incur the punishment of condemnation, then they would be humbled by penance and degraded. O wondrous reasoning of these preachers [?], for whom it is no longer, as the old proverb has it, "What we will is holy," but also "when we will and for as long as we will"! Let one of you happen to pray with us on board a ship: at once he is called defiled, at once a traditor. Yet those who condemned Primian share the altar with Maximian, adulterer of the truth, enemy of mother church, minister of Dathan, Korah and Abiram, and for eight months they remain innocent and undefiled! And so if any of them returned themselves to your communion on 24 December, you rejoiced at the return of the innocent — of those, naturally, whom "the shoots of the sacrilegious sprig did not defile." What did all those days of the eight months from 24 April to 25 December do to deserve from you that you should sanctify them so, that through them anyone who clung to the communion of the sacrilegious and condemned Maximian was neither defiled nor made guilty? And what offense did the most holy birthday of our Lord himself give you, that it alone, by its arrival and passing, should defile the innocent, so that in those who baptized in that schism the baptism of Christ remained holy through all those days and became unclean through the birthday of Christ?

What will human rashness not dare, once it is plunged headlong into an opinion of abominable error which vanity makes it ashamed to abandon, but which it is not ashamed to defend against the truth? But why say more on this, when even the most obstinate person, who has hardened himself against every voice of reason, must admit the following? Take those of whom it is said that "they returned themselves to the church and were restored before the appointed day" — words that you yourself used; take, finally, those of whom it is said, "We have permitted them to return to mother church"; "We rejoice at the return of the innocent"; "And lest the shortness of time for those returning, through the pressure of a confining day, take away the hope of salvation, we open the door of acknowledgment until that day, so that those who return may keep the foundations of their honor and faith intact. If anyone through sluggish idleness fails to enter it, let him know that the way to every avenue of pardon has been taken from him"; and "for those who return after the appointed day, fixed penance" — words which the three hundred and ten drove home again and again in their sentence. Any opponent whatever, I say, must admit that those of whom these things are said, before they returned themselves to you, before they were restored to you, before they came back to you, before they came back and entered the door of the grace period, were not with you, but baptized outside your communion, in the schism by which they had separated themselves from you. Returned and restored to you from the place where they had been estranged from you, coming back and returning to you from the place where they had been outside your fold, they both kept their ranks undiminished and brought in with them those they had baptized, who were not to be rebaptized.

Why do you go on defending a very bad cause so stubbornly? Give in at last, not to me but to the truth itself, by which you stand convicted. See how true my words were, which you tried in vain to undermine: "how much must be tolerated for the sake of peace." To use again and again the very words I used in that letter: "For the sake of the peace of Christ, return to the church, which did not condemn people without a hearing, since for the sake of the peace of Donatus you were pleased to recall the condemned." For if, out of those twelve whom they had condemned along with Maximian without any period of grace, they later received Felicianus and Praetextatus, how is it false that they recalled the condemned? And if a period of grace was given even to those of whom they said, "Know that they are condemned," then even if none of them had afterward come back, they were still pleased to recall the condemned. For after the sentence that said, "Know that they are condemned," a period of grace was granted, during which they could return with their condemnation cancelled. These points would be enough even if what you say were true: that when you were deeply troubled by this case of the Maximianists, you learned the facts from your bishops. But what will you do, since that too is false? Look up the date of the proconsular proceedings, or examine it if you have it. On that day Titianus presented the petition against Felicianus and Praetextatus, asking that they be driven from their places. See how long after the date of that period of grace this was done. The date of the Council of Bagai is the eighth day before the Kalends of May, in the consulship of the Augusti Arcadius for the third time and Honorius for the second. The period of grace ran from then until the eighth day before the [?] of January. But Titianus presented this petition after that consulship, on the sixth day before the Nones of March.

So it is clear that nearly the third month was under way when the proconsul was asked to drive Felicianus and Praetextatus from their sees as colleagues of Maximian, whom he had drawn into his madness. For when the advocate I mentioned had said in that same petition what seemed sufficient about Maximian, he went on: "Those too whom the error of another man's presumption had drawn away, it restrained with an admonition of equal force, first offering them the harbour of repentance if they wished to return within the time to the path of religion they had abandoned. But iniquity delights in its own ways and does not abandon itself once it has fallen headlong. For this same Maximian feeds the audacity he has begun and draws others into his madness. Among them is a certain Felicianus. At first he followed what was right, but he is now darkened by the defilement of this depravity. Settled in the city of Musti, he thought that walls consecrated to almighty God, a venerable church, should be held as if under a kind of siege. Praetextatus imitates him in the district of Assuras." Do you hear the advocate's perfectly clear and plain words? He says that these men we are discussing must be expelled from church premises because they despised the harbour of repentance offered to them, "while iniquity delights in its own ways, once it has fallen headlong." Even if the date of the proceedings could be hidden, it would be clear enough to anyone, however dull, that the proconsular power would not have been appealed to against them in this way unless one of two things were true. Either they had been condemned at that council without any period of grace, which seems more likely, or, if a period was granted to all, they had refused to be restored to you within it. But the date of the proceedings strikes the eyes and ears of anyone, however obstinate. It shows that even after the period of grace had expired, these men were so far outside your communion, and so firmly attached to Maximian, that this was why so fearsome a judicial order was obtained against them. What is said to this? Why do people still fight against so evident a truth with such astonishing and shameless blindness? Why do those who, for the sake of the unity of Donatus's party, were willing [?] to keep peace even with condemned and sacrilegious men still rebel so insanely against the unity of Christ? Why is the baptism of Christ, which was recognised with due reverence even in a sacrilegious schism, still rejected with impious presumption in so many catholic nations and violated by sacrilegious repetition?

I will not ask how long after the date of this petition, in which the words of the advocate Titianus accuse Felicianus and Praetextatus so gravely, they were received into your communion. It is enough that this same petition proves they were cut off from your communion, in Maximian's schism, long after the end of that fixed period of grace. Yet you later received them. You did not reduce their honours in any respect. And you were afraid to annul the baptism they had given, even though it was given in a sacrilegious schism, as indeed you had reason to fear. Would anyone's tongue, however stubborn, stir itself against us in this case if it felt that it moved in a human mouth and beneath a human brow? I admit I was plainly wrong in what I wrote in that letter about the sentence of the Council of Bagai. I said: "When it was read out among them to be decreed, they acclaimed it with wide-open mouths; but now, when we read it out, they fall silent." What you said is true: "Look, they do not fall silent." In matters so obvious, modesty can fall silent, and even shamelessness itself can; madness cannot. Do not take this as said of you, since you believed your bishops when they lied. Nor is it said of all of them, since you could not have consulted them all when you were troubled about this matter. It is said of those who knew what proceedings were taken against Praetextatus and Felicianus before the judges, and when. Yet they dared to tell you what you put into your letter: that Felicianus and Praetextatus were restored to your communion before the date of the fixed period of grace and so were not bound by the final sentence. Or if perhaps even they did not know these things, then now at least, as you read this, let modesty be silent, and let silence fall even on whatever shamelessness a human being has. Surely only madness will be left to cry out against so evident a truth. And perhaps even that can be healed, if those who are sane restrain it.

Now see how you spoke of me: "A false witness will not go unpunished," since you thought I had lied in this case of the Maximianists. I do not pay you back for this. Perhaps you said what you believed out of incautious friendship, not what you invented with a deceitful heart. We are human. With what vigilance, after all, can we make sure that we never slip in our opinions or our words? But we ought not to turn a deaf ear to the medicine of correction.

Now notice how easy this case of the Maximianists makes it for me to answer the other parts of your letter as well. You thought it necessary to say a great deal about the traditors as though they were ours, although it is rather your people who are shown to have done this, as I proved more than sufficiently in that work in three volumes. Still, look at this and answer it if you can. Whoever's crime this was, could it pollute Christians in the unity of so many nations, whether very far away or very long afterward? The crime of Maximian, that sacrilegious offshoot, could not stain his African associates. When your three hundred and ten bishops granted them a period of grace, they said of them: "whom the seedlings of the sacrilegious offshoot have not polluted." Nor could it stain you yourselves. With such harmony you received not only those you called innocent but also those already condemned in that sacrilege.

You say that the crimes of the traditors were known to the eastern churches. Yet you are an African, and the Maximianist schism committed in the capital of Africa was unknown to you until you read my letter and, deeply troubled, consulted your bishops. Even when you consulted them, you could not hear the truth from them at all. If you defend them by saying they did not lie, you concede that they did not know. And yet you will not allow us, or the many great peoples of East and West, even to be ignorant of the case of Caecilianus. Meanwhile these men are ignorant of the case of Praetextatus and Felicianus, whom the three hundred and ten, that is, all or nearly all the bishops of Donatus's party, condemned, Africans condemning Africans in Africa, and then received, Africans receiving Africans in Africa.

You insert the opening of the Council of Serdica, trying to prove that the eastern bishops, knowing the crime of the traditors, entered into communion with Donatus's party. Your one great piece of evidence is that the name Donatus is found among the bishops to whom they write. Yet nothing there says they had learned anything about the African traditors. In case you are unaware, that council belongs to the Arians, whom you yourself have already named among other heretics. It is usually read without the names of the cities added, because adding them is not the custom of the church when bishops write a letter to bishops. So I wonder whether this Donatus, whoever he is, has not been made "of Carthage" in your copies. Of course, those men, separated from Africa by such distant lands, might have asked at the very time they wished to write who the bishop of Carthage was, and found that it was Donatus. I leave aside the possibility that the eastern heretics had tried in some way to ally themselves with the African heretics. But you, a sensible man, wanted to settle the question, since someone could say to you: "If things were so, and the easterners wrote to your Donatus, how is it that the easterners later separated from the communion of your people?" You answered: "Because in receiving your people again they could not keep consistency in a case already condemned. And it is written: Whoever is joined to a prostitute is one body." With these words you have now fiercely accused your own people, since in this case of the Maximianists they could not [?] keep consistency: they condemned the sacrilegious with curses and received the condemned with honour. What you say about the easterners you do not prove at all; what is said about your own people you hear, read, see, and judge.

You order me to leave the church of the traditors. Yet neither you before us nor your forebears before ours could convict them or prove the charge. Even if you had proved it now, I would condemn their deed and their crime, but I would not abandon, on their account, the catholic fellowship of so many nations to whom they are unknown. But consider your reasoning. You do not want commemoration made in our communion of those dead men whose deeds we do not know, and who, as we have learned from their successors, had a good reputation among their own people. Meanwhile, living in your communion without any degradation are men whose evil you have experienced and whose sacrilege you have condemned.

You dare to say to me, sensible man that you are: "The man who handed over the Scriptures created you." In saying this you do not know that the one who is our creator as Christians is the same who is our creator as human beings. Nor, moreover, have you convicted of handing over the Scriptures the man you suppose to be my creator. But I do not repay this insult. I do not call Felicianus your creator, nor the creator of your sons, grandsons, or great-grandsons, if they are in Donatus's party. Only, since you permit it, I warn you that your Creator should not find you a deserter, running after a man's name with impious vanity. Then you think you add something persuasive: "The stream is drawn from its source, and the members follow the head. When the head is healthy the whole body is healthy, and if there is any disease or defect in it, it weakens all the members. Whatever grows from a stock looks back to its origin. One who does not follow the way of an innocent man cannot be innocent, especially since it is written: Do not walk in the statutes of your fathers." In all these words of yours I pass over the fact that your comparison with the human body does not fit, for the foot may ache while the head is healthy, and the head while the foot is healthy. I also pass over the fact that you have forgotten what you said a little earlier: "This is what we too want, this is what we urge, that Christ be the head of the Christian." Yet now you want some traditor or other to be the head of unknown Christian nations. Among them you refuse to recognise the baptism of Christ given and received, as though the baptized had been created only by that traditor. I pass over, too, how much the scriptural testimony you yourself cited helps me. It was said to the Jews: "Do not walk in the statutes of your fathers." Yet all who chose to keep this command at that time, like the holy prophets and the seven thousand men who did not bow the knee before Baal, did not separate themselves from their people or from the sacraments they shared. This is what I say, and whether you like it or not I drive it home by repetition, however tiresome I may seem to you: do not make Caecilianus, so often acquitted, the head of us who came after him. For I do not make Primianus, condemned by Felicianus, or Felicianus, condemned by Primianus, the head of those who came after you.

Now about the odium of persecution, which you boast of suffering from earthly powers on behalf of Donatus's party. Although I answered you fully and abundantly in that three-book work, I will not keep silent now about the brief answer this case of the Maximianists provides, even if you use this to commend yourselves to ignorant and unthinking people. For this is how Maximian himself, and this is how his associates, commend themselves to foolish and ignorant people. Your people persecuted them, and still they could not be made to give in and return to your communion. But those who think soberly understand that when people suffer some hardship, we must consider not the penalties but the causes. They understand that these men suffered disturbance even from secular courts rightly and justly, because of the crime of sacrilegious schism for which you rightly and justly condemned them. I do not even mention what you put in your letter, that it was not Optatus but the populace that demolished, not Maximian's basilica, but his cave. Even there, though it is uncertain whether your people did it, it is certain that he suffered persecution, and yet that he was not righteous but impious. So you are now forced to admit that we should attend not to what someone suffers but to why he suffers.

But it is not enough for me, for now, to show by this example of Maximian that whoever suffers persecution under the pretext and cover of Christ's name is not automatically righteous, since even the sacrilegious Maximian suffered it. I must also compel you to admit that the devout persecute the sacrilegious and the righteous persecute the impious, not out of a desire to harm, but rather out of the necessity of seeing to their good. I do not bring forward examples from the Old Testament, although you said you wanted to be taught by prophetic examples too. I do not bring forward those very ancient examples, I say, for they belonged to another dispensation and another time. But now, after gentleness had been revealed and commended at the proper time, your bishops [?], which we indeed call just. But as long as you defend such a cause there [?], you are forced to say: your bishops, I say, persecuted your schismatics.

So I do not now say, "Maximian suffered persecution, and Optatus inflicted it." You reply that we do not know this, and that he did it in such a way that I can cite no proceedings about it, although with the memory so recent, the cities themselves could not deny it if they were asked. This, then, I do not say. But I do say: Maximian suffered persecution, and Primianus inflicted it. And I cite proceedings to show that Primianus, acting through an agent he had commissioned, took away a house that Maximian claimed as his own, on the claim that it was a church exorcistery, with the legate Sacerdos favouring him, as the proceedings themselves show. But suppose the judge acted from justice, not favour; I do not deny or dispute it. Why, then, in the records of the magistrate of Carthage, among other insulting things he instructed his agents to say about us, did Primianus say: "They take away what belongs to others; we let go of what has been taken from us"? If the house was Maximian's, he himself had taken what belonged to another. If instead Maximian had usurped it, Primianus had not let go of what was taken from him. But if you will not have even this count as persecution, I say that your bishops and your clergy persecuted the Maximianists who remained in the sees where they had long ago been ordained. They accused them before proconsuls, obtained orders against them, and secured the pressure of officials and the help of the cities to carry out those orders. These men had already been condemned by the severity of the Bagai sentence and cut off from the body of your communion with a brief, sharp pain, so that the pestilent poison would not creep through all the members. They no longer posed any danger to you through the diseased contagion of their communion. Together with their congregations, cut off along with them, they attended their own conventicles, and with the people who adhered to them they held, in long-standing possession, places and basilicas they had not seized. Yet the aim was that they should be terrified, harassed, expelled, and if they resisted, brought before the court.

Read what the advocates said about them and against them in their pleadings: what crimes of sacrilege were charged, and with what force of accusation the authorities were stirred up. Ask what was done to Salvius of Membressa. The harassments of that persecution could not force him to return from his partnership in the crime. He preferred to submit to trial and answer his persecutors in the proconsul's court. I suppose he was confident that his adversaries could not use the laws issued against heretics before the judge without equally entangling themselves in them. But this calculation deceived him. Before Seranus, then proconsul, either favour carried more weight or, perhaps more likely, the Council of Bagai did, which was read out there too against this same Salvius. In one interlocutory ruling, in fact, the proconsul showed what was being sought through him. Either he was to return Salvius to the choir of bishops of Primianus's communion, or he was to drive him from his sees, so that Restitutus, whom Primianus had ordained against him, could hold without a rival all the places Salvius held. And yet in that same ruling he stated plainly that Salvius was suffering persecution. For this is what we read in those same proceedings: "Seranus the proconsul said: By law, a dispute between bishops must be heard by bishops. The bishops have judged. Why do you not either make satisfaction and return to the choir of long standing, or, as you have it written, turn your back on your persecutors?" What do you think of this? Will you call this Salvius righteous? He was being accused before the proconsul with your bishop Restitutus standing against him, and the proconsul even gave him advice from holy Scripture, to turn his back on his persecutors, since it is written in the gospel: "If they persecute you, flee." Surely you see what an image of a martyr or a confessor Salvius presents among his own people. With Restitutus persecuting him, he earned these words from the proconsul. And yet he is judged impious and sacrilegious not only by us but by you as well.

Then the proconsul's sentence was delivered to the people of Abitina, the neighbouring town, through whom your people had obtained that the judgment be carried out, since nearly all the people of Membressa loved Salvius. What these same Abitinians did to a man of great age I am ashamed to tell, because they did not do it on the record. But since, with the memory so recent, the testimony of the towns themselves is clearer than any document, I will briefly touch on what I learned there while travelling through. Relying on the crowd that favoured him, Salvius tried to resist them, even after the proconsul's judgment, in order to defend his sees to whatever extent he could. At length he was overpowered and seized. He was no longer to be brought before the judge, since the sentence between the parties had already been pronounced. Instead he was to be paraded in a pitiful triumph. They tied dead dogs around the captured old man's neck and danced with him like that for as long as they pleased. If I wished to amplify this in my speech, could I not perhaps show that this punishment can scarcely be compared even with the tortures of the Etruscan kings, who bound dead bodies to living ones? Suppose an old man who wanted to be regarded as a bishop were offered two punishments and had to undergo one of them. Would not everyone judge that he deserved to be banished from the company of both the living and the dead if he did not choose to be bound to human corpses rather than dance with dead dogs?

Now look at those words of mine which you thought you had refuted. Or rather, look not at those words themselves but at these, which I shall say in their place. See, I do not say, “If it is not lawful to persecute, Optatus did it”; I say, “If it is not lawful to persecute, Restitutus did it.” Nor do I say, “If whoever suffers persecution is to be held innocent, Maximian suffered it”; I say, “If whoever suffers persecution is to be held innocent, Salvius suffered it.” I am reading out the records and repeating words you do not want to hear: Restitutus did it, Salvius suffered it. Of these two, which will you tell me is the Christian, if not Restitutus, and which the sacrilegious one, if not Salvius? So two of your claims must fall flat and be rejected as unproven. One is your claim that no persecution is just. The other is your question, “Who refuses to accept the testament that has been produced, the one who suffers persecution or the one who inflicts it?” For there is such a thing as just persecution: the kind that Salvius endured and Restitutus inflicted. Salvius suffered it, and yet for you Restitutus is praiseworthy and Salvius damnable. Nor will you say that it was done in secret, or that something done in that city could have escaped Primian. He himself presided there as bishop, and it was so great a city, and the case was before so great a judge, that it could not have stayed hidden even from other cities. Or if this too is to be counted among hidden things, why will you not allow the world to be ignorant of whatever wrong Caecilian did in the time of persecution (though God forbid that he did any)? After all, Primian could apparently be unaware of the persecution that Salvius suffered at the hands of the man Primian himself ordained against him, in the very city where he holds primacy over his colleagues. So, like it or not, you will admit that not only can the unjust suffer persecution, but the just can also inflict it. Otherwise you will be forced to condemn Restitutus, Primian and the party of Donatus. Or if you think that what is done justly should not be called persecution, you will be unable to prove that you have suffered persecution from us, or your people from ours. Instead we shall show that we suffer it from your clergy and circumcellions. With hard and senseless hearts, neither understanding nor bearing that we are seeking their salvation, they rage against us with such fury that I cannot count, recount or adequately describe in words what they do to us.

So when a madman attacks his doctor and the doctor ties the madman up, either both are persecuting each other, or, if only what is done wrongly counts as persecution, then surely the doctor is not persecuting the madman, but the madman the doctor. Your savagery, then, and your most violent audacity, which everyone knows you exercise through your circumcellions, the henchmen of your clergy, had to be curbed and in a sense tied up by the laws passed against you. At the same time the laws were meant to make you at least willing, warned by that very fear, to reflect on and correct the error you are in and the sacrilege by which you are divided against the unity and peace of Christ. In the same way Felicianus and Praetextatus, harried by your own threats through orders of the secular authorities, corrected the schism they had made from you and returned to your communion and fellowship. Salvius, with an exceedingly hard and perverse heart, refused to do so. But the whole would be put right if all of you returned to the Catholic root. Whatever has been done against you beyond the moderation of Christian love is no more to be laid to the charge of the Catholic Church than I would lay to the charge of Primian or Restitutus what the people of Abitina did to Salvius.

You exaggerated the persecutions which you said the party of Donatus had endured, saying nothing at all of what your people did first and saying much about ours that is not proven. Then you added testimony from the Psalms and said, “Is it not of those who do such things that it is said, Their feet are swift to shed blood, and the way of peace they have not known?” Yet these very words, and many others far more severe, your bishops spoke against Felicianus and Praetextatus at that Council of Bagai. Those two certainly shed no one's bodily blood and made no violent physical attack on you. But the men who said these things against them judged that, through the sacrilege of schism, they were shedding spiritual blood, which is far more criminal. So if, after such grave and harsh words had been spoken against them, you made peace with them without tarnishing their rank and without annulling their baptism, there is no need to despair that you may come to agreement with us as well. The whole Christian world ought to draw you to make peace far more strongly than Praetextatus and Felicianus did. If the men you condemned on such atrocious charges did not defile you, far less does the unity of so many Christian nations defile you, a unity to which you have not proved the crimes of a few unnamed Africans. What does defile you greatly is the crime by which you have separated your fellowship from the fellowship of that Church for which so many and such great divine testimonies are cited. With human rashness you have dared to contradict these divine testimonies. And yet you yourself, compelled somehow by the same force of truth, have admitted that the whole world is daily turning to the Christian name.

You dared, I say, to resist God's testament. Yet the apostle says, “No one annuls or adds to a man's will once it has been ratified. The promises were made to Abraham and to his offspring.” You had not the least fear of annulling this testament and setting the party of Donatus above it. In that same testament God says to Abraham, “So shall your offspring be, like the stars of heaven and like the sand of the sea.” You annul this and set above it the party of Donatus, for which you cite no testimony, and you say, “Truth is often found among the few; error belongs to the many.” You do not understand how the Lord could say that few enter by the narrow gate, when he also said that many will come from east and west and recline at table with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and when the Apocalypse shows thousands clothed in white, from every nation and tribe and tongue, whom no one could number. They are certainly many in themselves, and yet the same people are few compared with the far greater number who are to be punished with the devil. This grain is destined for the divine granaries for ever and is joined throughout the whole world in the unity of love. Yet it endures the heat and threshing of this age until it is cleansed at the final winnowing. It suffers both from the scandals and violence of heretics and from its own inner chaff, so to speak: the many who do not live rightly. But against all this nothing answers you more readily than the case of the Maximianists. If truth is often found among the few and error belongs to the many, then allow the Maximianists to surpass you in truth by as much as they fall short of you in numbers. You will not. Then do not boast of how few you are compared with the multitude of Catholic nations, just as you do not want the Maximianists to boast of how few they are compared with your multitude.

As for your stories about African traditors: do you really not know, or not feel with any sort of human heart, how empty and foolish a story is in a debate that seeks the truth, when no proof follows it? I would not spend effort refuting it even if I did not have, in the case of the Maximianists, so easy and direct a shortcut. The sacred scriptures say, “The God of gods, the Lord, has spoken and summoned the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting; out of Zion comes the beauty of his glory.” The gospel agrees with this prophetic testimony when the same Lord says of himself, “It was necessary for the Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day, and for repentance and forgiveness of sins to be preached in his name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem.” What is said there, “summoned the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting,” is said here as “among all nations”; and what is said there, “out of Zion comes the beauty of his glory,” is said here as “beginning from Jerusalem.” For Christ did not only suffer there. There too he rose again, and from there he ascended into heaven. There, on the day of Pentecost, he sent the Holy Spirit from heaven and filled the hundred and twenty who were gathered together. There, converting them into his body, he received three thousand believers on one day and five thousand on another. From there the Church spread, and is still spreading, bearing fruit, into all Judea and Samaria and the other nations of the world. He foretold this to his disciples when he was about to ascend into heaven: “You will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria and to the ends of the earth.” This Church began from Jerusalem and is spreading through all nations with such evident fruitfulness that it forces even you to confess that, by God's providence, the whole world is daily turning to the Christian name. This Church, I say, is summoned from the rising of the sun to its setting as the Lord, the God of gods, speaks. It could in no way be polluted by African traditors of whom it knew nothing at all. For the shoots of the sacrilegious Maximian did not pollute those seedlings, so many of his colleagues, merely because they did not lay hands on him to ordain him. And this was so although they praised him when Primian condemned him, and themselves condemned Primian, and although they were given a period of grace in which to return while they stood in his schism.

I also said, “We charge you with handing over far more plausibly.” You reply that I thereby admitted that you charge us with it plausibly. You even teach a rule of speech: the comparative degree “intensifies what is set before it; it does not disapprove of what was said before.” You add that just as there are “well” and “better,” “badly” and “worse,” “horribly” and “more horribly,” so there are “plausibly” and “more plausibly.” From this you think you can draw a conclusion, and you say, “If you more plausibly, then we plausibly.” I answered you on this point sufficiently, perhaps more than sufficiently, in its proper place in that longer work of three books. There I showed from the literature in which we learned our words that the comparative degree does not always intensify what it compares, but sometimes disapproves of what it is compared with. Hence the lines “May the gods grant better things to the righteous” and “I could wish this under better auspices.” Read carefully, and you will find more for yourself. But I beg you, are you not amazed that in this case of the Maximianists, from which I have now decided to answer you on every point, I have not lacked an example of this way of speaking either? In that most splendid and eloquent sentence of the Council of Bagai they say, “A more healthful course has been found: so that the pestilent poison may not creep through all the limbs, the wound that has arisen is to be cut away with a brief pain.” By your rule they certainly ought to have said “healthful,” not “more healthful.” For it was not healthful but ruinous for the pestilent poison to creep through all the limbs. So cutting away the wound with a brief pain was the more healthful course, although the alternative, letting the poison creep through all the limbs, was not healthful but deadly. In the same way, we charge you with handing over more plausibly, although you do not charge us with it plausibly.

Next, I said that Silvanus, your bishop of Cirta, was a traditor. The municipal records drawn up there at Cirta by Munatius Felix, the curator of the city, bear witness to this. As we read written there, when the library was opened the cupboards were found empty. Silvanus then produced a silver casket [?] and a silver lamp, saying that he had found them behind a chest. Victor, son of Aufidius, said to him, “You would have been a dead man if you hadn't found them.” And when Felix the curator said to him, “Search more carefully, in case anything is left here,” Silvanus said, “Nothing is left here; we have thrown it all out.” These records were read out in the proceedings before Zenophilus the consular and entered into them along with many other pieces of witness evidence. The consular then asked, “What office did Silvanus hold in the clergy at that time?” Victor replied, “When the persecution broke out under Bishop Paul, Silvanus was a subdeacon.” To weaken belief in this most evident public record, you think you are setting up something important against it. You mention the sentence he pronounced against Caecilian, as though he were punishing traditors, and you argue that a man who showed himself so severe an avenger of handing over could not possibly have been a traditor. As if anything had seemed more severe than those utterly wicked elders, when they raged so insistently to have Susanna put to death, while their conscience was pierced by the very crime they pretended to want to punish in her! But let us leave such things aside. What of Felicianus? Does he not now, together with Primian, condemn what he himself committed together with Maximian? Clearly, though, he has been corrected by a better judgment and is not more shameless for it. If Silvanus had been willing to do the same, he would have condemned, in a wholesome act of amendment, not a false handing over in Caecilian but a true one in himself. He would then have passed over to the innocent Caecilian, even if not as a bishop, yet with his wickedness corrected. After all, Felicianus had likewise condemned the innocent Primian, as Silvanus had condemned Caecilian. Yet Felicianus could pass over to Primian with no stain to Primian or to himself, and even keep his episcopal rank.

I also said that your forebears ought to have convicted certain traditors whom they accused, if their accusations were true. You should not have taken this to mean that they ought to have done so among themselves. You answer that they did, and that this is why they judged that our people had lost baptism. First read carefully what you are writing against, and either understand what is said or stop twisting what you do understand into something else. I said that those men ought to have been convicted not among your people but before the churches overseas, which considered the men your people accused to be innocent. The Maximianists too think that they convicted Primian before condemning him. But they did not do it before people who were placed farther away and further removed from favor or envy, and who could therefore have passed a judgment on him that the whole party of Donatus would readily accept. As it is, a hundred condemned him and left him to be acquitted by more than three hundred, before whom they themselves ran the risk of condemnation. They ought, of course, to have persuaded these far more numerous bishops of their judgment, so that they themselves would be inside with them and Primian outside, if after his condemnation he had rejected penance. But suppose they could not persuade so much larger a number of colleagues, and so many churches of their communion spread throughout all Africa. Then they should have rescinded their sentence on sounder advice, since, being men judging a man, they could have been mistaken. Or, if they had learned beyond any doubt that his crimes were real but still could not persuade so many more of the others, they should have tolerated a man they knew to be guilty, more wisely and patiently, rather than separate themselves by an impious schism from so many innocent men who did not know these things. They should have held to that saying of the blessed Cyprian, so full of charity and piety: “For even if there seem to be tares in the Church, our faith or charity ought not to be hindered, so that, because we see tares in the Church, we ourselves withdraw from the Church.” This would indeed have done them great good, if they had been cleansed within the bosom of the Catholic Church and had tolerated the refuse that they could not separate before the time. But what we say they ought to have done within this fellowship of your error, which you think is the true Church, your forebears ought to have done in that plainly true Church in whose unity they stood, so as not to be separated from it. Take any man of your party who knows nothing at all about Primian's case. Even though a hundred Maximianists condemned Primian, he simply believes him innocent, because Primian proved himself to so many more. In the same way, a member of the Catholic communion who does not know the facts of Caecilian's case is quite right to be persuaded that Caecilian was innocent. For not only throughout Africa but throughout the lands of so many Christian nations, there were so many more other bishops before whom one of three things happened. He could have been recognized as innocent, and so earned acquittal from those who knew him. Or he could have hidden his guilt, and so not earned condemnation from those who did not know. Or, if a corrupt judge acquitted him against his deserts, his guilt could not be shown to others who had not judged him. You, then, by a sacrilegious separation, cut yourselves off from the unity of so many great and innocent peoples. Since they could not be judges in this case, either they did not know that there had been any judges in it, or whether anything had been judged or what, or else they believed the chosen judges rather than the defeated litigants.

This also shows how easily you are defeated on the point you chose, the last option in my fourfold division; indeed you could choose no other. I said that if documents proving the crimes of handing over were produced by both sides, then either both sets are true, or both are false, or ours are true and yours false, or ours are false and yours true. I showed that our victory was very easy under the first three options. As for the fourth, either you did not fully understand that you are beaten there too, or, as I rather believe, you tried to cover it with some sort of shadows so that others would not understand it, and you thought you should argue about the type of reasoning instead. Perhaps I will deal with you on that elsewhere if need be, so as not to waste time now on matters that are not necessary.

So consider whether I can show this too in that clear mirror of yours, the case of the Maximianists. When all those by whom and before whom these things were done have died, a dispute over communion may one day arise between your descendants and theirs. They will say that their forebears, a hundred or more bishops, condemned Primian, and they will produce the sentence written against him first at Carthage and then the other at Cebarsussi. Against this your people will read out the Council of Bagai. They will demand to be shown that the crimes of Primian recorded in their forebears' sentence were cleared away. Will not your people answer, with much more justice: “These crimes that you lay against a man now dead may be true. If so, prove that you brought them before our forebears and showed them to be true. If you tried to do this and failed, then other people's crimes, however true, could not defile our forebears, because they had not been shown to them. How much less, if you did not even try to show them! So how could the guilt of that case pass to us, when, being unknown and unproven, it did not touch even those who were alive with Primian at the time? We therefore convict you of the guilt of schism by plain truth. For we see that you are separated from us, your brothers, because of other people's crimes that were not demonstrated to our forebears when they should have been.” The congregations and clergy of the places that sent the three hundred and ten bishops who drew up the Council of Bagai against the Maximianists will say this most justly. If, I say, Africans will rightly say this to Africans, and great numbers of Numidians and Mauretanians to a few from Byzacena and the Proconsular province, how much more justly does the whole world say this to Africans about the crimes of certain traditors in Africa, even if those crimes were real! This is all the more so since the Catholic Church in Africa itself is so large and is joined to the other nations by the bond of unity. And it still cries out: “Even the documents of other people's crimes that you are now trying to show me do not make the peoples of the nations guilty, since those documents were not shown to them when they should have been, either because you could not or because you did not bother. These peoples are innocent in this case. If I cut myself off from them because of other people's crimes, I cannot be innocent of the sacrilegious crime of schism. So even suppose you were entirely in the right and could now teach me that these charges are true: we condemn the dead traditors, but we do not desert the living innocent.”

I said that if any of your documents were true, you ought to have proved them to the Church, that is, the Catholic Church, so that you would be inside and those you convicted would be driven out. Why, then, did you choose to answer that the separation took place because we were driven out, while your people remained in the full and Catholic Church? If the Maximianists said this to you in exactly those words, what would you answer except that they do not deserve refuting, only laughing at? For they dare to claim to be the full Church with now fewer than a hundred bishops, against so great a number and multitude headed by more than three hundred. And throughout all the regions of Africa where the Maximianists are, the communion of Primian is present too, while in the other, far more numerous and extensive parts of Africa no one would find a single Maximianist, except perhaps the odd traveller. With what face, then, do you dare to call the party of Donatus the full Church, against the Church that the voice of truth promised from the rising of the sun to its setting, and that has now been delivered? The party of Donatus exists only in Africa, while that Church exists among so many nations and in Africa as well. ("But of course this one sent that one out.") Please, do not you send that word out: a man's forehead is on his face, not under his shoulder. So this one sent that one out, did it? Do you not see what follows if that Church is sent out? It is the Church of which God says to Abraham: In your seed all nations shall be blessed; of which we read the prophecy that in the last days the mountain of the Lord shall be made manifest, and all nations shall come to it; of which the psalm sings the prophecy: All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations shall worship in his sight; of which it is preached that it bears fruit and grows in the whole world; which the Lord himself says is spread through all nations, beginning from Jerusalem. Do you not see, I say, that if this Church is sent out, then the law of God, the prophets, the psalms, the apostles, the gospel itself, in short the whole testament, and the heir himself are sent out with it?

If you pay attention to this wickedness, if you shudder at it, if you tremble at it, then see where you all stand, and come back inside. You did not send others outside; rather, it is you who went out. See what headstrong blindness does! When people say that Maximian sent Primian outside, everyone laughs. When they say that the party of Donatus sent outside the labours of the apostles, which are bearing fruit and growing throughout the whole world, no one shudders.

So that you are not deceived and do not deceive others, I must say something more. You fail to notice, or pretend not to have noticed, what I have mentioned so often, and you claim that I said that the Catholic Church, which I uphold, is not the Lord's grain, [?] as though I had upheld it in a way that divine Scripture does not. Grain alone will be stored in the granary; now the Church is being threshed like a threshing floor, together with the chaff. This is what presses and weighs on you, and it will destroy you unless you are corrected. You have shown that you yourselves are the chaff of this threshing floor, yet you said that you could not tolerate the chaff, and you shamelessly declared that you are the purified grain. So, stirring up trouble with empty slanders, you have left the threshing floor itself before the final time of winnowing, like the lightest dust of the threshing carried off into the void. In short, that most arrogant and most false saying is yours, not ours: "What has chaff to do with grain?" Jeremiah said this about the dreams of foolish men and the revelations of false prophets, and Parmenian writes it as though it had been said about us and you. Ask Maximian too; he will say nothing else about himself. For all who tear themselves away from the unity of Christ share one and the same swelling of impious pride: they boast that they alone are Christians, and they condemn everyone else, not only those who know about their quarrel but even those who have never heard their name.

Next, how clever you thought you were being! I had said of God's testament: "Now let it be read, wherever it was brought out from." You thought you should reply that this already amounted to a confession of the crime, and that I said "let it be read, whoever brought it out" because I know that it was burned by our people and preserved and brought out by yours. But suppose that, trusting in the truth, you wanted Maximian to bring out a copy of the Law from which you could read about Dathan, Korah and Abiram, who were swallowed alive when the earth opened up, the men to whom the sentence of Bagai compared him. Would the passage not be read against him all the more forcefully because it is found in his own copy? So when I said, "let the testament be read, wherever it was brought out from," that was not a confession of crime but confidence in the truth. What could be more fitting, or more splendid, than that, if possible, what is read against you should be brought out by you? It is not that I have nothing on my side. But the refutation is easier and surer when you hold in your own hands what tells against you, which would become something in your favour if you were corrected.

Since you chose to repeat empty arguments against the universal Church, I will answer you on this point too. In Africa you are the party of Donatus, and it is plain that the party of Maximian made the schism from you. It does not reach throughout Africa, as you do, while you are present even in the regions where it is found. Other schisms have also broken off from you, such as the Rogatists in Mauretania Caesariensis, the Urbanists in a small corner of Numidia, and a number of others. But they stayed where they were cut off. From this it is obvious that they went out from you, not you from them, since you are present even in the lands where they are, while they are not found wherever you are, except perhaps as travellers. In the same way the Catholic Church, which, as Cyprian says, "stretches out its branches over the whole earth in rich abundance," bears everywhere the scandals of those who are cut off from it, chiefly through the vice of pride: some here, others there and elsewhere. They point to their own parties and say, "Look, here is Christ!" or "Look, there he is!", and he himself warned us beforehand not to believe them. For they do not point to the way of which the psalm prophesied: "That we may know your way on earth, your salvation among all nations." Each points instead to the regions of its own communion: "Look, here! Look, there!" Where they fall, there they remain; where they are separated, there they wither. So the Church from which they are cut off extends even into the lands where those fragments lie, each in its own region. But those fragments are not present wherever the Church spreads, although now and then the wind of pride may scatter a very few dry leaves from their withered wood into foreign lands.

This Church, then, which, to use the same words again, "stretches out its branches over the whole earth in rich abundance," will go on growing until it reaches many barbarian nations beyond the Roman world as well. I think you have looked into this and found it out, for you said: "I pass over the peculiar religions of the barbarian nations, the rites of the Persians, the stars of the Chaldeans, the superstitions of the Egyptians, the gods of the magi, as though none of these existed, since by the providence of God the whole world is turning daily to the Christian name." What you said is true, and in this way the promise made to Abraham is fulfilled: "In your seed all nations shall be blessed." He said "all nations"; he did not say "all the people of all nations." So the whole world must be filled until the end, when the judgment separates them, not only by the fruitfulness of the growing Church but also by the multitude of its enemies mixed in with it, through whom its devotion can be exercised and tested. This testament was also recalled to Abraham's son Isaac, when the Lord said: "I will establish the oath that I swore to Abraham your father, and I will multiply your seed like the stars of heaven, and I will give you and your seed all the earth, and in your seed all the nations of the earth shall be blessed." And to his grandson Jacob: "Your seed shall be like the sand of the earth, and it shall spread out beyond the sea, and toward the African quarter, and toward the north and the east, and in you all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed." Anyone who reads Scripture knows that when it says "beyond the sea" it usually means the west. If you had been willing to accept this testament once it was brought out, you would not have stayed in the African quarter alone.

So, as you say, we are not in communion with the Novatianists, Arians, Patripassians, Valentinians, Anthropians, Apellians, Marcionites, Ophites and the rest of the sacrilegious names, to use your words, "of wicked plagues, not sects." Yet wherever these are, the Catholic Church is there too, just as it is in Africa where you are. But it is not true that wherever the Catholic Church is, either you or one of those heresies is there. From this it is clear which is the tree that "stretches out its branches over the whole earth in rich abundance," and which are the broken branches that have no life from the root and lie withering, each in its own place. But if they do not remain in unbelief, as the apostle says of the Israelites, they will be grafted in, for God is able to graft them in again. This does not mean that they receive the sacrament of baptism again, since they did not change it when they were broken off from the tree. It means that they come back to life through the root of love and unity, separated from which they wither in the barrenness of their hostility. In the same way you thought that Praetextatus and Felician, whom Maximian had cut off along with himself, should be grafted back in, and you did not reject the baptism of those who had been cut off. You would truly do them some good if you restored both them and yourselves, not to your own fragment, but to the Catholic root.

Now, what shall I answer to your claim that I seemed to have spoken on your side? I said that baptism does no good to those who depart from unity, yet that they still have it is proved by the fact that it is not given back to them when they return. You declared that you too say this: that the baptism our forefathers had received in the Church did them no good once they did not return to it. If that is what you were saying, there would be nothing else in dispute between us except which is the Church where baptism does good. But you do not say that baptism is in us and does no good. You say that what we received from those who had lost it by departing is not baptism at all. So you could not answer, and you will not be able to answer, the point I made: that departing people still have baptism is proved by the fact that it is not given back to them when they return. If Felician had lost his baptism by leaving you, why was he not baptized again when he came back, so that what he had lost might be restored to him? Indeed, if Maximian himself were to return to you, he would not be baptized, which he certainly ought to be if he had lost his baptism. These are your own words: that those held in his schism under the sentence of condemnation "lost both baptism and the Church together." Then, just as the Church is restored to them when they return, let baptism be restored too. Let them be baptized when they return, I say, if they lost baptism when they left. Since you do not do this, you too admit that those who leave the Church still have baptism, but that it does them no good. So they give it in the way they have it: those who receive it from them outside the Church have baptism, but it does them no good. Therefore, just as the returning schismatics are not given back what they never lost, so those who received baptism from them should not be given what they had already received. Rather, the aim should be that what both could have outside the Church, though without benefit, may benefit both through the Church. So I said nothing in support of your error, and you have not answered what I did say.

You also add something about the enclosed garden and the sealed fountain, without understanding at all where it comes from. "If the garden is enclosed and the fountain sealed," you say, "how can someone who stands outside, separated from the garden, that is, the Church, and from its fountain, that is, baptism, give what he does not have?" Ask Felician whether he was in the enclosed garden when the door of the time-limit was opened for him to return, as it were, into that same enclosed garden. Or did he perhaps steal the fountain from it, so that he could baptize his laypeople in the schism of Maximian? If so, where were your people washing theirs at that time? Or did your people also make them wait for the length of that time-limit, until those thieves came back to the garden with the fountain? Were those men not false prophets then, when they lied about Primian's crimes and led the people they had deceived into their sacrilege? Were they not ravening wolves when they dragged those they had led astray from Primian's flock into the little fragments of their cutting-off? You deny what I said about the tyrannical lordship your people exercise on other people's estates and their drunken revels. Deny it as much as you can; I am not afraid that this will make you reluctant to come to agreement with us. I said nothing of the kind against you compared with what the Maximianists you condemned deserved to hear from you. You deny the frenzy of the Circumcellions and the sacrilegious and profane cult of the corpses of those who threw themselves off cliffs of their own accord. Yet you do not deny that, when the shores were full of the dead bodies of those who perished, very much after the example of the Egyptians, whose greater punishment in death itself was that they did not even find a burial, you clung to these unburied corpses. For Praetextatus and Felician lay among them. Or if they came back to life among you, what do you do about the baptism that they gave while they were dead?

You say that I did not keep the peace and gentleness I had promised at the beginning of my letter, because I called Petilian Satan. I did not compare Petilian, or any person in the party of Donatus, to Satan. I compared the very error of the party of Donatus to him, and I long for the people I love to be set free from its snares. Read more carefully and you will find this. And even if I did say something rather harsh, read what you yourselves said, not against the error of the Maximianists but against the men themselves. So let Petilian imitate Felician, and not be angry with me, who long for peace.

I am certainly not angry with you for thinking you should obliquely throw the Manichees at me because of the error of my youth. In that matter I do not so much grieve over my past unhappiness as rejoice in the everlasting glory of my deliverer. Still, if you like, I advise you to look for and read what I have written against the most pestilent heresy of the Manichees, how much and in what way. There you will see how faithfully I have defended Christian truth against them, and how clearly I have demolished their deceptions. Do not be unwilling to believe me, when you believe that Felician has faithfully held to Primian, though on Maximian's behalf he pronounced such great crimes against Primian in a sentence of condemnation, and though, once separated from Maximian, he may perhaps have written something against him. Felician did not fall into Maximian's schism as I fell among the Manichees, as a young layman and catechumen. He was an old man and a bishop, and he had made an old man and a bishop the adversary of the one to whom he is now joined. You also mentioned, with the same urbane obliqueness, the letter that our primate wrote about me in anger. When he was pressed in a council of bishops to prove what he had charged, he corrected himself and asked pardon on this matter, and I can read that the letter was condemned by his own sentence. You go and see whether you can read anywhere that Felician, having been corrected, condemned what he said against Primian, not as an accuser but as one condemning him; or at least that Primian himself annulled what he said in condemning Felician. Even if you were to find this, the two cases would still not be equal. Our primate had brought an accusation, and when he saw that it was false he condemned it and asked for pardon. He did not scorn the humility of amendment because of his rank as primate, but wisely remembered what is written: "The greater you are, the more humble yourself in all things, and you will find favour before God." Those men, however, had not accused each other before others; they had sat as judges against each other. So they condemned each other, and once condemned, they came to an agreement. We do not begrudge the condemned their peace within the party of Donatus, provided that they do not reject the peace of Christ throughout the world as well.

You see now, I think, how emptily you said that you thought you had answered everything my letter contains. If you answered simply because you did not want to keep silent, then you did answer, though not everything. But if you answered in order to refute what I had said, I see that you replied to many points, but I do not see that you refuted anything. Considering everything I have said, I think you will very easily understand that your people refuse to confer with us, not in order to avoid contention, which does not exist when truth is being sought and people are not quarrelling for empty glory, but because they have no confidence in their bad cause. For if we bring forward only this one case of the Maximianists, perhaps you now recognize at last that nothing can be said against it. So I did not arrogantly commend it as if it were unconquerable eloquence of mine, as you believe or falsely allege. I wanted rather that readers should see that the case is such that no advocacy of eloquence is needed to assert it, or rather to demonstrate it.

Look: I no longer speak of your error as a three-headed beast, since you are such a delicate corrector of words. I say instead "a threefold slander." Nor do I say that we must resist it with this case of the Maximianists as with a three-pronged weapon; I say "with a threefold defence." Nor do I say "pierce them in the forehead" or "stop their mouths"; I say "curb their impudence and check their speech." Now that the words have been changed and the figurative ones made literal, has the case of the Maximianists changed as well? By it you are so briefly overcome that, if you ever come to your senses, nothing remains for you but to put an end to your obstinate hostility and make peace.

If the question is about communion, not in other people's sins but in divine sacraments: you have held communion with those you condemned, and of other sacrilegious men who were in communion with the condemned Maximian it was said that "the sacrilegious shoots did not pollute the plantings." If the question is about persecution: you have persecuted those you condemned, and you have corrected hostile people by persecution. If the question is about baptism: you have accepted baptism given in a sacrilegious schism. Why, then, are testimonies from Scripture, not understood, still brought forward in vain, to prevent the truth from being known and error from being shunned? It is written: "If anyone thinks he is contentious, we have no such custom." But you did not regard Restitutus as contentious when he fought it out with Salvius of Membresa in the noise and litigation of the courts over little cells and plots of land, in order to drive him from those places. How much less should a man be thought contentious who argues in good faith, not to seize or take away an inheritance, but to share the heavenly inheritance with those who think otherwise! It is written, you say: "Do not say anything in the ears of a fool, lest he mock your sensible words." Do not speak into our ears as if in secret, then, if you do not think us wise, just as Christ did not speak into the ears of the Pharisees, though he brought forward in their hearing what would refute them. Show us openly, so that if we are not corrected we may at least be convicted, how the Christian world would defile you if you came into unity, when the condemned Felician does not defile you. It is written: "Do not answer a fool according to his folly, lest you become like him." Does it not go on: "But answer him against his folly, lest he seem wise in his own eyes"? Do this yourselves. Do not let your answer go along with what you think is our folly; answer in a way that can refute it. Answer, I say, how you accepted without any undoing the baptism the Maximianists administered in a sacrilegious schism, while you undo the baptism given in the churches that Christ spread through the apostles.

At the end of your letter you thought you should run briefly over everything you had said more fully above, to refresh the reader's memory. Take my reply in the same order, so that you may not deceive yourself or others. First, it is not arrogance to seek or to assert the truth. And what you think could never have been settled has been settled, not only for the wise and those who fear God; you yourselves also brought to an end the whole matter, which you thought endless, when you took back the Maximianists. Second, we call you not to contention but to conference: you who struck the Maximianists even with lawsuits in the courts. In those who were baptized in Maximian's schism, though they should never have been baptized there, you nevertheless recognized the baptism of Christ. By accepting baptism that sacrilegious men had given outside, you declared that the fountain of the Church, which no one approaches unless he is good, must be understood in another way. Third, you are forced to admit that our forefathers, or the holy Church that we hold, could not have been polluted by other people's crimes of offering incense and handing over the Scriptures, even if you had ever proved them, which you never have. For you said that the sacrilegious shoots of Maximian did not pollute the plantings, meaning Maximian's associates, to whom you gave a time-limit for returning. So we, born so long afterwards, can much less belong to that same origin of traditors and incense-offerers, if their crimes could not stain the fellowship of our forefathers who lived at the same time. Fourth, though you are accustomed to reproach us with persecutions, which you say were most savage, against the truth, you yourselves to some extent corrected the Maximianists by persecutions. And though the time-limit had not been granted to those who had already been condemned, you still received them after it expired. The baptism given outside your communion by those to whom you opened the door of return by the time-limit you recognized and approved, and did not annul, even after that time-limit had passed. You see, then, that you have been able to say nothing that this one case of the Maximianists does not refute and overturn. Forgive me if perhaps I have offended you by some harsher word that escaped me. And if you, an African in Africa, have only so late, prompted by my letter, looked into the great case of the Maximianists, which arose in the capital of Africa, and even after looking into it have been unable to find out about it because your people told you false stories, as you now see, then fear God, all of you. Do not smear so many Christian nations, spread so widely across the world in Christian unity, with the crimes of unknown Africans, crimes unknown to them. If for the sake of Donatus' peace you were pleased to recall the condemned, then for the sake of Christ's peace return to the Church, which did not condemn people it did not know.
Augustine, Retractations, Book II, Chapter 52 (26)
(p. 162, line 4, Knöll's edition). To Cresconius, a Grammarian of the Party of Donatus: Four Books.

A Donatist grammarian named Cresconius also came upon my letter in which I had refuted the first parts of Petilian's letter that had then come into our hands. He thought he ought to reply to me, and he wrote this very reply to me. I answered his work in four books, though in fact I finished in three what a complete reply demanded. But I saw that everything he wrote could be answered from the case of the Maximianists alone. The Donatists had condemned these as their own schismatics, yet received some of them back in their former ranks and did not repeat the baptism they had given outside their communion. So I added a fourth book as well, in which I showed this very point as carefully and clearly as I could. When I wrote these four books, the emperor Honorius had already issued laws against the Donatists.
This work begins: "Not knowing, Cresconius, when my writings might reach you."
